## Dedication.

[...cast] aside, so that the bright light of truth cannot be darkened by the darkness of the world. Indeed, even among the common crowd <note>original: *rohen Hauffen*; literally "raw heap," referring to the uneducated or unrefined masses</note>, one daily perceives that various individuals—after having tasted the pleasures of the world and found that no peace is to be met therein—finally turn inward and realize that they have hitherto been driven by nothing other than the senseless lusts of youth to cast off the yoke of Divine discipline. Meanwhile, in the midst of their foolish undertakings, they nevertheless constantly felt the power of God and clearly saw that they could not deny their **Creator**. <meta>catchword: Creator</meta>

The same situation applies to those who devise their own form of worship <note>original: *GOttes-Dienst*</note> and—so that they are not entirely without discipline—invent for themselves a law and guideline. In other respects, however, they cast behind them all true knowledge of God and despise the investigation of eternal truth as mere scholastic bickering <note>original: *Schul-Gezänck*; refers to the pedantic arguments often associated with academic theology</note>. For even these people must tolerate the fact that there are others—to whom they can as little deny a sound mind as they can to themselves—who hold from their hearts to the truth revealed in Holy Scripture and view such self-devised worship as foolish and ill-advised. 

Not to mention that one can easily show such people that their **pretended justice, equity, and honesty** <note>original: *prætendirtes justum, æquum & honestum*</note> goes no further than their own **passions** <note>original: *passiones*</note> wish to see it **extended** <note>original: *extendirt*</note>. <meta>This page begins the "Vorrede" (Preface). Following the formal dedication to Count von Reventlau on the previous pages, the author, Michaël Christian Rusmeyer, shifts to a personal, autobiographical tone to explain his motivations for writing this work on the Trinity.</meta>

# Preface.

## Honored Reader!

It has now been quite a long time since—upon perceiving my own corruption and that of all **Christendom**—the doctrines of faith of our churches began to seem suspicious to me. (For it happens that the unbelief which lurks within us only becomes truly manifest when, in the midst of spiritual trial <term>Anfechtung: a specifically Lutheran concept describing a deep state of spiritual crisis, doubt, or temptation where one's faith feels under attack</term>, one wishes to pay heed to the **Word**; for otherwise, one does not concern oneself much with it.) Among these doctrines, the article of the **Holy Trinity** caused me all manner of doubt, although I hardly knew why myself.

In particular, however, my thoughts tended toward **Arianism** <note>Arianism: an early Christian belief—deemed heretical by the mainstream church—that Jesus Christ was a created being and subordinate to God the Father, rather than being of the same substance or co-eternal.</note>; for **Socinianism** <note>Socinianism: a rationalist theological system that denied the pre-existence of Christ and His divinity, viewing Him instead as a human prophet who was later granted divine status.</note> caused me no difficulty, because I recognized all too clearly that **Christ** had existed before His birth from Mary. Now, I did indeed strongly support myself with the name of the Son—

<summary>In this opening of the preface, Rusmeyer confesses to a period of intense spiritual doubt where he questioned the central doctrines of the Church. He describes how his personal crisis led him to struggle specifically with the doctrine of the Trinity and a temporary intellectual attraction to Arianism.</summary>
<keywords>preface, spiritual doubt, Trinity, Arianism, Socinianism, Christology, Anfechtung, 18th-century theology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface" (Vorrede). On the previous page, the author began describing his internal struggle with the doctrine of the Trinity, specifically how his mind drifted toward Arianism and how he wrestled with the relationship between the Father and the Son.</meta>

# Preface.

and I judged that a son must indeed be equal in essence <term>Wesen: the fundamental nature or substance of a thing; in this context, the "ousia" or divine substance shared by the Trinity</term> to his father; nevertheless, I could not well conceive how it should come about that the Son should be co-eternal with the Father, because in my ignorance I wanted to compare the divine essence absolutely with created beings. But in a short time, I noticed that every birth has its own manner and time, and that therefore the divine birth <note>original: "göttliche Gebuhrt"; in theological terms, this refers to the "eternal generation" of the Son by the Father, a process occurring outside of time</note> must also have its own manner and must occur without time in pure eternity.

Since my doubt was now removed, I immediately wished for an opportunity to communicate this to others, in the hope that it might yet serve one person or another. However, it had to remain as mere thoughts, partly because I did not find myself capable of writing, and partly because I first had to learn whether these thoughts on the divine birth were not as old to other people as they were new to me; for I afterwards discovered that people generally—if not in every specific detail, then at least as a whole—argued in that manner.

But when I had the opportunity in a large city to learn the differing opinions of people in *matters of religion* during *conversation* <note>original: "Conversation"; here referring to the social and intellectual discourse among the educated classes</note>, and often noticed with dismay that they were *Socinian* <note>Socinianism: a rationalist school of thought that rejected the Trinity and the divinity of Christ, viewing Him instead as a remarkable but human prophet</note> in their thinking, I felt a longing to fully investigate the matter and to demonstrate the truth thoroughly. In this, I was to some

# Preface

...strengthened in such a way, when I—through a conversation brought about by <term>Divine Providence<note>The author attributes this chance encounter to God's guidance rather than mere luck.</note></term> (as I cannot judge otherwise from the circumstances)—once again encountered <term>Socinian principles<note>original: "Socinianische Principia." Socinianism was a rationalist Christian movement that emerged in the 16th century; its followers rejected the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ.</note></term> in someone where I would not have suspected them. However, I had to travel in great haste and thus had no opportunity to think further about it; I even set aside all such thoughts to avoid any further complication.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nevertheless, it so happened that soon after, I had some completely idle time which I could use at my own disposal. I then resolved to set aside some spare hours from my regular studies and to turn them toward a draft of my thoughts on the <term>Holy Trinity<note>original: "H. Dreyeinigkeit."</note></term> and the <term>Divinity of Christ<note>original: "Gottheit Christi."</note></term>; yet, I was not yet willing to carry it out fully. But it eventually came to a full resolution to properly take up the subject and, according to God's will, to bring it to light through printing.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To be sure, among other reasons, the weightiness of the subject matter might have reasonably deterred me from the work, especially since I had to consider that it ought to be handled with "holy hands" <note>A common expression of the time suggesting that sacred topics should only be approached with spiritual purity and great reverence.</note>. But when I looked upon the clear truth in the Scriptures and considered the unanimous testimony of the faithful, I became joyful and did not let myself be deterred from carrying out the matter to the best of my ability, with heartfelt <term>humility<note>original: "Demühtigung."</note></term> before God and a plea for the enlightenment of His Spirit.

# Preface

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I do not doubt that those who <term>worship God in spirit and in truth<note>A reference to John 4:24, emphasizing sincere, internal faith over mere outward ritual.</note></term> will approve of this undertaking, and all the more so because the path to a great <term>atheistic anti-Christianity<note>original: "Atheistischen Anti-Christenthum." In this period, "atheism" was often used broadly to describe any belief—such as Socinianism—that the author felt undermined the traditional doctrine of God.</note></term> is being paved more and more through the neglect of investigating the truth.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Initially, it took much effort for me to resolve to add my own few thoughts on this matter to the learned testimonies that have come to light until now. But when I reflected that <term>Satan<note>original: "Satanas."</note></term>, despite such powerful testimonies, nevertheless does not cease to spread his weeds further and further, and is especially busy doing so now in <term>Germany<note>original: "Deutschland."</note></term>, I felt I had reason to bear witness to the truth according to my ability, even if it could not equal the others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Satan is an impudent guest; even when his lies have long since been thrown back at him, he always brings them forward anew and sings his old songs. If one now becomes weary, allowing oneself to be cornered and exhausted by his impudence, then he finally gets his way and cries out, <term>"The Philistines are upon you!"<note>original: "das Philister über dir." A biblical allusion to Judges 16, where Delilah calls out to the weakened Samson before his capture. It suggests that if believers grow tired of defending their faith, they will be easily overcome by their enemies.</note></term> Thus, it is only right that one pushes his filth back at him as much as possible and does not—through total silence—leave the tempted and partly hardened <term>souls<note>original: "Seelen."</note></term> in the delusion that all has already been lost.

<meta>catchword: Man (One)</meta>

### Preface

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;However, this treatise should not be seen as a <term>polemic<note>original: "Streitschrifft." A text written specifically to attack or challenge an opposing viewpoint, often in a harsh or confrontational manner.</note></term>; for it is not the intention here to confront those who have already actually separated themselves from the confessors of the <term>Holy Trinity<note>original: "H. Drey-Einigkeit." The Christian doctrine that God is one being in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note></term>, but rather to strengthen the weak, the doubting, and those who are already wavering. Nevertheless, it could not be otherwise than that—given the aroused and highly driven conflict—one must, even against one's will, touch upon and answer the points of contention. Therefore, this modest writing must also, as if by chance, be a public testimony against all enemies of the Holy Trinity.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If there is anyone who, without a quarrelsome spirit and in a pure investigation of the truth, wishes to read through this work and still finds offense in it, or thinks that some <term>doubt<note>original: "Zweiffel."</note></term> remains in matters that have not been addressed, he can, after careful investigation, communicate his <term>doubts<note>original: "dubia." Latin for uncertain things or questions.</note></term> through letters and be assured of all loyalty and confidentiality; for he shall be answered as far as possible. For spiritual matters wish to be investigated spiritually and freely, but also humbly and purely; however, where one has been <term>tempted<note>original: "versuchet." In this context, it refers to experiencing spiritual trials or intellectual doubts oneself.</note></term> oneself, there one also knows how to have compassion for others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Should something be found that not everyone can grasp because the matters are unknown to them, then one can stick to that which is easier to understand and which is also the most important. But to him who is familiar with these things, he will find pleasure even in that which might otherwise seem somewhat <term>obscure<note>original: "obscur." From Latin "obscurus," meaning dark, hidden, or difficult to understand.</note></term> to an unlearned person and which, to my knowledge, has not yet been touched upon by anyone. The people who are inclined toward <term>Socinianism<note>original: "Socinianismo." A rationalist Christian movement that emerged in the 16th century, which notably rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and the divinity of Christ.</note></term> are generally sharp and critical minds; one must indeed meet these mostly with the simplicity of the Scriptures, but it also does no harm if one gives their sharp reason something to do in the process.

### Preface.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Regarding the Jewish testimonies / these are for the most part taken from the famous French theologian among the English / **Pierre Allix’s <note>original: "Petri Allix." Pierre Allix (1641–1717) was a prominent French Protestant divine who lived in England.</note> *Judgment of the Ancient Jewish Church Against the Unitarians <note>A religious group that rejects the doctrine of the Trinity, believing God is only one person.</note> in the Controversy Regarding the Holy Trinity*** etc. / specifically from the translation / which, with a preface by Mr. Gottfried Arnold, has made this treasure known in Germany. The cited page numbers are to be understood as those found in the English edition / and placed in the margins of the translation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In investigating the <term>Socinian<note>A non-trinitarian movement following the teachings of Lelio and Fausto Sozzini, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note></term> propositions and objections, I have made use of the work of <term>S. D. Spener<note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), a highly influential German theologian and the "Father of Pietism."</note></term> in the defense of the testimony of the eternal deity of **JESUS Christ** etc. / whom I have hesitated so much the less to trust / as his integrity is so well known : just as he has also, to my knowledge, not yet been accused of any <term>falsehood<note>original: "falsi." In this context, it refers to the intentional misrepresentation of an opponent's writings.</note></term> in the passages cited from Socinian writings. The kind reader will find a few other authors always faithfully cited / and will therefore always know how to distinguish my own work from that of others.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I could indeed have made an index / as such a thing is usually of no small benefit; however, everything is so arranged / that those / who read it through / can create a <term>memory of location<note>original: "memoriam localem." A traditional study method where a reader remembers information by visualizing its specific place on the page.</note></term> for themselves without effort. But whoever will take the time to read it through / will find in it one or another important matter / which / if not more / will at least give cause for riper and better thoughts.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, I wish the honored reader the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit from the Father / for the revelation of his Son. But to God / from whom / and through whom / and in whom are all things / be honor and praise for eternity! Amen.

Stockholm, June 29,
1714.

## A Sufficient
# Account
### Of the
## Dispute Raised Concerning the Article of the Holy Trinity,
### From the Beginning of the New Testament Until the
### Present Day.

->§. I.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a miniature landscape scene with a tower and trees.</image-desc>
Just as I am in the process of committing my humble work on the mystery of the most holy Trinity to the press, I am reminded by a sensible and learned man, my highly esteemed friend, to preface <note>original: "*præmittiren*"</note> it with the history of the dispute raised over this matter. Since it is easy to understand that there are many who not only lack a sufficient account of this matter (which they nevertheless wish to have), but also that the truth itself becomes much more distinct and understandable through a rational and pure investigation of the dispute and its opposition: I find not only reason not to contradict my friend's opinion, but must also acknowledge his reminder with all thanks.

->§. II.<-

In this regard, however, I must necessarily remind the reader in advance that I do not intend to touch upon all those disputes which have otherwise been raised on various occasions concerning the God of peace, and concerning his child Jesus Christ, who has himself made peace through the blood of his cross. For it would be a labor unsuited to our purpose if we wished to investigate the names of the **Valentinians**, **Anthropomorphites**, **Melchizedekians**, **Patripassians**, **Nestorians**, **Eutychians**, <note>These groups represent various early Christian sects deemed heretical: the Valentinians were Gnostics; Anthropomorphites attributed human form to God; Melchizedekians held unorthodox views on the biblical figure Melchizedek; Patripassians believed God the Father suffered on the cross; and the Nestorians and Eutychians held conflicting views on the union of Christ's divine and human natures.</note> and the many different **sects** of the latter two. Those, however, who actually concern us here, are the ones

### Report of the Raised Dispute

who have primarily attacked the mystery of the Trinity and the true divinity of the Son. And it is these people whose history, teaching, and various names I now wish to present to the gracious reader, according to the truth as far as it can be known from written reports.

->§. III.<-

We intend, however, to go through all the centuries <note>original: "Secula"</note> from Christ's birth onwards; and even if we encounter nothing on this matter in some of them, I still wish to pass through such empty centuries by indicating as much, so that we may be more thoroughly informed of the entire situation. This is why we immediately look into the first, apostolic century and ask: was there also at that time a dispute over the question of the Trinity and the true divinity of the Son?

->§. IV.<-

When we look at the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists, we find that the dispute began with the person of our **Lord** and Savior **JESUS**, namely whether he was the **Christ** and **Son** of the Father. This is found so clearly in the first Epistle of John that one finds it there in those very words; see chapter 2:22, 4:2–3, 5:5 <note>original: "vid. Cap. II. 22. IV. 2. 3. V. 5."</note>. At that time, many "Antichrists" emerged who denied that **JESUS** was the same **Christ** and **Son of GOD**; against whom the Apostle fights with great zeal, excluding them from **GOD** and eternal life. However, since he proves in the cited place of chapter 5 <note>original: "l. c. V."</note>, by citing the three witnesses in heaven, that **JESUS** is the Son of **GOD**, he presupposes <note>original: "præſupponirt"</note> the Trinity as a doctrine then known among the Jews. From this it is clear that at that time the dispute was not so much whether there was a Trinity in **GOD**, but rather whether **JESUS** was the one with whom—according to the hope of the Israelite Church—the *Shekhinah* <note>the "Divine Presence" or dwelling of God</note> or the second *Sefirah* <note>in Jewish mysticism, an emanation of divine light</note>, *Chokhmah* (Wisdom), had united?

->§. V.<-

If we now look at the history of that same time outside of Holy Scripture, specifically as it was recorded by **Irenaeus**, the student of Saint **Polycarp**, we find among the anti-Christian people that **Cerinthus** <note>an early Gnostic leader who lived at the end of the 1st century</note>, above all others, is noted for considering our **Lord JESUS** to be a mere man. However, this must not be understood as if he held the same opinion as the **Socinians** <note>a later 16th-century group who also denied Christ's divinity but from a different philosophical perspective</note>; rather, he divided **JESUS** and **Christ**, saying that **Christ** was from above, someone who could not suffer, and had descended upon **JESUS**, but then flew back up into his fullness, etc. From this it is clearly evident that he originally attacked not so much the doctrine of the Trinity as the person of **JESUS**. But since an error rarely stays alone, it is not surprising that he and his companions, when investigating the union of the other *Sefirah* or divine Wisdom with the children of men, brought his own wares to market <note>a German idiom meaning to promote one's own ideas</note> and spoke in the following way: One is the Maker, another the Father of the **Lord**

### §. VI.

This historical note gives us not only the key to the writings of St. John / but is also perfectly confirmed by those same writings. For regarding the person of *Christ* / the Apostle shows / that Jesus is the Christ and Son of GOD / and that one must make no distinction between the two: In view of the union of divine and human nature in the God-Man, he shows / that the Word in the Godhead / which was from the beginning and is God Himself / became flesh. Generally, however, he declares himself regarding the heavenly persons / when he says: There are three that bear witness in heaven / the Father / the Word and the Spirit / and these three are one. <note>This refers to the "Johannine Comma," a famous verse in 1 John 5:7 traditionally used to defend the Trinity.</note> From this we see / that by explaining the true nature of the Triune GOD / and the mystery of the manifestation of GOD in the flesh / he puts to shame the self-invented chatter of the deceivers. And this is what we find from the historical record / regarding the dispute over GOD and his child Jesus / in the first century.

### §. VII.

In the second *century* <note>original: "Seculo"</note> it was of almost the same nature / as we *observed* <note>original: "observirt"</note> in the first. We will not dwell at all on the recounting of the strange thoughts / which the *Valentinians* <note>A Gnostic sect named after Valentinus who believed in a complex hierarchy of divine beings.</note> and others held regarding the Godhead; but rather recount only for completeness / that once again some were found among the notorious heretics / who did not consider Christ to be the true GOD. Thus it is told of *Carpocrates* <note>A second-century Gnostic leader in Alexandria.</note> / from the writings of *Irenaeus*, *Tertullian* and others / that he and his followers taught: Jesus was begotten of Joseph / and differed from others only in that his soul was firm and pure / and therefore remembered what it had seen in its circulation near the unbegotten GOD.

### §. VIII.

However, in this *century* <note>original: "Seculo"</note> the well-known *Justin Martyr* was famous / whom today's *Unitarians* <note>original: "Unitarii"</note> blame / as being the one / who first really set the doctrine of the Trinity in motion. Yet it has been proven by others / that the mystery of the Trinity in itself is an eternal truth / which is unfairly counted among the new inventions of individual persons. Whoever takes the trouble / to read through this book / will be convinced of this without difficulty. But as for the explanation of the faith of the Trinity / which is attributed to him / some think / it is obvious / that it does not belong to him.

# Report on the Stirred-up Dispute

who have mainly attacked the mystery of the **Trinity** and the true **Deity of the Son**. And these are those whose history, doctrine, and various names I will now set before the eyes of the kind reader, according to the truth, as far as it may be recognized from the written records.

->§. III.<-

We wish, however, to go through all the **centuries** <note>original: "Secula"</note> from the birth of Christ onwards; and even if we encounter nothing on this subject in some of them, I will nevertheless—precisely by indicating that fact—pass through such empty centuries, so that we may be much more thoroughly informed of the entire nature of the situation. This is why we immediately look around in the first, **Apostolic**, century and ask: was there also at that time a dispute over the question of the **Trinity** and the **true Deity of the Son**?

->§. IV.<-

If we look at the writings of the Apostles and Evangelists, we find that the dispute took its beginning with the person of our **Lord and Savior Jesus**, namely: whether he was the Christ and the Son of the Father? This lies so clearly in the first Epistle of John that one finds it therein in those very words; **see Chapter II:22, IV:2, 3, V:7**. At that time, many **Antichrists** <note>original: "Wiederchristen," literally "Against-Christians"</note> were found who denied that Jesus was the same Christ and Son of God; against whom the Apostle fights with great zeal and excludes them from God and eternal life. However, while he proves in the cited place <note>original: "l. c." / "loco citato"</note> in Chapter V, by citing the three witnesses in heaven, that Jesus is the Son of God, he **presupposes** <note>original: "præsupponirt"</note> the Trinity as a doctrine already known among the Jews at that time. ->§. V.<-

If we now look at the history of that same time outside of the Holy Scriptures, specifically as it was recorded by **Irenaeus**, the student of Saint **Polycarp**, we find **Cerinthus** <note>An early Gnostic leader who was a contemporary of the Apostle John</note> noted above others among the anti-Christian people for holding our Lord Jesus to be a mere man. However, one must not understand this as if he held the same opinion as the **Socinians** <note>A later 16th-century sect that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ</note>; rather, he divided **Jesus** and **Christ**, saying that Christ was from above, who could not suffer, and had descended upon Jesus, but had flown up again into his **fullness** <note>original: "fülle," likely referring to the Gnostic "Pleroma" or divine realm</note>, etc. From this it clearly appears that he originally attacked not so much the doctrine of the Trinity as the person of Jesus. But since an error seldom remains alone, it is also not surprising that he, together with his companions, brought his own wares to market <note>A metaphor for spreading one's own ideas or "baggage"</note> when investigating the union of the other **Sephira**, or divine Wisdom, with the children of men, and spoke in the following way: **One is the Maker, another is the Father of the Lord.** <note>Cerinthus argued that the world was created by a lower power (the Maker/Demiurge) rather than the supreme Father of Christ.</note>

### §. VI.

This Historical Note gives us not only the key to the writings of *St. John* / but is also through those very same writings perfectly confirmed. For as concerns the person of Christ / the Apostle shows / that *Jesus* is the Christ and Son of *God* / and that one is to make no distinction between the two: In view of the union of divine and human nature in the *God*-Man he shows / that the Word in the Divinity / which was from the beginning and is *God* himself / has become flesh. ### §. VII.

In the second *Century* <note>original: "Seculo"</note> it had almost the same nature / that we *observed* <note>original: "observirt"</note> in the first. We do not linger / however / at all with the recounting of the strange thoughts / which the *Valentinians* <note>Followers of Valentinus, a mid-2nd century Gnostic teacher</note> and others have held concerning the Divinity; but recount only as an addition / that again some were found among the notorious heretics / who did not hold Christ to be the true *God*. ### §. VIII.

But there was famous in this *Century* the well-known *Justin Martyr*, whom the modern *Unitarians* <note>original: "Unitarii," those who reject the Trinity in favor of the uni-personality of God</note> blame / that he be the one / who first really brought the doctrine of the *Trinity* into use. Yet it has been proven by others / that the Mystery of the *Trinity* in itself is an eternal *Truth* / which is unjustly counted among the new inventions of individual persons. Whoever takes the trouble to read through this book / will be convinced of it without difficulty. But as concerns the explanation of the faith of the *Trinity* / which is attributed to him / some mean / it is manifest / that it does not belong to him.

# Report on the Stirred Dispute

->§. IX.<-

Around the middle of the third <term>century</term> <note>original: "Seculi"</note>, the <term>Noetians</term> <note>Followers of Noetus of Smyrna, who taught that God the Father and Christ were the same person</note> became known, who received their name from a certain **Noetus** of Asia. It is thought that even before him, **Hermogenes** and **Praxeas** taught the same thing. The doctrine itself, however, consisted of this: there is only one single, independent divine essence <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis), here referring to a single underlying substance or person</note> which has only three names: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This [essence] gave the Law in the Old Testament as the Father; in the New Testament, it became man in the person of the Son; and as the Holy Spirit, it came upon the Apostles. These are the ones otherwise known as <term>Patripassians</term> <note>From the Latin for "Father-suffering," because their view implied that God the Father himself suffered on the cross</note>; but it is not our purpose to deal further with them here.

->§. X.<-

It comes closer to our purpose to briefly recount that the notorious **Sabellius**, a native of **Cyrene** in **Libya**, is said to have learned or borrowed this opinion from **Noetus**. Indeed, there is no difference between what is attributed to **Noetus** and that which **Sabellius** taught, perhaps with greater skill. However, the <term>Sabellians</term>, more than others, may have allowed themselves to be led astray by their corrupted reason in that they—against their own knowledge and thought—violated the prohibition where God says that one should make no image of Him. For, because they always envisioned the divine being under the image of a <term>Monarch</term> or a single supreme ruler, they were labeled with the name of <term>Monarchians</term> <note>original: "Monarchicorum," a group emphasizing the "monarchy" or sole-rule of God the Father</note>. Furthermore, some wish to observe regarding this time of <term>Sabellian</term> error that it was precisely then that the opportunity was given to introduce new <term>technical terms</term> <note>original: "terminos"</note>, and they specifically point to the word **hypostasis** <note>original: "ὑπόστασις"</note>; the extent to which this word has a proven foundation may be investigated, among other things, from this small work.

->§. XI.<-

What we have just said about the <term>Sabellians</term>—that they envisioned God under a human image beyond what is proper—we can confirm with even more right regarding the Bishop of Antioch, **Paul of Samosata**, who made himself known toward the end of this <term>century</term> <note>original: "Seculi"</note>. For, as one finds in the writings of **Athanasius** and others, he taught: God is a single person, in whom the Word and the Holy Spirit always reside, just as the word resides in a man's heart. Christ is not the essential Son of God, but rather he is *in* God. The Word, however, dwelt in the man Jesus as the only God. Jesus, meanwhile, was called a Son of God because of his divine works, and was called "the Word" because he was sent from God to men. From this, one sees all too clearly that he felt the testimony of Scripture regarding the Word and Spirit quite strongly, but—following the forbidden depiction of the Divine Being—he simply compared it to the image of a human being. Otherwise, so much is told of his boasting and haughty nature that even those who, for significant reasons, often doubt the accounts given about heretics, do not in any way [excuse him]...

### §. XII.

We come now to the fourth <term>century</term> <note>original: "Seculo"</note>, which is most pitiable, both for other disputes and especially for the cruel bickering over the divinity of **Jesus Christ**. The occasion for this was given by **Alexander**, Bishop of **Alexandria**, who, in a convention, wishing to display his intellect and wisdom, disputed somewhat subtly concerning the unity and Trinity of the unfathomable **God**. Because of this, he fell under suspicion of <term>Sabellianism</term> <note>The belief, previously mentioned in §. X, that Father, Son, and Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three modes of one God</note> by one of his elders, **Arius**. Since the Bishop said in his speech, among other things, that the Son was of equal honor and of the same essence with the Father; this **Arius** could grasp it so little that he instead concluded: If the Father begat the Son, then the Son must necessarily have a beginning of his essence; and consequently, there must once have been a time when the Son was not, so that he derives his self-subsistence from that which did not exist.

### §. XIII.

That **Arius** is said to have contradicted **Alexander** out of envy—because the latter had been preferred over him for the bishopric—I do not wish to defend. For even **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century church father known for his "Panarion," a catalog of heresies</note> testifies that in the beginning, he was held dear and worthy by his Bishop; and this lends credibility to the otherwise suspicious **Philostorgius** <note>An Arian church historian whose works only survive in fragments</note>, who relates that **Arius** had willingly deferred to **Alexander**. However, that he did not thoroughly investigate the mystery of the birth of the Son of God from the Father is easily judged from his unfounded conclusion. For it is manifest even in nature that a father can never exist even a moment earlier than a son; since "father" and "son" inevitably relate to one another, and all fatherhood ceases to be as such until a son appears at that very moment. But that a father must nevertheless exist earlier as a complete human being—if not yet functioning as a father—is due to his own beginning, which is finite, for which time and growth are required. How little one can conclude from the <term>pre-existence</term> of one human before another regarding the nature of the divine birth is tangibly recognized from this: because in **God** no beginning or growth is found, consequently that <term>irrational</term> <note>original: "irraisonnable"</note> deduction <term>ceases</term> <note>original: "cessiret"</note>. To say nothing of the fact that it is entirely against Scripture, which does not want one to take an image of **God** from anywhere. However, this belongs to the detailed exposition itself; we shall proceed further with the history.

# Account of the Stirred-Up Dispute

### §. IX.

Around the middle of the third <term>century</term> <note>original: "Seculi"</note>, the **Noëtians** became known, who received their name from a certain **Noëtus** of Asia. It is thought that even before him, **Hermogenes** and **Praxeas** taught the same things. The doctrine itself consisted of this: **That there is only one single, subsistent divine essence** <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis)</note> **which has only three names: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.** This essence supposedly gave the Law in the Old Testament as the Father, became human in the person of the Son in the New Testament, and came upon the Apostles as the Holy Spirit. These are those otherwise known as <term>Patripassians</term> <note>From the Latin words for "Father" and "suffering"; a group believing that God the Father himself suffered on the cross since they saw no distinction between the persons of the Trinity</note>; however, it is not our purpose to deal further with them here.

### §. X.

It is more relevant to our purpose to briefly recount that the notorious **Sabellius**, a native of Cyrene in Libya, is said to have learned or borrowed this opinion from **Noëtus**. For in truth, there is no difference between what is attributed to **Noëtus** and that which **Sabellius** taught, perhaps with greater skill. The **Sabellians**, however, more than others, may have allowed themselves to be led astray by their own corrupted reason, in that—contrary to their own knowledge and intention—they violated the prohibition where God says one should make no image of Him. Because they always envisioned the divine being under the image of a <term>monarch</term> <note>a single, absolute ruler</note> or a sole supreme sovereign, they were labeled with the name of **Monarchians** <note>original: "Monarchicorum"</note>. Furthermore, some observing this period of Sabellian error note that it provided the occasion to introduce new <term>technical terms</term> <note>original: "terminos"</note>, and they specifically point to the word **hypostasis** <note>original: "ὑπόστασις"</note>; the extent to which this word has a proven foundation may be investigated, among other things, in this little work.

### §. XI.

What we have just said of the **Sabellians**—that they envisioned God under a human image beyond what is proper—we can confirm with even more justice regarding the Bishop of Antioch, **Paul of Samosata**, who distinguished himself toward the end of this century. For, as found in the writings of **Athanasius** and others, he taught: that God is one single person in whom the Word and the Holy Spirit always reside, just as the word resides in a man’s heart. He claimed Christ was not the "essential" or "substantial" Son of God, but rather that he existed within God. He argued the Word dwelt in the man **Jesus** as the eternal God, but **Jesus** was called a "Son of God" only because of his divine works, and called "the Word" because he was sent from God to humanity. From this, one sees all too clearly that he felt the weight of the Scriptural testimony regarding the Word and Spirit, but—following the forbidden practice of imaging the Divine Being—he simply compared it to the image of a human being. Otherwise, so much is told of his boastfulness and haughty character that even those who, for significant reasons, often doubt the accounts given of heretics, by no means [can]

I do not wish to defend the claim that **Arius** contradicted **Alexander** out of envy because Alexander had been preferred over him for the bishopric. To say nothing of the fact that it is generally against the Scripture, which does not want one to take an image of God from anywhere else. # Report on the Stirred-Up Conflict

### §. XIV.

In the meantime, we cannot deny that Arius sinned not so much out of malice as out of ignorance; and that he perhaps would have gladly allowed himself to be convinced of a better way if only his conscience could have been satisfied and he had not been oppressed with unchristian persecution. However, it was by then an obvious judgment upon the Christian Church that such major schisms had to come; for the clergy had now, for the most part—if not for the greatest part—surrendered themselves to the spirit of the world. They consumed divine knowledge with the pleasure of their own pride, engaged in disputes over precedence <term>Præcedenz-Streit; arguments over who held higher rank or status</term>, and allowed the bond of faith to bind them so little that they even had to be exhorted to it by the Emperor Constantine himself. Not to mention that their great ignorance can be inferred from many circumstances: particularly the story that at the Council of Nicaea <note>Held in 325 AD, this was the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church</note>, a certain philosopher could not be refuted by a single person; until finally a layman—whom some believe to be the confessor Spiridion <note>Saint Spiridion (c. 270–348), a shepherd turned bishop known for his simple but profound faith</note>—took pity and cornered him in argument. Given these circumstances, one can easily imagine that Arius likely received no full satisfaction in such an important matter.

### §. XV.

Just as they were unable to satisfy Arius, it also could not be prevented that not only various elders and deacons in Alexandria but also many great bishops from abroad joined his side. Therefore, Alexander thought the best way to remedy the evil was to have the Arian party publicly declared guilty and condemned through a great Council and under the power of the Emperor. This was made easier because Bishop Hosius of Cordoba <note>A prominent advisor to Constantine</note> was sent by Constantine to Alexandria with letters to both parties and was incited against Arius. For Hosius—though he himself later faltered and leaned toward the Arian side—knew how to sway the Emperor upon his return. Thus, while the Emperor had previously considered the whole affair a mere dispute over words, he now arranged a Council with all diligence and had the assembled multitude of bishops magnificently entertained.

### §. XVI.

At this great and highly famous Council, Athanasius had to do the best work in the discussion with the Arians (who, for reasons I know not, offered little defense). He served as the spokesman in place of the old bishops, even though he was only a deacon and, by his studies, a legal scholar <note>original Latin: "Juris-Consultus"</note>. Consequently, he later became the foundation pillar of this Council, and a Creed <note>original Latin: "Symbolum"</note> against the Arians was drawn from his writings on this matter; to this day, it is called the Athanasian Creed and is held in great value, though it must not be confused with the Nicene Creed. Yet, as highly as he was regarded and as great a following as he had, he was nevertheless subjected to many persecutions and was even forced into exile by Constantine the Great himself—not to mention other persecutions. One also finds very harsh accusations against him, which are recorded by the writers <note>original German: "Scribenten"</note>...

->§. XVII.<-

One sees, however, from the generally cited fate <note>original: "Fatis"; the circumstances or history of his life</note> of this famous man / that the intended purpose of this Council <note>original: "Concilii"; referring to the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD</note> was by no means achieved. For depending on whether the Emperors were of an *Arian* or *Orthodox* mind / either these or those had to suffer.

->§. XVIII.<-

And / as it is wont to happen / that no one in error wishes to recognize himself as being in error / but rather accuses his opponent of the error ; so too the *Arians* were not slow / to label the *Orthodox* with such names / which were intended to be the sign of the alleged error. Accordingly, the *Orthodox* were not only scolded as *Sabellians*, *Samosatenians*, and *Photinians* <note>These were terms for different "heresies" that either denied the distinction between the persons of the Trinity (Sabellians) or the divinity of Christ (Samosatenians/Photinians)</note> ; but they also had to let themselves be called *Homoousiasts* from their so-called *shibboleth* <note>A Hebrew term for a password or custom that distinguishes one group of people from another</note>, the word <term>homoousios; "of one substance" or "consubstantial," the key term used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son</term>. For the Nicene Fathers / regardless of the anathema <note>original: "Anathematis"; a formal curse or excommunication</note> that had been placed upon those / who would use other words / than those found in the Scripture / had found it necessary / to take this word in order to show / that the Son is of the same essence as the Father. Because the *Arians* now saw / that this was, as it were, contrary to the agreement <note>original: "Accord"</note> that had been made / they knew how to cause their adversaries vexation with it. Although it cannot be denied / that / if the *Orthodox* might have overstepped a little with their critiquing / (as they are even accused by our own modern theologians ;) on the other hand, the *Arians*, with far too vehement hostility toward a word made for the clear explanation of the matter / betrayed their own obstinacy. For to devise new things and doctrines in religion / is rightly called acting against the pattern of healthy doctrine; but to declare a word that corresponds to the matter itself as a heresy out of a perceived necessity / is a sign of poor understanding / and a deep deviation from the aforementioned pattern. Even granted / that *Paul of Samosata* and other heretics just

# Report on the Conflict Aroused

### §. XIX.

After the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius who believed Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father</note> were thus separated from the *Orthodox* / they then also had their particular principles and customs; of which we only need to touch upon those that pertain to the matter at hand. They confessed / that God was neither one essence nor one subsistence <note>original: "ουσία" (ousia) and "υπόστασις" (hypostasis); Greek philosophical terms used to define the nature of the Trinity</note>; [they claimed] Christ was indeed made from nothing by God / but in such a way / that through Him all things were created; He was a Creator of all things / the Word of the Father / who must also be worshipped and honored as God / just as all power and the highest name have been given to Him. Furthermore / some of them say / they also denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit and said / He was made by the Son. Others, conversely, conclude from this / that *Arius* had thought nothing of it / because nothing was decreed against it at the *Council of Nicaea* <note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD which established the Nicene Creed</note>. Be that as it may / it is nonetheless certain / that those who do not hold the correct opinion regarding the Son cannot judge rightly regarding the Holy Spirit.

### §. XX.

Those who remained with the doctrine just mentioned / actually kept the name of *Arians*: And because they would not grant at all / that the Son was of the same essence as the Father / they were for that reason called *Anomoeans* <note>original: "Anomoei"; from the Greek for "unlike," referring to the belief that the Son's essence was unlike the Father's</note>. They also received other names / partly from their most prominent teachers / hence they were called *Aetians* <note>After Aëtius of Antioch</note> and *Eunomians* <note>After Eunomius of Cyzicus</note> / and partly from the doctrine itself / for which they were called *Exucontians* <note>original: "Exucontii"; from the Greek phrase "ex ouk ontōn," meaning "from what did not exist"</note> / because they taught / the Son was created and begotten by the Father "from non-existence" <note>original: "εξ ουκ όντων"</note> / out of that which had not been. Distinct from these "coarse" *Arians*, however, were the *Semi-Arians* / who did not so simply contradict the truth / but still did not want to agree fully with the so-called *Homoousians* <note>original: "Homousiasten"; those who believed the Son is of the same substance as the Father</note> / instead of the word *Homoousios* <note>original: "ομοούσιος"; "of the same essence"</note> / they devised another word that sounds almost the same / *Homoiousios* <note>original: "ομοιούσιος"; "of a similar essence"</note> / which signifies a similarity of essence / but for that very reason they were condemned by the others at the *Synod of Sirmium* <note>A series of church councils held between 347 and 359 AD</note>. Finally / there was the party of the *Acacians* / named after the Bishop of Caesarea, *Acacius* / who simply confessed / Christ was like the Father / without adding / whether He was like Him in essence or in all things. And that was the lamentable state of affairs on that side.

### §. XXI.

But this was not yet enough / rather / when *Marcellus*, Bishop of Ancyra in Lesser Galatia / fell into a dispute with the *Arian*, *Asterius* / and through carelessness lapsed into the error of *Paul of Samosata* <note>A 3rd-century bishop whose teachings were considered a precursor to various heresies regarding the nature of Christ</note> / it gave rise to the *Photinian* disputes <note>original: "Photinianischen Händeln"; referring to Photinus, a student of Marcellus whose teachings on Christ were later condemned</note>.

For although Marcellus soon found his footing and complained that his words were being misinterpreted—and since he otherwise had a good testimony regarding his teaching and life, he was eventually reinstated to his bishopric—his disciple and successor, **Photinus**, would not yield so easily. Instead, he sought to defend his propositions with all earnestness. It may be that he allowed his good and perhaps fiery intellect to lead him astray, as he felt confident in arguing his case against his opponents. For he is praised as having been a very learned, sensible, and eloquent man who conversed very well in both the Greek and Latin languages, and thereby drew many to himself. Thus, at the Synod held on his account at Sirmium in the year 359 AD—where he was declared a *Sabellian* and a *Samosatenian* <note>Followers of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata, who were accused of denying the distinct personalities of the Trinity or the divinity of Christ</note> and was deposed from his bishopric—he rejected everything else that was attempted by way of a kind agreement and demanded that the matter be decided through a formal debate. Perhaps his honorable office also made him somewhat bold, for he was the Bishop of Sirmium in Hungary, and he did not wish to yield to the other bishops simply based on authority <note>original: "pro auctoritate"</note>.

->§. XXII.<-

However, writers differ in uncovering his actual opinion. Most agree that he taught: **GOD** is one, and not three persons, but only three names: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Christ was a mere man and had his beginning with his birth from Mary. Also, the Holy Spirit was not actually a distinct person. Others, however, express his opinion in the following way: The Son (by which he understood the humanity, or the man Jesus Christ) was one thing, and the Word was another. The latter [the Word] had indeed been from the beginning, according to the words of John, but not the former [the Son]. The Word and the Spirit had always been in **GOD**, but the man Jesus was always outside of the Trinitarian essence. Now, whichever way we take this, we see that within it lie the *Sabellian*, *Samosatenian*, and even the *Cerinthian* errors <note>Cerinthus was an early Gnostic who distinguished between the human Jesus and the divine Christ</note>. According to the first account, the *Sabellian* opinion is more obvious; but according to the second, the imagination of Paul of Samosata shows itself quite clearly, as does the teaching of Cerinthus, insofar as he wished to separate the man Jesus from the divine nature. Following this observation, it should be noted that the *Socinians* <note>A 16th-century theological movement that denied the pre-existence of Christ and the Trinity</note> who were active in the sixteenth century, although they come closest to the *Photinians* in that they consider the man Jesus to be a mere man—and are therefore not improperly compared to them—are nevertheless quite far removed from them. On the other hand, it is evident that those who have emerged in our time as *Unitarians* in England hold to the party of Photinus.

->§. XXIII.<-

Certainly, if one considers the opinion of Photinus somewhat more closely, one must necessarily arrive at the thought that the great **Athanasius** <note>A central figure in the development of the Nicene Creed and a staunch opponent of Arianism</note> did not have such a bad intention in receiving him when he was driven out by the Synod of Sirmium, as some would otherwise attribute to him. For it was indeed the case that Athanasius, along with the Orthodox, was of a completely different opinion than Photinus and his followers; but Athanasius had reason

# Report on the Stirred Controversy

to believe that Photinus's teaching was better than that of the Arians. For the latter held Christ, even according to his divinity, to be a creature of **GOD** <note>The Arians believed Jesus was the first and greatest creation of God, but not eternally God himself</note>; Photinus, however, asserted that the Word—as St. John describes it—is *in* **GOD**, and consequently not a creature, but **GOD** Himself. We have already noted that Photinus's propositions harmonize particularly well with the thoughts of Paul of Samosata. When we also take into account the term <term>of one substance</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιον (homoousion); the central term of the Nicene Creed asserting that the Son is of the same essence as the Father</note> which was borrowed from him at the Council of Nicaea—a reproach to which Athanasius did not particularly wish to respond—it is indeed highly probable that Photinus held more to the opinion of Athanasius than to that of the Arians, and consequently had no malicious intention. Indeed, what should we think of the confidence Photinus had in Athanasius, such that he took refuge with him? Especially since the origin of his error consisted in his opposition to the Arians, as shown above in §. XXI. When we further consider that Photinus may have been made quite pliant by his persecution and spoke fair words, even conforming himself more to the teaching of Athanasius, all suspicion rightly falls away. At the same time, it is not incorrectly concluded that the same may be true of many other evil reports that this famous man had to suffer.

### §. XXIV.

This may also be the cause why this error, although it spread quickly at the time, did not last long. For it is to be suspected that those of the Photinian mind—especially when they saw that their leader had turned to Athanasius—willingly turned back to the Orthodox faith, as they more closely considered the personal nature of the Word (which they believed according to the writings of John) and its personal union with human nature. For this sect vanished so quickly that even Epiphanius records that it had become scattered and unknown; and after him, Theodoret writes that not the slightest trace of it remained. Nevertheless, Photinus, even though he was later condemned at various Synods, continued constantly to defend his opinion both orally and in writing, in the Greek and Latin languages.

### §. XXV.

The Priscillianists in Spain, who came to prominence around the year 380 AD, are also usually accused of *Sabellianism* <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different modes or "masks" of a single person, rather than three distinct persons</note> among other things; which, if correct, would be a sign of Photinianism existing among them. However, we shall not trouble ourselves further with that; it is enough that this fourth century was, alas! far too fertile in erroneous opinions regarding the most holy Godhead. We have sought these out in such a way that all the rest belongs there. What is written of the Macedonians regarding the doctrine of the Holy Spirit cannot be taken so particularly to heart, because they are expressly given testimony that they taught correctly regarding the Son of **GOD**. Now, one does not easily expect an error regarding the personality of the Holy Spirit where the person of Christ is taught correctly.

### §. XXVI.

But to return to the Arians, it should be noted that as much as they began to spread in the fourth century, they also managed to endure—though with alternating fortune—until the end of said century, when they suffered another powerful blow under **Theodosius the Great** <note>Theodosius I (reigned 379–395 AD), the Roman Emperor who established Nicene Christianity as the official state religion and campaigned against Arianism</note>. The entire Orient was so flooded with the Arian heresy that **Basil the Great** and **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>Two of the "Cappadocian Fathers" who were instrumental in defining the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity</note> were almost the only ones who still resisted them; it is said that for this very reason they had to abandon the solitary life they otherwise loved so much, so that they could withstand the heretics. It happened not only that some of the Christian Emperors were devoted to their party, but they were also better tolerated by the apostate **Julian** <note>Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), who rejected Christianity and attempted to restore Roman paganism</note>, who believed that they were more rational than the others. On the other hand, however, they also encountered resistance from various Emperors.

### §. XXVII.

It fared no differently in the following fifth century, when the Arians indeed had to endure resistance in the Orient; conversely, however, they spread all the more in the other regions of the world and plagued the Orthodox under their dominion with many persecutions. For the invading **Goths** turned—I know not in what manner—almost entirely to the Arians, as did the **Vandals** in Africa. Indeed, the Arians had the opportunity to convert the **Burgundian** nation to their faith and thereby make themselves even more formidable. From this, cruel persecutions arose from them against the Orthodox; yet the latter had to view these as nothing other than a just judgment of **GOD** that came upon them for the sake of their sins, and especially as a <term>Law of Retribution</term> <note>original Latin: "Jus Talionis"; the principle of "an eye for an eye" or like-for-like punishment</note>. For in addition to their otherwise unchristian lives, they had particularly stained themselves with many unmerciful persecutions of the Arians, and therefore now had to see the same game played against them as they had played against others. For this reason, one rightly views the Edict of **Hunneric** <note>King of the Vandals (477–484 AD) in North Africa</note> in Africa as fatal, when in it he ordered those very same punishments which the Orthodox had used against the Arians to be reversed and directed against the Orthodox.

### §. XXVIII.

At the beginning of the sixth century, the Arians still acted as masters, both in Europe and in Africa, as it is remembered that **King Clovis** <note>original: "Ludwig"; Clovis I, King of the Franks, whose conversion to Catholicism was a turning point for Europe</note> in France was almost the only Orthodox king in his time; although shortly thereafter **King Chilperic** <note>Chilperic I, a Merovingian king known for his conflicting religious policies</note> introduced Arianism everywhere. They were also still so strong in the Orient that **Justin** and **Justinian** had much work to do with the persecution of them. Indeed, if one may believe **Procopius** <note>A prominent Byzantine historian of the 6th century</note>, who claimed that the Arian churches were so rich that everything in them was made of gold, silver, and precious stones, it can be recognized from this that they were no small or insignificant crowd there. Meanwhile, however, they received a deadly wound through the persecution of Justinian in the Orient, as well as in Africa, from which they could never again recover. For although the Emperor had to spare the sect of the **Hexacionites** <note>A sub-sect of Arians</note> because he [did not wish to provoke] the Gothic kings in Italy who were devoted to them, since

It is also customary for the Priscillianists in Spain, who appeared around the year 380, to be accused among other things of <term>Sabellianism</term> <note>The belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons, but merely three modes or "masks" of one God</note>; which, if it were correct, would be a sign of the Photinianism that existed among them. However, we shall not trouble ourselves further with that; it is enough that this fourth century was, alas! far too fruitful in erroneous opinions concerning the most holy Divinity: which we have sought out in such a way that everything else belongs there. What is written of the Macedonians regarding the doctrine of the Holy Spirit cannot be taken so particularly to heart, because testimony is explicitly given of them that they taught rightly concerning the Son of **GOD**: now, however, one does not easily expect an error regarding the personality of the Holy Spirit where the person of Christ is rightly taught.

## §. XXVI.

But to return to the *Arians* / it is to be noted / that as much as they began to spread in the fourth *century* / they also / though with alternating fortune / made their way through / until the end of said *century*, when they suffered another mighty blow under *Theodosius the Great*. The entire *East* <note>original: "Orient"</note> was so flooded with the *Arian* heresy / that *Basil the Great*, and *Gregory Nazianzen* were almost the only ones / who still opposed them / and for this reason they are said to have left the solitary life they otherwise loved / so that they could resist the heretics. It happened not only / that some of the Christian Emperors were devoted to their party; but they were also better tolerated by the apostate *Julian* <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who attempted to revive Roman paganism</note>, who believed / that they were more reasonable / than the others. On the other hand, however, they also found resistance from various Emperors.

## §. XXVII.

It fared no differently in the following fifth *century*, when the *Arians* indeed had to suffer resistance in the *East*; but on the other hand spread all the more in the other regions of the world / and plagued the *Orthodox* under their dominion with many persecutions. For the invading *Goths* turned / I know not in what manner / almost all to the *Arians*, as did the *Vandals* in *Africa*. Indeed the *Arians* had the opportunity to convert the *Burgundian* nation to their faith / and thereby make themselves even more formidable. Thence arose cruel persecutions by them against the *Orthodox*; which the latter, however, had to regard as nothing other than a just judgment of **GOD** / which came upon them for the sake of their sins / and especially as a <term>jus talionis</term> <note>original: "Jus Talionis," the law of retaliation, often expressed as "an eye for an eye"</note> that came over them. For in addition to their otherwise un-Christian lives / they had particularly stained themselves with many unmerciful persecutions of the *Arians* / and therefore now had to see / that the same game was played with them / as they had played with others. For this reason one rightly views the edict of *Hunneric* in *Africa* as fateful / when in it he turned those very same punishments / which the *Orthodox* had used against the *Arians* / and had them directed back against the *Orthodox*.

## §. XXVIII.

At the beginning of the sixth *century* the *Arians* still played the master / both in *Europe* and in *Africa*, in so much as it is remembered / that King *Ludwig* <note>Clovis I (Chlodwig), King of the Franks</note> in *France* was almost the only *Orthodox* one in his time; although shortly thereafter King *Chilperic* introduced *Arianism* everywhere. They were also still so strong in the *East* / that *Justin* and *Justinian* had much to do with the persecution of the same. Indeed / if one may believe *Procopius* / that the *Arian* churches were so rich / that even all things therein were made of gold / silver and precious stones; then it can be recognized from this / that they were no small or insignificant crowd there. Meanwhile, however, they received a deadly wound through the persecution of *Justinian* in the *East*, as also in *Africa* / from which they could never again recover. For although the Emperor had to spare the sect of the *Hexakionites* <note>A subgroup of Arians in Constantinople, named after the "Hexakionion" or "Six Columns" district where they gathered</note> / because he [feared] the *Gothic* kings in *Italy* / who were devoted to the same—

->§. XXIX.<-

In the same manner, things also went more and more toward the decline for them in the *West* <note>original: "Occident"</note>. Already *in the year* 517, the Burgundian King *Sigismund* allowed himself to be persuaded by *Avitus*, Bishop of *Vienne*, / to join the *Orthodox*. From which one sees / that / however gloriously the beginning of this *century* <note>original: "Seculi"</note> had shone upon the *Arians* / the end turned out just as miserably for them.

->§. XXX.<-

However / when we consider that they nonetheless hesitated / to name three deities; we cannot indeed approve of the good *John's* critical rationalizing; yet we must also confess / that people interpreted his meaning more harshly / than he perhaps intended.

### §. XXXII.

This Mahometh, or as he must properly be called / Muhammad, who became known around the year 622 / is said to have first been a camel driver in Arabia. It is easily observed, however / that he must have possessed great natural intelligence: and there is no reason to doubt the truth of what the writers say of him / that he was inclined toward deep reflection and a solitary life. Otherwise, he was an enemy to superstition and all idolatry / viewed the confusion of the Christians with resentment / and noted the wretched condition of the Jews. From which observation it is most likely to be concluded / that he was not entirely without the fear of God; but rather that in his deep reflection he weighed everything carefully / and as he was left to himself in his proud heart / being without the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit / he resolved / to trust no man further / but to choose from everything that which seemed good and rational to him. By this, he indeed had the appearance / of acting more rationally than others / who bickered and consumed one another aimlessly without reason; but he did not perceive the Divine judgment / which is pronounced over those / who will not humbly and calmly follow the Spirit of God / namely, that they shall be given over to the thoughts of their own hearts and a vain mind.

### §. XXXIII.

After he had looked around at all religions and sects / and specifically allowed himself to be instructed by the <term>Arians</term> <note>A sect that denied the full divinity of Christ, arguing he was a created being</note>, <term>Nestorians</term> <note>Followers of Nestorius who emphasized the separation between Christ's human and divine natures</note>, and <term>Jacobites</term> <note>A Monophysite Christian sect in the Middle East</note> / he organized his teaching into some order: And because he noticed / that he would not lack followers in such a completely confused state of religion / he accepted the honor of inventing a new religion / and first scattered its seeds in Mecca, a city / which was all the more convenient for him because the inhabitants / although they were pagans / had nevertheless broken away from polytheism <note>original: "Vielgötterey"</note>. Although he did not immediately succeed there / but had to flee from there to Medina. In this latter place, however, more and more people gathered to him / so that after 8 years / during which he completed a good part of his <term>Alkoran</term> <note>The Quran, the central scripture of Islam</note> / he was able to take Mecca, and thereafter all of Arabia. For because he was of an ambitious and yet melancholic <note>In the 17th-century sense: brooding or intensely serious</note> temperament / he permitted the religion to be spread by weapons / and made the beginning of this himself.

### §. XXXV.

Besides this, he also forbade the reading of the holy books; and although he allowed Moses and other writers of Holy Scripture to pass as good and holy people / he nevertheless asserted many things / that ran directly contrary to them.

### §. XXXVII.

However, the violent expulsion of the Arians <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> throughout the world helped his rise not a little. For since the people may have possessed little of true Christianity / and perhaps because of the sharp <term>Præsidiī</term> <note>original: "Præsidiī" — referring here to the strict legal authority or oversight of the official church</note> had little desire left for disputing / it fell very conveniently for them / that they finally found someone / whom they could hold onto / and under whom they were permitted to safely cherish their opinions in their hearts. ### §. XXXVIII.

In such a way, however, the sect of the Arians vanished completely in this seventh <term>Seculo</term> <note>century</note>. To be sure, I do not wish to say / that all the Arians joined themselves to the Muhammadans / as that would certainly be an unprovable statement: nevertheless, the history of <term>Muhammedismi</term> <note>Muhammadanism, an old term for Islam</note> shows clearly / that a great part of them must have turned that way. Meanwhile, it is to be believed / that very many through persecution were brought to a confession against their conscience / among whose descendants the Arian tenets were finally forgotten. It is also not unbelievable / that many among them, upon the rising of <term>Muhammedismi</term>, looked inward / and through the obvious apostasy of their own people, conceived a total loathing for all Arian doctrine.

### §. XXXIX.

If one indeed wished to draw it to one of the previous heresies / it might perhaps have more similarity with <term>Nestorianismo</term>. <note>Nestorianism, the doctrine that there were two separate persons in the incarnate Christ, one divine and one human.</note>

Information about the Stirred-up Dispute

### §. XL.

And so, by the ninth century, it was completely over for the Arians. Even if some of them remained here and there in secret—which is more than certain—no one dared to show themselves for fear of the zeal of Charlemagne <note>original: "Caroli M." — Charles the Great (r. 768–814), King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. For just as he was eager to spread the Christian religion according to his understanding through sword and weapons among the heathens, he was also inflamed to exterminate heresies in the same manner. Consequently, he launched a formal military campaign in Spain to root out, root and branch, the alleged heretics there who were still accused of Arianism. It remains uncertain, however, whether those so-called Arians were true Arians, or whether they were simply blackened with this dreaded name by their adversaries. Otherwise, it seems likely that many Arians may have stayed under assumed names during this century. In this same way, the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between light and dark; they were frequently persecuted alongside Christians.</note> in the East should be viewed, of whom it is said that the Emperor Basil <note>Basil I (r. 867–886), Byzantine Emperor.</note> exterminated and executed a great number.

### §. XLI.

In the tenth century, things were quite silent regarding the Arians. This is a sign that those who search for some of them in the following eleventh century are mistaken. For while one reads here of a dangerous heresy that arose from an Italian woman and was strongly promoted by Heribert and Lisoius at Orleans, some also count the doctrine of the divinity of Christ among their errors, and for this reason, Sandius <note>Christoph Sandius (1644–1680), a scholar who wrote a history of Arianism and often tried to identify historical figures as secret Arians.</note> wants to present these people as Arians. But even granted that they had erred in the doctrine of the divinity of Christ, it has not yet been proven that it happened in an Arian manner; and even if it were so, it would not follow that these people were descended from the old Arians, who were completely buried in the previous tenth century. However, it is well known that Sandius was concerned with nothing else than refusing to admit that the teachings of these people had entirely vanished; for which reason his thoughts are rightly held in much more suspicion.

### §. XLII.

In the twelfth century, when the witnesses of the truth emerged so powerfully under the name of the Waldensians <note>A medieval movement that advocated for poverty and lay preaching; they were often declared heretics by the Catholic Church.</note> that they flooded almost all of Europe, and more than 70,000 of them sacrificed their lives for the sake of the truth, still none were found who were supposed to have revived the Arian error. To be sure, they were decried as Arians by the corrupt clergy, but not according to the truth; rather, it was done to inflict that much more misery upon them. On the contrary, they generally had the testimony even from their enemies that they believed rightly concerning God in everything and also kept all the articles contained in the Creed. In this century, however, the learned Frenchman Peter Abelard is particularly set up as an Arian, whose doctrines on the Trinity were condemned at the Synod of Soissons in the year 1139 in the presence of Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a powerful abbot and primary critic of Abelard's philosophical approach to faith.</note>. Now, the learned readily admit that he allowed philosophy to lead him into several incorrect propositions;

It appears, at the very least, that he could not have been truly devoted to *Arianism* <note>A belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-equal or co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, because the embittered clergy still had to let him die a natural death in the monastery of *Cluny* in *Burgundy*, where even after his death he was praised as blessed by the monks.

->§. XLIII.<-

In the thirteenth *century* <note>original: "Seculo"</note>, the orthodox Waldensians <note>A medieval movement following the teachings of Peter Waldo, emphasizing poverty and the Bible; they were frequently targeted by the Inquisition.</note> still had to endure being labeled with the horribly detested name of "Arians," among other insults. We have shown in the previous *paragraph* <note>original: "Paragrapho"</note> with what little justification this was done. Therefore, it also seems that this shameful naming finally ceased. For in the fourteenth *century*, when the Wycliffites <note>Followers of the English reformer John Wycliffe.</note> caused such a great stir, and in the fifteenth, when the Hussites <note>Followers of the Czech reformer Jan Hus.</note> emerged so powerfully, this name was—to my knowledge—heard no more. This is an infallible proof that this doctrine was finally buried for many *centuries*. I will not deny that there may have been some here and there who had an incorrect *concept* of the Godhead; for how can one find a time when a thousand different opinions do not wander through the thoughts of men? But it is enough that God also wished to testify to His displeasure externally by the complete overthrow of this false doctrine. And truly, these two *centuries* are all the more remarkable because, even during the first heat of the Reformation, no one was found who allowed it to be noticed, even once, that he harbored a doubt regarding the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

->§. XLIV.<-

However, when a particular freedom in religious matters began to emerge in the sixteenth *century*, after *Dr. Luther, Zwingli*, and *Calvin* everywhere powerfully opposed and weakened the Papacy, people began once more to assault the doctrine of the Godhead both secretly and openly. The beginning of this was made by *Michael Servetus* or *Rennes* <note>While the text says "Rennes," this refers to Michael Servetus (c. 1511–1553), who also used the name Reves.</note>, a *physician* <note>original: "Medicus"</note>, born in *Tarragona* in *Catalonia*, who as early as the *year* 1525 attacked the doctrine of the Trinity in writing and speech, and especially in the *year* 1531 published seven books *On the Errors of the Trinity* <note>original: "de Erroribus Trinitatis"</note>. His errors are made known from his suppressed writings in the following manner: God is one both in essence and in person; before His birth from Mary, Christ existed only in the mind of God as an image (*by way of an idea* <note>original: "per Ideam"</note>); Christ is called God because of His conception by the Holy Spirit, the indwelling of divine grace, and His anointing; the divine essence is a part of all *creatures*, etc. This man—who perhaps did not mean it for evil, as he directed his whole heart toward the Reformation along with others—had the misfortune of falling into the hands of *Calvin's* zealous spirit. While passing through *Geneva*, *Calvin* had him seized, and by obtaining theological *opinions* <note>original: "Responsa" — formal legal or theological judgements requested from authorities.</note>, persuaded the authorities to have him burned alive. The *theologians* generally praised this deed of *Calvin*, but they were constantly forced to have it thrown back in their faces whenever they complained about the cruel *proceedings* of the *Papists* against the *Huguenots* <note>French Protestants who were often persecuted for their faith.</note> and others.
