# Account of the Stirred-Up Conflict
<meta>catchword: year</meta>

### §. XLV.

In a similar manner, others who accepted and defended the teachings of **Servetus** <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish physician and theologian executed in Geneva for heresy regarding the Trinity.</note> also had to suffer a violent death. Among these was **Valentinus Gentilis**, a native of **Cosenza** in **Calabria**. Although he had escaped death in **Geneva** in the year <note>original: "anno"</note> 1558—having signed a confession <note>original: "Confession"</note> of the Trinity out of fear—he returned to **Switzerland** in the year 1566 after spending several years in **France**. He was imprisoned in **Bern** and beheaded there in that same year. His doctrine is recounted as follows: **GOD** the Father alone is the one true **GOD**; the Son is **God made into a being** <note>original: "Deus Essentiatus"</note>, or made into an essence by the Father; the Father, Son, and **Holy Spirit** were three **substances** <note>original: "substantien"</note> or independent beings, and three eternal spirits, but the Father was greater than the Son and the **Holy Spirit**, and existed before the Son; the Father alone is an **unbegotten Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus ἀγένητος"</note>, the Creator, while the Son was begotten of **GOD** in an unspeakable way to carry out the Father's will, and so forth. He claimed the **Athanasian Creed** <note>original: "Symbolum Athanasii"; a Christian statement of belief focusing on Trinitarian doctrine and Christology.</note> was composed sophistically, that it created four gods, and that it tore the **Lord Christ** into many parts. At a **Synod** in the year 1562, he is said to have confessed: **GOD**, in the vastness of eternity, had brought forth an excellent spirit, who afterwards, in the fullness of time, became man.

### §. XLVI.

Others of these people, who were executed one by one in various places, we shall rightly pass over in silence as individuals who had no significant following. However, we must still remember the famous Royal Polish Physician <note>original: "Medici"</note> and Privy Councilor, **Georgius Blandrata**, who was likewise an Italian from **Saluzzo**, and had been driven out of **Geneva** because of **Servetus’s** teaching. It was through this man that this doctrine was specifically introduced into **Poland**, where it gradually found many followers and even many patrons among the nobility. It is true that **Calvin** <note>John Calvin, the influential French reformer in Geneva.</note> pursued him even there through letters; but Prince **Nicolaus Radziwiłł** <note>A powerful Polish-Lithuanian noble and reformer.</note> protected him. By the Prince's efforts, he was sent to a **Synod** of the Reformed in the year 1561, where he received a testimonial for a confession he delivered as follows:

> I confess that I believe in one **GOD** the Father, in one **Jesus Christ** His Son, and in one **Holy Spirit**, each of whom is essentially **GOD**: I reject the plurality of gods, because we have only one **GOD**, who is inseparable in essence: I confess that there are three distinct **persons** <note>original: "ὑπόστασεις" (hypostases)</note>; and **Christ’s** eternal divinity and begetting; also one **Holy Spirit** as true and eternal **GOD**, who proceeds from both.

However, the aforementioned **Gentilis**, his **teacher** <note>original: "Præceptor"</note>, is said to have been dissatisfied with him because of this confession, saying that he had accepted the errors of **Sabellius** and **Samosatenus** <note>Early Christian figures associated with "Modalism" (the idea that Father, Son, and Spirit are just roles/modes of one person) and "Adoptionism" (the idea that Jesus was a man who became divine).</note>.

### §. XLVII.

And up until this point, such people still remained among the Reformed; but

# Concerning the Article of the Holy Trinity
<sig>C 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: must /</meta>

In the year <note>original: "anno"</note> 1562, they were separated from the others in a colloquy <note>A formal theological discussion or conference.</note> and subsequently attracted many followers, both from among the common people and from the preachers themselves. It was also around this time that **Faustus Socinus** arrived in Poland; from him, and from his relative **Lælius Socinus**, they eventually received the name **Socinians**. We therefore have reason to remember these two in particular.

### §. XLVIII.

The elder among them, **Lælius Socinus**, traveled in the year 1541—in the 22nd year of his age—through France, England, Holland, Germany, and Poland, and finally settled in Zurich in the year 1551. In Wittenberg, he was welcomed by **Melanchthon** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a primary leader of the German Reformation alongside Luther.</note> and remained there for three whole years, because Melanchthon saw that he had a great desire to investigate the disputes of that time. In Zurich, however, he lived with the learned **Conrad Pellikan** and exchanged letters with the most famous Protestants, who may have esteemed <note>original: "æstimirt"</note> him for his talents. Regarding his temperament, he was timid and modest, and therefore skilled not only in harboring all sorts of notions and thoughts but also in masterfully concealing them. For he had seen **Servetus** burned <note>Referring to the 1553 execution of Michael Servetus in Geneva.</note>, and for that reason, he not only took great care but also knew how to explain himself in a fairly orthodox manner when he was hard-pressed. However, I do not wish to say that he did this out of fear alone: for because he had a modest disposition, he was suited to reflect on the truth and not to break out immediately with all his doubts <note>original: "dubiis"</note>. Perhaps the unchristian persecution of Servetus and others might have driven him, against his will, to a general doubt of the doctrine, which he might otherwise have considered more calmly and accepted more securely if he had been out of danger. For it cannot be expressed what a prejudice <note>original: "præjudicium"; here meaning a negative predisposition or stumbling block.</note> grows against pure doctrine from the unchristian behavior of its confessors. Truly, it is so piercing that the mind can fall into such a natural impotence <note>original: "Impotenz"</note> and weakness that it is unable to prevent an anxious and trembling wavering, despite the strength of the most powerful arguments.

### §. XLIX.

This will become even better known to the reader from the following private letter, which he wrote in the year 1555, and in which he explains himself thus: He holds the ancient creeds <note>original: "Symbola"</note>—the **Apostolic**, **Nicene**, and **Constantinopolitan**—in honor as well as he can and should; nor does he deny, alongside those who lack understanding, that the words **Trinity**, **Person**, <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "ὑπόστασις"; a Greek term for the distinct "substance" or "person" of the Godhead.</note>, **Consubstantiality** <note>The doctrine that the Father and Son are of the same substance.</note>, **Union**, **Distinction**, and the like, were not just recently invented, but have been in use for a good 1300 years. But he would much rather approve if one still explained the Evangelical and Apostolic faith using the words of Christ, the Apostles, and the Evangelists. Yet he did not deny that those terms <note>original: "Termini"</note> were necessary for the Church Fathers <note>original: "Patribus"</note> to present the Catholic <note>Used here in the sense of the "universal" or "established" church teaching.</note> doctrine more respectably; much less did he cast doubt upon the foundation of Christian doctrine, which should be certain among all the orthodox...

# Report of the Aroused Controversy

### §. XLV.

In the same manner, others who accepted and defended the teachings of **Michael Servetus** <note>A Spanish theologian executed in Geneva for heresy in 1553.</note> also had to suffer a violent death. Among these was **Valentinus Gentilis**, a native of Cosenza in Calabria. In Geneva in the year 1558, he had escaped death by signing a confession regarding the Trinity out of fear. However, after staying in France for several years, he returned to Switzerland in 1566, where he was imprisoned in Bern and beheaded that same year. His doctrine is recounted as follows: God the Father alone is the one true God; the Son is "God given essence" <note>original: "Deus Essentiatus"</note>, or made into a being by the Father; the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three substances or independent beings, and three eternal spirits, but the Father is greater than the Son and the Holy Spirit, and existed before the Son; the Father alone is an "unbegotten Spirit" <note>original: "Spiritus ἀγένητος"</note>, the Creator, while the Son was begotten from God in an inexpressible way to carry out the Father's will, and so forth. He claimed the Athanasian Creed <note>A Christian statement of belief focusing on Trinitarian doctrine and Christology.</note> was composed sophistically, creating four gods and tearing the Lord Christ into many parts. At a synod in the year 1562, he is said to have confessed: God had brought forth an excellent spirit in the expanse of eternity, who later became man in the fullness of time.

---

### §. XLVI.

We rightfully pass over others of these people in silence, individuals who were executed in various places over time but had no significant following. However, we must mention the famous Royal Polish Court Physician and Privy Councilor, **Georgius Blandrata** <note>Giorgio Biandrata (1515–1588), an influential Italian physician and theologian in Poland and Transylvania.</note>, who was likewise an Italian from Saluzzo and had been driven out of Geneva because of **Servetus's** teachings. For it was through this man that this doctrine was specifically introduced into Poland, where it gradually found many followers and even many patrons among the nobility. Although **Calvin** pursued him even there through letters, **Prince Nicholas Radziwiłł** <note>A powerful Polish-Lithuanian noble and reformer.</note> protected him. By the Prince's influence, he was sent to a Reformed synod in 1561, where he received a testimonial based on the following confession he delivered:

> I confess that I believe in one God the Father, in one Jesus Christ His Son, and in one Holy Spirit, each of whom is essentially God: I reject the multiplicity of gods, because we have only one God, who is inseparable in essence: I confess that there are three distinct persons <note>original: "ὑπόστασες" (hypostases); the underlying states or persons of the Trinity.</note>; and Christ's eternal deity and birth; also a Holy Spirit as true and eternal God, who proceeds from both.

However, the aforementioned **Gentilis**, his teacher, is said to have been dissatisfied with him because of this confession, claiming that he had accepted the errors of **Sabellius** and **Samosatenus** <note>Refers to Sabellianism (merging the persons of the Trinity) and Paul of Samosata (who taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine).</note>.

Yet he does not deny that those terms were necessary for the **Church Fathers** <note>original Latin: "Patribus"</note> to present the **Catholic** <note>In this historical context, meaning the "universal" or "orthodox" Christian teaching as opposed to a specific denomination</note> **doctrine** more respectably. Much less does he cast doubt on the foundation of Christian teaching, which must be certain among all the orthodox...

I reject the multiplicity of gods, because we have only one God, who is inseparable in essence. ### Account of the Stirred Conflict

...he would have to and would want to wish that it <note>referring to the doctrine of the Trinity</note> were made quite certain to him, because he does not dispute that the Father is the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit. He does not imagine three Jehovahs, or three equally essential Gods; he does not divide Christ, but allows for one person; but he is afraid of those frivolous minds, and for that reason guards himself against all harmful paradoxes. He also avoids all the errors of the Anabaptists <note>a radical reform movement often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants</note>, and he condemns and abhors the teaching of *Servetus* <note>Michael Servetus, executed in 1553 for heresy</note> and the whole of *Arianism* <note>the belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God</note>: He demanded no new way of teaching, etc. One sees from this letter that he judges quite moderately, and was not of one opinion with *Faustus Socinus*. Although, if one wishes to judge him most harshly, one must confess that he reveals nothing else in this letter than the opinion of *Paul of Samosata* and *Photinus* <note>early Christian bishops whose views—denying the pre-existence of Christ—were declared heretical</note>. Nevertheless, I must confess that a great uncertainty shines through the letter, especially if one considers the rest of it, which has been omitted here to avoid long-windedness. Perhaps we do not err if we believe that he died in uncertainty, yet remained in constant anxiety and laborious research, because he may have looked more to the power of his reason than to the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit. Under these circumstances, it is then so much less to be wondered at that he died so very young, namely in the thirty-seventh year of his age in the year <note>original: "anno"</note> 1562.

->§. L.<-

After his death, his brother's son, *Faustus Socinus*, took the writings left behind for himself, which were afterwards published either without his name or with it. In my opinion, however, one would do *Lælius* an injustice if one simply wanted to judge his faith based on the writings found with him: for one can put many things on paper as if they were *problems* <note>original: "problematice," meaning as a hypothetical or for the sake of argument</note>, in which one does not yet have certainty. *Faustus*, however, gathered the actual Socinian doctrine together and spread it in Poland and Transylvania <note>original: "Siebenbürgen"</note>; he also ventured in the year 1594 at the University of Krakow to publish a public disputation *concerning Christ the Savior* <note>original: "de Christo Servatore"</note>. However, previously in the years 1568 and 69 at Weißenburg in Transylvania, several preachers had already scattered various such writings and called themselves: Ministers of the congregations who agree together concerning one God the Father.

->§. LI.<-

But one must marvel that these people, who still had the blood of their fellow believers in fresh memory and had until now resisted the dominion over consciences with all their might, now themselves began to persecute their own brothers as soon as they enjoyed some measure of freedom and authority. For *Francis Davidis* <note>Ferenc Dávid, a key figure in the Unitarian Church of Transylvania</note>, who was preaching at Klausenburg at that time, fell into conflict with the aforementioned *Blandrata* <note>Giorgio Biandrata, a physician and influential religious reformer</note> at Weißenburg because of the adoration of Christ, which he <note>Davidis</note> denied. When *Faustus Socinus* was brought in during the year 1577 to settle this matter, poor *Francis* had to crawl into prison, in which he also died, and thus bore a poor testimony of his brothers. In the meantime, *Faustus Socinus* went back to Poland, where there was likewise no lack of bickering and divisions among these peo-

### §. LII.

Specifically mentioned among those Lutherans who joined Socinus are: Johannes Sommerus, a schoolteacher in Klausenburg <note>modern-day Cluj-Napoca</note> in Transylvania; Christopher Ostorod, who, after being removed from his post as a school rector in Pomerania, came to Poland in 1585 and became a preacher there, also writing extensively; Johannes Völkel from Grimma in Meissen, also a pastor in Poland, who made himself known especially through the five books *On True Religion* <note>original Latin: "de vera religione"</note>; Valentin Schmalz, born in Gotha in Thuringia, who is one of the most famous Socinians, being—next to Faustus Socinus, Peter Statorius, and Hieronymus Moscorovius—the principal author of the *Rakow Catechism* <note>a foundational statement of Socinian/Unitarian belief published in 1605</note>, not to mention his other writings; Ernest Soner, who was first a physician and Professor of Medicine at Altdorf; Johannes Crell, first a rector, then a pastor among these people, whom one regards as the sharpest defender of <term>Socinianism</term> <note>a branch of Christian theology that denies the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note>; Matthew Radeck, first a syndic <note>a legal representative or magistrate</note> in Danzig <note>modern-day Gdańsk</note>, later a pastor among the Socinians; Martin Ruar, from Krempe in Holstein, who after many travels became a pastor at Straszyn near Danzig, and after being expelled by the Danzigers, finally enjoyed the freedom to hold his church meetings again as a Royal Polish Minister; he is otherwise praised as a pious man, highly beloved everywhere for his great erudition and gifts of spirit. Others we pass over in silence for the sake of brevity.

### §. LIII.

Among these people, the Socinian doctrine found great reception in Poland, as they turned especially toward the newly-built little town of Raków, and distinguished themselves there through both teaching and writing. At the beginning of the seventeenth century, they were in considerable bloom; they had their own schools and printing presses, founded their own college in the aforementioned town of Raków, and held their annual synods. The school at Raków was established in the year 1602 and increased in such a way in a short time that often over 1,000 students lived there—not only Socinians, but also <term>Papists</term> <note>a contemporary, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics</note> and <term>Reformed</term> <note>followers of the Calvinist tradition</note>. They attracted the great lords of the Polish realm to such an extent that they could make long registers of them in their writings, while others complained that the poison of the <term>Photinians</term> <note>a term for followers of the 4th-century heretic Photinus, used here as a label for Socinians who denied the pre-existence of Christ</note> had spread so far that over 1,000 great lords in Poland had turned to them. Indeed, it is believable that Socinianism may also have spread widely in Germany at this time. For one finds in some letters of our theologians that they complain greatly about the Photinian nature and its expansion.

# Report on the excited dispute

...century, when their condition changed greatly and they fell into great persecution. The first occasion arose in the year 1638. At that time, several students from the *Rakow Gymnasium* <note>The intellectual center of Socinianism in Poland</note> broke a wooden crucifix outside the city into pieces with stones. Because it was believed that this had happened with the prior knowledge of the local Lord and the teachers, it was decreed at the Diet <note>The *Sejm*, or Polish parliament</note> in *Warsaw* to abolish the school, to ruin the printing presses, and to drive the Socinian pastors and teachers out of the country; which was indeed carried out. Now, some betook themselves to a neighboring place called *Kisselin*, but they were driven out from there in the year 1644, and the churches there, along with others in the neighborhood, were torn down. In the year 1648, most were robbed of their goods in the *Cossack War*, and further on, when the *Swedes* invaded *Poland*, they were in the year 1655 partly cut down and slain by several thousand peasants—whom the priests themselves led—and partly deprived of all they owned through robbery and fire.

->§. LV.<-

Before we further relate the external history <note>original Latin: "fata"</note> of <term>Socinianism</term> <note>A rationalist Christian movement that rejected the Trinity</note>, it will be necessary that we finally provide the required report on the actual nature of their faith and doctrine, which is recognized nowhere better than from the *Rakow Catechism*. Regarding the actual point which we have to look at here in particular—namely, the Godhead—their own confession in the aforementioned book, Chapter I, page 37, reads as follows:
> "Among other things, this is the most important: to know that in God's essence there is only one Person. Prove this to me? I prove it thus: since the divine essence is only one in number, there can in no way be many persons within it. For a person is nothing other than an intelligent, inseparable being. Tell me, which is the single divine person? It is the only God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, John 17:3; 1 Corinthians 8:6, etc."
Regarding Christ, the *Rakow Catechism* explicitly denies on page 55 that he has a divine nature, because it would be contrary to <term>right reason</term> <note>The Socinian principle that religious dogma must not contradict logical reasoning</note>, and because the Holy Scripture shows only one who is God by nature, namely the Father of Jesus Christ, and so forth. But because Christ is here and there explicitly called GOD in Holy Scripture, they generally answer that they gladly recognize Christ as their God and Lord, but also believe of him that he cannot be the most high God, because he was made a Lord and Christ by God the Father through his resurrection, but most of all through his subsequent exaltation. See: Johann Ludwig von Wolzogen in the *Christian Instruction*, page 56 and following. In this way, deceptive reason has found such a twist that it can almost never be properly set right. Regarding the Holy Spirit, the *Rakow Catechism* will in no way admit that he is a person in the Godhead, because such things are attributed to him in the Holy Scripture which would suit no person, such as Acts 5:32; 1 John 4:13, etc. And because the Spirit of God is compared with the spirit of man; therefore he must also be natural in God, just as the spirit of man is natural in man, etc. Nevertheless, there are some among them who, with the name of the Trinity or Three...

### §. LVI.

Just as they err in this main article, they also hold great errors in other important matters which have the closest connection to salvation. Thus, they refuse to recognize human corruption, which has come upon mankind through **Original Sin**, even though they carry it in their own bosoms; they do not even admit that Holy Scripture mentions it, but rather reject all obvious pronouncements with the most contemptible excuses. For example, it says in the **Rakow Catechism** <note>The primary statement of faith for the Socinians, published in Raków, Poland</note> page 284 and following:

> But what do you think of David saying in the 51st Psalm that he was conceived in sin, and that his mother warmed <note>or "conceived"</note> him in sin? Here one must consider that David does not speak of all men, but only of himself, and this not simply, but in view of his fall; and he speaks in such a manner as one reads in the same David, Psalm 81. Therefore, Original Sin is not proven from this word. But St. Paul says that they all sinned in Adam, Romans 5:12. One does not find it in St. Paul that they all supposedly sinned in Adam; rather, in the Greek language there are words <note>The Greek phrase "ἐφ᾽ ᾧ" (*eph' ho*)</note> which are commonly translated as "in whom," but which one can translate with the little word "because" or "insofar as," as can be seen from similar passages, Romans 8:3, Philippians 3:12, Hebrews 2:18, and 2 Corinthians 5:4. And therefore, it cannot be concluded from this passage either that there is an Original Sin.

In the same way, and based on this foundation, they will not and cannot admit that the **free will** of man is corrupted by Original Sin, although out of urgent necessity they must otherwise admit that in man by nature, regarding free will, there is very little power—not considering what a poor impression this makes on their other propositions. But we will let the indication of these mentioned errors suffice, because they are precisely the ones that belong to our purpose and are cited in the work itself. The rest—concerning the three offices of Christ, justification, faith and its obedience, and whatever else belongs there—we leave to those who take it upon themselves to deal with them in such matters.

### §. LVII.

In the meantime, we follow our oppressed <term>Socinians</term> <note>A group of anti-Trinitarian Christians who emphasized reason and rejected the divinity of Christ and Original Sin</note> further and see how things finally came to an end for them in **Poland**, and where they ultimately remained. Thus it happened in the year 1658 that King **John Casimir** banished them all together from the kingdom forever, with the addition that whoever should be caught in Poland in the future should be punished in body and life <note>a phrase indicating the death penalty</note>, as this was indeed later very strictly carried out. To be sure, mercy was still shown to them in that they were given 2 years to sell their goods, during which time several also held a *Colloquium* <note>A formal theological discussion or debate</note> with the Catholics <note>original: "Papisten"</note>...

# Report on the Stirred-Up Conflict

Regardless, no further mercy was shown to them; instead, they were forced to leave the country outright on **July 10, 1660**. Because of this, many became Papists <note>Catholics</note> or Reformed out of fear; others, however, after being unable to sell their immovable property at all, or perhaps for only the tenth, fifteenth, or twentieth penny <note>an idiom meaning they sold their assets for a tiny fraction of their actual value</note>, had to depart the realm naked and bare, so that even the most prominent and noble among them did not have enough bread to eat in foreign lands. Those who moved to Hungary and **Transylvania** <note>original: *Siebenbürgen*</note>, numbering over 500, were additionally stripped almost to their shirts by the Imperial soldiers at the borders, so that a large portion of them later died of hunger and the plague in Transylvania.

### §. LVIII.

After the expulsion from Poland, others of these people turned to various places. Many went to **Silesia** and found refuge for a time in the small town of **Kluczbork** <note>original: *Creutzburg*</note>, where the Duke of Brieg permitted them to hold services in their homes; for this, they praised the kindness of the Duke and the preachers themselves. Some came to **Mannheim** in the Palatinate, where the Elector, to make the land populous again, granted all foreigners the freedom to come; however, after three years, they had to depart from there as well. Since then, they have distributed themselves across Prussia and the March <note>the Margraviate of Brandenburg</note>, as well as Silesia, and especially in **Holland**. They are not lacking in other regions of Germany, particularly in these parts; however, they generally keep quiet and find opportunities here and there to attract certain well-meaning souls—who, at the beginning of their turning away from the world, tend to snap at every wind of doctrine—through their modest conduct and outward practice. Therefore, it is to be suspected that there may be more of them than anyone ever imagined, especially since everywhere people are now beginning to stop putting themselves in danger by disclosing the thoughts of their hearts in religious matters, but instead keep them hidden. It also cannot be denied that in some places, even among the highest **Ministers** <note>original: *Ministris*</note> at court, some may harbor Socinian opinions. For one easily sees that they are gradually beginning to raise their heads again, both secretly and openly, even though until this hour they have not yet dared to step forward properly anywhere. In the meantime, however, they have maintained themselves to this day in Transylvania, Hungary, and in the **County of Baranya** <note>original: *Graffschafft Barau*</note>, where about 15 congregations are still counted; these are said to have not only the free **exercise of religion** <note>original: *Religions-Exercitium*</note> but also their **vote** <note>original: *Votum*</note> at the Imperial Diets.

### §. LIX.

Furthermore, the Socinians, in addition to persecutions, have had to suffer all kinds of other vexations, which especially include the burning and confiscation of their writings and the epithets <note>derogatory nicknames or slurs</note> given to them. Thus, it is also common to call the **Socinians** by the name **Photinians** <term>Photinians: Followers of the 4th-century bishop Photinus, who taught that Jesus was a mere man and not eternally divine</term>, even though they are otherwise quite distinct from one another. Most of all, the **Socinians** prefer to be called **Unitarians**, a name they gave themselves because they acknowledge one GOD the Father, and His only-begotten Son JESUS Christ our LORD, along with the Holy Spirit. However, one easily sees that—where they do not speak this way merely to better justify themselves before their adversaries—they prove themselves to be very poor **Unitarians** under such a given reason, since in such a manner they ought rather to be called **Trinitarians** than **Unitarians**. Otherwise, they also tend to call themselves **Collegiants** and **Prophetants** (from the freedom of their practice), and others call them **Monarchians** <term>Monarchians: Those who emphasize the "monarchy" or absolute oneness of God, often denying the distinct persons of the Trinity</term>.

### §. LX.

Among the teachers of these people, besides those previously mentioned, the **Lubieniecki** family <note>original: *Lubienicii*</note> are famous. Among them, **Stanisław** <note>Stanisław Lubieniecki (1623–1675), a Polish astronomer and theologian</note> unsuccessfully petitioned the Danish King **Frederick III** in the year 1660 for freedom for the **Socinians**; he eventually died in 1675 and is buried in **Altona** <note>then a Danish-controlled city near Hamburg</note>. Also from the previous 16th century was **György Enyedi** <note>original: *Georgius Enjedinus*</note>, who was Hungarian by birth and died in the year 1597 in the prime of his life while serving as the Superintendent of the **Socinian** congregations in Transylvania and overseer of the **Gymnasium** <note>a high-level secondary school</note> at **Cluj-Napoca** <note>original: *Clausenburg*</note>. In the seventeenth century, **Lodewijk van Wolzogen** <note>original: *Ludwig von Wolzogen*</note> distinguished himself through various writings; he was a Baron from Austria who was first driven out of Hungary by the Papists <note>Catholics</note> as a member of the Reformed Church, but then went to the **Socinians** in Poland and finally died near Breslau <note>modern-day Wrocław, Poland</note> in 1658. Most notably, **Andrzej Wiszowaty** <note>original: *Andreas Wissowatius*</note>, who was a preacher among the **Unitarians** in various places and had to endure all the persecutions in Poland, demonstrated the sharpness of his intellect among friends and foes alike, until he finally died in exile in Amsterdam in the year 1678. No less did **Johann Preuß** make a name for himself through his writings as the preacher for the Polish exiles in the Margraviate of Brandenburg <note>original: *Marck*</note>, which was his fatherland; many others have done the same, whom we shall pass over for the sake of brevity.

# Report of the Conflict that was Stirred Up

...shown that some have declared themselves **Arian**, while others have declared themselves purely **Socinian**; and so it has always continued until now: for the time being, we shall not mention the various other changes in their teachings on this subject, though something more will be said of them below. In the seventeenth century, **Jeremias Felbinger** of Brieg in Silesia identified as an **Arian** while living among the **Socinians**. Consequently, he found little comfort among them during his exile, but instead had to struggle along poorly by providing private tutoring to children and working as a proofreader in printing houses. He was first a school rector in Cöslin, Pomerania, until he was removed from his office there because of his teachings and driven out of the country. Finally, in the year 1672, he wrote against the **Socinians** themselves an *Epistle to Christians regarding the one highest God the Father etc., in which the more serious errors of Socinus etc.* <note>original: "Epistolam ad Christianos unum altissimum Deum Patrem &c. in qua Socini errores graviores &c."</note> which was also published in Rotterdam in 1681. Similarly well-known as **Arians** were the **Sandii**, father and son. The former was an Electoral Brandenburg Councilor and Chief Secretary in Königsberg, but was removed from his office in the year 1657. The son <note>Christopher Sandius (1644–1680), a noted historian and Arian scholar</note>, who stayed mostly in Amsterdam working as a proofreader and died in the year 1680 in the 36th year of his age, made himself famous particularly through various learned writings. He was praised by scholars in Holland as a diligent, learned, helpful, and pious man. In addition to the **Arian** opinion which he held regarding the Son of God, one particularly notices in him strange thoughts regarding the **Holy Spirit**, as if a type of **Holy Angel** could be understood by that term. Shortly before his end, a rumor was spread that he had turned from **Arianism** to the **Arminians** <term>Arminians: Followers of Jacobus Arminius who disagreed with strict Calvinist views on predestination, often seen as a middle ground between orthodoxy and radicalism</term>; others, however, who say that people would have liked to draw him away from **Arianism**, do not wish to acknowledge this.

### §. LXII.

It is no wonder, however, that the **Arians** and **Socinians** have tolerated one another fairly well until now. Because they have been suppressed and persecuted everywhere, and were thereby forced to cry out for **Tolerance**, they finally had to forget about persecuting one another—which otherwise would certainly have occurred. And this is precisely the reason why one finds so much outward modesty and good works among these people. For under the rod <note>meaning: under the threat of punishment or discipline</note> one learns to bow, and amid tribulations, one seeks refreshment in the "purity of one's hands" <note>a biblical metaphor for living a blameless or moral life</note>. But as soon as one no longer has anything to fear, the insolence of the natural heart becomes apparent; which they will have to confess even against their will, even if they wish to know nothing of the "universal corruption of innate wickedness" <note>The author is critiquing the Socinian rejection of Original Sin</note>. Meanwhile, they find their way in here and there through this means, and cause much confusion in many honest souls.

### §. LXIII.

As for the **Unitarians** or those of **Socinian** mind, they began to stir themselves mightily in England, especially toward the end of this century. They spread a great multitude of all kinds of writings and particularly mocked the various explanations of the **Trinity** which the defenders of that doctrine made, each according to his own concept. To the **Unitarians**, this gave the appearance that the defenders themselves were not in agreement regarding the teaching. Whe—

### §. LXIV.

I do not know, however, if there is cause to rank the learned *Peter Allix*—who made himself known through various fine writings and particularly distinguished himself regarding this subject with his excellent book, *The Judgment of the Ancient Jewish Church Against the Unitarians*—behind anyone else. > „Nearly six years have now passed since someone from this sect wrote a Latin treatise concerning the **Word** <note>original: "λόγῳ" (Logos)</note>, explaining how it is to be understood in the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>The Targums, ancient Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, as an answer to *Wechner* (who proved that Saint *John*, in the first chapter of his Gospel, uses this word in the same sense as the Chaldean Paraphrase used it at the time of Christ; and that it must consequently be understood as a person properly so called within the highly praised Trinity). And now they freely accept what this *Socinian* author so vehemently fought against: that the **WORD**, mentioned by St. John, is an eternal, essential power of **GOD**, through which He created the world, and which worked within the person of *Christ*. They deny only this: that the Word is a person distinct from the Father, as we confess. It explores the uneasy alliance between Arians and Socinians under the pressure of persecution and moves toward the rise of Unitarianism in England.</meta>

->Report on the Ignited Dispute<-

...that some have declared themselves Arian <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, believing that Jesus was the first and greatest creation of God, but not equal to God the Father.</note>, while others have declared themselves purely Socinian <note>Socinians, following Faustus Socinus, denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing Jesus as a human who was granted divinity after his resurrection.</note>; and so it has continued until now. For the time being, we will not mention the various other changes in their doctrines regarding this matter, though something more will be said of it below. In the seventeenth century, *Jeremias Felbinger*, from Brieg in Silesia, identified as an Arian while living among the Socinians. Because of this, he found little comfort among them during his exile, and instead had to struggle through a meager existence by teaching children and working as a proofreader in printing houses. He was initially a school rector in Cößlin, Pomerania, until he was deposed from his position due to his teachings and driven out of the country. Finally, in the year 1672, he wrote a work against the Socinians themselves titled *Letter to Christians concerning the one highest God the Father etc., in which Socinus’s more serious errors etc. [are addressed]* <note>original: "Epistolam ad Christianos unum altissimum Deum Patrem &c. in qua Socini errores graviores &cc."</note>, which was also published in Rotterdam in 1681. Likewise, the *Sandii* <note>The Sandius family.</note>, father and son, are also known as Arians. The father was a counselor and Chief Secretary to the Elector of Brandenburg in Königsberg, but was removed from his office in 1657. The son, who spent most of his time in Amsterdam working as a proofreader and died in 1680 in the 36th year of his age, made himself famous particularly through various learned writings. He was also praised by scholars in Holland as a diligent, learned, helpful, and pious man. Aside from the Arian opinion he held regarding the Son of God, one particularly notes his strange thoughts concerning the Holy Spirit—as if the Holy Spirit could be understood as a type of holy angel. Shortly before his end, a rumor was spread that he had turned from Arianism to the Arminians <note>A branch of Protestantism that emphasizes human free will in salvation, often seen as more moderate than Socinianism.</note>; others, however, who say that people would have liked to draw him away from Arianism, claim to know nothing of this.

### §. LXII.

It is no wonder, however, that the Arians and Socinians have tolerated one another fairly well until now. Because they were suppressed and persecuted everywhere, and were thus forced to cry out for tolerance, they eventually had to forget their internal persecutions of one another, which otherwise would certainly have occurred. And this is precisely the reason why one finds so much outward decorum and good works among these people. For under the rod <note>A metaphor for living under discipline or punishment.</note> one learns to bow, and amidst tribulations, one seeks refreshment in the "purity of one's hands" <note>An idiom for living a blameless or moral life.</note>. But as soon as one no longer has anything to fear, the arrogance of the natural heart becomes noticeable; they will have to admit this even against their will, even if they refuse to acknowledge the general corruption of innate human nature. In the meantime, they find their way in here and there through these means, causing much confusion in many honest souls.

### §. LXIII.

As for the Unitarians <note>A general term for those who reject the Trinity in favor of the "unity" of God.</note> or those of Socinian leanings, they began to stir themselves mightily in England, especially toward the end of this century. They scattered a great multitude of all kinds of writings and directed their mockery particularly at the various explanations that the defenders of the Trinity made—each according to his own concept—thereby gaining the appearance that even the Trinitarians were not in agreement in their doctrine. ->concerning the Article of the Holy Trinity.<-

...in which the main accusations amounted to the claim that the Trinitarians either fell into Sabellianism <note>A belief, named after Sabellius, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three different "modes" or roles of one God.</note>, or into Tritheism <note>The heretical belief that the Trinity represents three separate gods rather than one God in three persons.</note>, or finally that they contradicted themselves and did not know what they were proposing. This was pushed so far that even the House of Commons felt compelled to submit their complaints regarding the matter to King William; he then issued a specific decree on the subject, forbidding the use of any "new terms" in the Article of the Trinity. At that time, among many others, John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Edward Stillingfleet, Bishop of Worcester, became famous in the struggle against the Unitarians; both have now been departed from this world for a good while.

->§. LXIV.<-

However, I do not know if there is any reason to consider the learned Peter Allix—who made himself known through various fine writings and especially distinguished himself regarding this matter with his excellent book: *The Judgment of the Ancient Jewish Church Against the Unitarians*—as inferior to anyone else. He not only diligently collected the Targumic and Rabbinic testimonies of the Holy Trinity (which Stephanus Rittangel had also done before him in his *Scale of Truth* <note>original: "Libra Veritatis"</note>, though he was refuted by Henricus Vorstius in the so-called *Two-Pound Scale of Truth* <note>original: "Bilibra Veritatis"</note>), but also well-defended such testimonies against the excuses of his adversaries. This same Allix also shows the difference between the old and new Socinians <note>Followers of a rationalist Christian movement that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> in the first chapter of the aforementioned book on page 2, in the following words:

> "Nearly six years have now passed since one of this sect wrote a Latin treatise concerning the word 'Logos' <note>original: "$\lambda\text{ó}\gamma\text{o}\varsigma$," meaning "The Word" as used in the Gospel of John.</note>—specifically how it is to be understood in the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>Aramaic translations and interpretations of the Hebrew Bible, also known as Targums, used by scholars to understand ancient Jewish theology.</note>—written as a response to Wechner. (Wechner proved that Saint John, in the first chapter of his Gospel, uses this word in the exact same sense as the Chaldean Paraphrase did in the time of Christ; and that it is consequently to be understood as a properly named Person in the highly praised Trinity). Since this way of explaining the word 'Logos' directly overthrows the Socinian doctrine (which was: that Saint John understands nothing else by the word 'Logos' than Christ in his capacity as a human being), one should not wonder that this author brings forth all his wit and scholarship to see how he might escape it. The explanation that Socinus smeared onto the first chapter of Saint John was commonly followed by his pupils at that time; but in the years since then, they have cast it aside as something tasteless and absurd. And now they voluntarily accept what this Socinian author so vehemently fought against: that the WORD, of whom mention is made in Saint John, is an eternal, essential power of GOD, through which He created the world, and which worked in the person of Christ. They only deny this: that the Word is a person distinct from the Father, as we confess. And whereas Socinus previously taught that Christ was a created GOD, and therefore a proper object to whom divine worship was due, the Unitarians now reject this, who..."

# Report on the Provoked Dispute

...believe of him that he is nothing other than a human creature; [they reject] the divine worship attributed to him entirely, as they follow the principles of Christianity better than Socinus <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604) was an Italian theologian who denied the pre-existence and essential divinity of Christ, forming the basis of Socinianism.</note> did.

->§. LXV.<-

Just at this time, when such movements were arising in England, several sermons by the late Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), known as the "Father of Pietism," a movement within Lutheranism that emphasized personal piety and individual devotion.</note>—which he had delivered in Berlin to his congregation regarding the eternal deity of Christ—provided an opportunity for the patrons of Socinianism to begin stirring there as well. For in the year 1700, when the aforementioned sermons had already been delivered over seven years prior, a writing of eight sheets was brought to his house under the title: *Some Reflections on Dr. P. J. Spener’s Sermons Delivered on the Eternal Deity of Christ from Matthew 22:41, etc.* When he read it through after some time, he immediately testified how greatly he wondered at the weakness of this writing, yet he wished to accept this public attack as a divine calling. Thus, it finally happened that, despite many obstacles, the book so highly esteemed by many was perfectly completed by him: **Defense of the Testimony of the Eternal Divinity of Jesus Christ**, etc., and was published with a preface by Mr. Paul Anton <note>original: "Paulo Antonio"</note>, the highly renowned Professor of Theology in Halle. In this regard, it is remarkable what he [Anton] adds at the end of page 13 of the preface, after recounting all the circumstances and the final completion:

> „And behold! hardly had that happened when our dear teacher lay down once more (for he had become mortally ill in the midst of the work), after having frequently testified that God would soon call him away from this temporal life once he had fully concluded the work. For this reason, he did not like to be hindered in the work. He thanked God heartily that he was to complete his course with the testimony of the Lord's Christ. And God fulfilled that, as he had been called to it, so to speak, in a special way.

So far Mr. Anton. Afterward, however, this beautiful book was summarized—not without benefit—by Bartholomaeus Kanngießer <note>The original uses the term "epitomirt" (epitomized), meaning to condense or summarize a larger work into a shorter version.</note> under the title: **Foundational Stone of Salvation**, which makes itself popular among other things because of its clarity, and would be even more popular if it did not somewhat spoil its otherwise good flavor with several weak-seeming arguments.

->§. LXVI.<-

Finally, in this currently running eighteenth century, there has been such a lack of Antitrinitarians <note>Those who reject the doctrine of the Holy Trinity (one God in three persons).</note> that instead, especially in England, another significant movement and uprising has occurred. It seems, however, that they have once again collectively abandoned the party of Socinus and wish to follow Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) taught that Jesus was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to God the Father; this view is known as Arianism.</note> for the time being. For it is known that the now so notorious William Whiston <note>original: "Guilielmus Whiston," an English theologian and mathematician (1667–1752) who succeeded Isaac Newton at Cambridge but was expelled for his Arian views.</note> defended Arianism as vehemently as ever...

# in the Article on the Holy Trinity.

He certainly does not wish to take his name from Arius and rejects several expressions that were condemned at the Synod of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea in 325 AD was the first ecumenical council, which defined the relationship of the Father to the Son and condemned Arianism.</note>; nevertheless, he calls Christ a created being <note>original: "κτίσιν" (ktisin)</note>, and does so in a purely Arian sense. He also professes the teachings of that part of the Church which, in the fourth century, was labeled "Arian" out of hatred, as he calls it. After this, Mr. Samuel Clarke—a man famous in the fields of philosophy and mathematics—stepped forward. In his book, *The Scripture-Doctrine of the Trinity*, he set forth such propositions regarding this article of faith that, in truth, they contain nothing other than a subtle Arianism <note>Arianism is the theological belief that Jesus Christ was created by God the Father and is therefore distinct from and subordinate to Him.</note>; he even accuses the Orthodox, in the manner of the ancient Arians, of Sabellianism <note>Sabellianism (or Modalism) is the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different modes or "masks" of a single divine person, rather than three distinct persons in one essence.</note>. For this reason, the aforementioned Mr. Whiston received that book with joy and stated that it gave great luster to his own opinion, except that he does not agree with Mr. Clarke in all things and accuses him of being a "people-pleaser" <note>This implies Clarke was being too cautious or diplomatic in his phrasing to avoid trouble.</note>.

->§. LXVII.<-

Because these people may have a large following, both secret and public, not only was the former [Whiston] actually removed from his office and the other [Clarke] kept his only with great difficulty, but an order was also issued by His Majesty King George I to the Archbishops and Bishops. This was done to maintain unity in the Church, to keep the Christian religion pure in the doctrine of the Holy Trinity, and to preserve the peace and stability of the state. We will not mention at this time the orders given regarding this by the previous Queen Anne.

->§. LXVIII.<-

But now that we have heard how much Arianism is increasing in England, and find cause to believe that they do not lack followers in other places as well, we must not think that the Socinian party <note>Socinianism was a rationalist movement that denied the pre-existence of Christ and the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.</note> has come to an end or will do so in the future. Rather, one can be quite certain that the Socinian weed continues to spread further and lies hidden everywhere, as was mentioned before and could be demonstrated with specific examples. Thus, this modest writing owes its origin not so much to those of Arian mindsets as to those of Socinian mindsets.

### General Outline of the Doctrine of GOD/ the Father/ Son and Holy Spirit/ and of the Incarnation of the Son.

->§. 1.<-

If **GOD** in the **Old Testament** did not wish to be represented under an image / it was not so much for the sake of the depiction itself / as if He could not endure images; but rather because His essence is incomprehensible / and nothing may be found either in heaven or on earth or in the water / that could [represent] the form of His essence <note>original: "Bildung seines Wesens"</note> **Exodus 20:4**. <note>The author refers to the Second Commandment, arguing that the prohibition was based on the impossibility of depicting the divine essence rather than a total rejection of visual art.</note> For it is evident that **GOD** had no abomination for images themselves / from the fact that He Himself had images made / and wrapped the entire worship of the **Old Testament** in images. <note>This refers to the "types" and "shadows" of the Old Testament law, including the ornate decorations of the Tabernacle like the Cherubim.</note> Indeed, He even allowed Himself to be depicted to a certain extent / when He presented Himself as a great **Monarch** / had a house and a special room built for Himself / wherein He had His throne / and governed His people. <note>The "house" refers to the Tabernacle or the Temple in Jerusalem, which was viewed as the earthly dwelling of the divine King.</note> Only **Moses** had to take care / that he [did] not [make] any...

### General Sketch of God, etc.

...they would contend with one another—and does one apply this to the most holy, only God? Indeed, how defiantly people insist upon the pronouncements of those passages of Holy Scripture where the only God is mentioned; they claim these for themselves with full right and wish to accuse others—who confess the same—of **polytheism** <note>original: *Vielgötterey*; the belief in or worship of more than one god</note>. What can the worshippers of the most holy Trinity do if the reason of their adversaries is so coarse that they cannot grasp any Trinity within the Unity at all, and therefore pour out blasphemous speeches which one should be afraid even to take into one's mouth? If one had such special understanding as one claims to have, one would finally notice that it is not spoken in vain when the Holy Spirit, in countless instances, places the **plural form for "Gods"** <note>original: *Pluralem Götter*; a reference to the Hebrew name *Elohim*, which is plural in form but singular in meaning when referring to the Creator</note> alongside the word **Jehovah**. However, this will soon be spoken of separately.

§. 5. But corrupt reason has rubbed itself against this mystery primarily during the times of the New Testament; and Satan has particularly sought his advantage therein, so that he might dispute the eternal deity of our Savior **Jesus Christ** among men. He did this so that, if the foundation of faith fell, the entire work of redemption might be hindered. But thanks be to God, who until now has not let it succeed, and will further make room so that one will be able to worship God the Father through His Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit, unseparated and undivided. One can, however, conveniently divide the attackers of Christ's eternal deity into two classes: the **Arian** and the **Socinian**; unless one wishes to make a special sect of those more recent ones who have emerged in England and have been contested by **Mr. Allix** <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717), a prominent Protestant theologian who defended the doctrine of the Trinity against the rise of Unitarianism in England</note>. 

The **Arians**, who arose in the **fourth century** <note>original: *vierten Seculo*</note> and received their name from an **Elder** <note>original: *Aeltisten*; meaning a presbyter or priest</note> in Alexandria, **Arius**, taught that the Son was created out of nothing by the Father, and that therefore the Son is not of the **same essence** <note>original: *gleiches Wesens*; the theological term for this is *homoousios*</note> or equally eternal with the Father. In this, they nevertheless admitted that the Son, as the **Word**, created the world, and in the fullness of time became flesh and was born of a woman. 

At that same time, the seed of **Socinian** errors was sown by a Bishop of Sirmium in Hungary, **Photinus**, who wished to maintain that Christ was a mere human being who did not exist before His birth from the **Virgin Mary**. Just as the Photinian error is more easily recognized than the Arian, so too the passages of Holy Scripture—which testify that Jesus existed before His birth from Mary—shine all too brightly into the eyes of an unbiased reader:

# And of the Incarnation of the Son

...ten: Consequently, those former groups could not make as much of an issue of the divine essence as these latter ones did. For the Arians <term>Arians: followers of Arius, a 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father</term> became so powerful that they even incited great persecutions against the Orthodox <term>Orthodox: those who held to the established creeds of the early Church, specifically the belief in the Trinity</term>. However, the providence of **God** finally let this error vanish completely, and through such a total downfall, He proved that such a doctrine was not from **God**. Such a disappearance is never found in a true doctrine, which always remains like a light upon a lampstand for at least some people. 

However, when the light of the Gospel began to shine forth again in Luther’s time, the Devil also wanted to appear as an angel of light. Therefore, he created confusion here and there and took special pains to strike a blow against his enemy—the one who crushes the serpent's head <note>A reference to the messianic prophecy in Genesis 3:15</note>. Consequently, he used the newfound freedom of teaching and the previous darkness of the Papacy <note>original: *Pabstthums*; the Roman Catholic Church system</note> as a cloak. He presented people with an irrational logical conclusion: "The Papacy has corrupted everything; therefore, one must immediately adopt the exact opposite of whatever it believes." 

Following this principle, people found the most "wonderful" opportunity to test themselves against the stumbling block of **Jesus** Christ. For there once again appeared a foolish logical conclusion: that One could not be Three, and Three could not be One. Yet, if one had been truly reasonable, one could have perceived "One in Three" and "Three in One" everywhere—or at the very least, as tending toward One. 

But so that one would not find it necessary to believe the Holy Scripture until the eyes of reason were opened, people used—following Smalcius <term>Valentin Smalcius: a prominent Socinian theologian (1572–1622) known for rejecting the Trinity and emphasizing human reason</term>—this axiom: "that religion holds much that is *above* reason, but nothing that is *against* reason." But they did not consider that proud reason, in its corrupted state, considers everything that is merely *above* it to be *against* it. And so that this would not be noticed, the spirit of lies had so arranged their entire system of doctrines <note>original: *Systema doctrinarum*</note> that they were forced to remain ignorant of the corruption of their own reason. 

I confess, Satan may have truly tormented many good-hearted souls with this; among whom—if what is occasionally told by historians is true—the good Servetus <note>Michael Servetus: a Spanish physician and theologian executed in 1553 for his radical views on the Trinity</note> is to be counted. For it is well known how it is with troubled hearts: they often do not know how to find peace even in the plain letter of Scripture, especially when they feel they have reason to distrust their opponents and feel so much more secure while under the impression of the Cross. However, just as one cannot simply declare such people innocent—even though one feels compassion for them and leaves them to their Judge—one can trust the rest of their fellow believers even less...

### General Outline of God, etc.

...so they would struggle with one another / and how does one apply that to the most holy, single **God**? What can the worshipers of the most holy Trinity do / if the reason of their adversaries is so coarse / that they cannot grasp any trinity within unity at all / and therefore pour out blasphemous speeches / which one should be afraid even to utter? If one had as much special understanding / as one pretends to have / one would finally notice / that it is not spoken in vain / when the Holy Spirit, countless times, places the plural "Gods" alongside the word Jehovah <note>This refers to the Hebrew word *Elohim*, which is grammatically plural but used with singular verbs, often cited by theologians as a hint of the Trinity in the Old Testament</note>. But of this, we shall soon speak separately.

§. 5. However, corrupted reason has mainly struggled against this mystery during the times of the New Testament; and Satan has particularly sought his advantage therein / that he might dispute our Savior **Jesus Christ’s** eternal divinity among men / so that / if the foundation of faith fell / the entire work of redemption might be hindered. But thanks be to **God** / who has not let it succeed so far / and will continue to make room / so that one will be able to worship **God** the Father through his Son **Jesus Christ** in the Holy Spirit, undivided and unseparated. 

But the attackers of the eternal divinity of Christ can be conveniently divided into two classes / the Arian and the Socinian; unless one wants to make a special sect of those modern ones / who have appeared in England / and have been contested by Mr. Allix <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717), a prominent French Protestant theologian who fled to England and wrote extensively against Unitarianism</note>. The <term>Arians: followers of Arius, a 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father</term>, who arose in the fourth century / and received their name from an elder in Alexandria, **Arius**, taught / that the Son was created out of nothing by the Father / and that therefore the Son is not of the same essence or equally eternal with the Father: though they did admit / that the Son, as the "Word," created the world / and became flesh in the fullness of time / and was born of a woman. 

At that very same time, the seeds of <term>Socinian: a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</term> errors were sown by a bishop of Sirmium in Hungary / **Photinus**, who wanted to claim / that Christ was a mere human / who did not exist before his birth from the Virgin Mary. Briefly and simply: it is against all sound reason to deny that a **plural noun** <term>nomen pluralis numeri|a noun in the plural number</term> which has its own singular form, and which must otherwise be taken everywhere as a plural, should be regarded as a singular based on mere human whim.

and a twofold Arabic version, a powerful testimony which we wish to cite from Dr. Spener’s <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and the founder of Pietism.</note> book on the eternal divinity of Christ. However, we are not so much concerned with this verse as with the following one, where the leading of the people of Israel out of Egypt is attributed to our Lord Jesus Christ. From this we learn that God did and spoke everything, even in the Old Testament, through His Son. If it stands written there that the Lord helped the people out of Egypt, this can be no one other than the Lord Jesus. For, as a rule, we must envision our Savior Jesus whenever we find the word "Lord" in the New Testament; because, as Spener also notes from Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686) was a leading representative of Lutheran Orthodoxy.</note>, the name "Lord" is assigned to the Lord Jesus in contrast to the Father in 1 Corinthians 8:6. Diligent Bible readers will find this confirmed by experience. Not to mention that Socinus <note>Fausto Sozzini (1539–1604) was a theologian whose followers, the Socinians, denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ. The author notes that even this theological opponent agrees on this specific grammatical point.</note>, as Spener observes once more in the same place <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> (Chapter 3, Paragraph 33), admits himself that the word "Lord," when used as a subject, refers to the Lord Jesus.

Furthermore, we make this powerful conclusion: The one who is the Lord—the one who helped the people out of Egypt—is the same one spoken of in the preceding verse as being denied by certain people. But that person was Jesus Christ, as we have just proven; therefore, it was that very same Jesus Christ who helped the people out of Egypt. Finally, we could also repeat from what came before that the one who must be understood is He who was not to be denied. Since it was not so much the Father as His Son and Christ who was being denied, the Son must necessarily be understood here. But these points all hang together; it is enough that we clearly see that God accomplished the exodus from Egypt, and thus everything else, through His Son.

# General Sketch of God, etc.

§. 12. Fourthly, we wish to clearly demonstrate this truth from the Old Testament itself. For in Numbers 12:8 <note>referred to here as the 4th Book of Moses</note>, it is written concerning Moses: **"and he shall behold the likeness of the LORD"** <note>original Hebrew: וּתְמוּנַת יְהוָה יַבִּיט (u-t’munat Yehovah yabbit)</note>. Luther rendered this as: **"he sees the LORD in His form"**; however, Junius and Tremellius <note>Francis Junius and Immanuel Tremellius were 16th-century scholars famous for their precise Latin translation of the Bible.</note> seem to have understood the power of the word <term>Temunah</term> <note>Hebrew: תמנה</note> better when they rendered it thus: *so that he beholds the appearance and likeness of Jehovah* <note>original Latin: "adeo ut speciem similitudinemque Jehovæ intueatur"</note>. We now briefly note that <term>Temunah</term> signifies a likeness, image, or representation of another thing, such that the thing itself is distinct from the <term>Temunah</term> or representation. This is shown irrefutably in Exodus 20:4, where it says: **"You shall not make for yourself a carved image or any likeness"** <gloss>Temunah</gloss> **"of anything that is in heaven above, or etc."** Thus, **Moses** saw **the likeness of the LORD, or His image**, and therefore necessarily saw something distinct from the Father. Thus, nothing remains but that Moses saw either an assumed form of the Lord, in which He represented His form physically, or else God’s essential Image—that is, His eternal Son and almighty Word.

The first option cannot be true, because it is explicitly stated: **"I speak with him mouth to mouth, and he sees the Lord in His form, not through dark words or parables etc."** and his beholding of God is distinguished from others <note>meaning other prophets</note>, **"to whom God <insert>Note Well</insert> makes Himself known in a vision, or speaks with them in a dream."** A common representation had been seen by all the children of Israel in Exodus 19:16 and following; and especially by Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders in chapter 24:9–10. But because Moses saw the image of God in another way—namely, mouth to mouth and face to face—it must necessarily have been His essential Image, His own Form, Beauty, and Glory. Indeed, the word <term>Temunah</term> itself indicates such a proper and essential likeness, such that any other external representation (which is not the essence itself) is only an improper meaning of the word. We see this first, irrefutably, in this passage, where everyone must confess that the Lord Himself must be understood. Furthermore, we see this clearly from the relationship to another word that shares the same *Radicem* <note>Latin: "root"</note> or <term>Min</term> <note>Hebrew: מין</note>—*see Schindlerus in Lexicon Pentaglotton* <note>Valentin Schindler’s 1612 polyglot dictionary was a standard reference for Hebrew and Semitic languages.</note>. Namely, the word <term>Min</term> <gloss>species, likeness</gloss> signifies such a

For we find the word used several times in the first chapter of Genesis, chapter 1, verse 11: "And God said, let the earth bring forth... fruit trees, that bear fruit according to their **kind** (form or likeness)." <note>The author is comparing the Hebrew word for "kind" or "species," *min* (מין), to the word for "likeness," *themuna* (תמונה).</note> Just as the word *min* <note>original Hebrew: מין</note> signifies a form in which the essence shapes and forms itself, so too does the word **Themuna**. For just as a tree bears a fruit that contains its entire essence, and which itself grows into the full size and form of the same tree from which it came, in a complete equality: so must that which is to be another’s **Themuna** <note>original Hebrew: תמונה, meaning likeness or representation</note> be equal to it in its essence and in all things, even though it has sprouted forth from the other.

That we have judged correctly in this matter is testified to us by the Holy Scriptures of the New Testament in Hebrews 1:3, where Christ is expressly called the **imprint of his essence** <note>original Greek: χαρακτηρ της υποστασεως αυτου (*charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou*), often translated as "the express image of His person."</note>. This teaches us, firstly, that Christ is God's *Themuna*; and secondly, that He is not a merely external portrait <term>Contrafait</term> <note>From the French *contrefait*, meaning a likeness, portrait, or even a counterfeit/imitation.</note> or a dissimilar likeness—such as one usually finds in artistic depictions—but an **essential Image, which comes forth from the essence, and is the essence itself**, much like the seed within herbs; though in this comparison, we must not imagine any created imperfection in God.

Furthermore, it may be noted that Paul, in this same passage, calls the precious Savior the **Brightness** or **Reflection of the Divine Glory**, which assures us all the more that in the Old Testament, the "Image" or "Form" of God was understood to be none other than the Son of God. For the translators of the Septuagint <note>The "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> rendered the aforementioned passage in Numbers 12:8 as: "he sees the **glory of the Lord**" <note>original Greek: την δοξαν κυριου (*tēn doxan kyriou*)</note>; of which more will be said shortly.

But these figures of speech do not fully correspond with one another. It was not at all absurd that He, who left the bosom of His Heavenly Father and wished to dwell among men, should demand the rain of fire and sulfur from His Father out of heaven while on the earth. If one were to treat this with mockery, one might as well mock Scripture itself, which says that GOD caused it to rain from GOD out of heaven—as if GOD were only in heaven and not also on earth. But who would judge so recklessly? Other arguments <note>original Latin: *argumenta*</note> that are otherwise brought forward I will not despise, yet I will not dwell on them. Menasseh Ben Israel <note>A prominent Portuguese rabbi and author based in Amsterdam (1604–1657).</note> confesses that the passage is far too difficult for him, unless one understands the "Lord" who was on earth to be the angel Gabriel, who as God's messenger bears the name of God. However, the ancient Jews found no such great difficulty in it as he and the *Socinians* <note>A group who denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ.</note> now encounter; for Philo the Jew <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria.</note> holds that it was the <term>Word</term> <note>original: λόγος (Logos)</note> that caused the fire to rain from heaven. Again, Philo says in the history of Sodom: "It speaks of God and His two powers." Now, the Father, Son, and Spirit have the same; therefore, the three are the one Jehovah.

## What is His Son’s Name?

He found himself in a very deep contemplation of nature and its Creator: he considered the space between heaven and earth, how it was so immeasurable and inaccessible; yet he saw their connection and union. He saw the power of the wind, that it could not be held back with hands, nor restricted by any power; yet he noticed that at its time it must suddenly let itself be checked and fold its proud wings, no differently than if it were grasped with hands. He saw the waters, both above and below, that they must allow themselves to be held in their power, no differently than if they were wrapped in a cloth or garment. He considered the ends of the earth; but could not grasp how they were so wonderfully fixed and ordered. Although he already knew that someone had done it, and it had not come about by chance, he still had to experience that he knew even less of the Creator than of the creature, which he at least saw before his eyes. At all this, his soul was terrified in holy awe; he humbled himself, recognized his misery and ignorance, and said: **I am the most foolish of all, and human understanding is not in me.** <note>original: "ich bin der allernärrischste und Menschen Verstand ist nicht bey mir." He knew that God did all this, who must have His name from His essence. Finally, he also knew that this Creator or God had a Son; only he could not grasp how the works of God were so wonderful, and what kind of being God must be to do such great things, and likewise, in what circumstances the Son must be, through whom the Father accomplished all this. Finally, thirdly, the same Spirit must necessarily be God Himself, because he is God's Spirit, and thus may not be separated from Him; therefore, even those who allow only one person in the Godhead must hold him to be God Himself, because God is a Spirit. Yet from this very fact—that God is a Spirit, and he is nevertheless called the Spirit of the Gods <note>The author refers to the plural Hebrew name for God, *Elohim*.</note>, and consequently the Spirit of the Spirit—we see that he must be a Spirit distinguished in a divine manner from the other two. I do not see even the slightest tint with which one could paint over another meaning and make it popular with the appearance of truth. And these three—Father, Word, and Spirit—are also they who alone constitute the plurality in the Holy Godhead. For otherwise, no one bears the name Jehovah, which is known to be the proper name of God. Therefore, we conclude herewith irrefutably: Whoever has the name Jehovah, the same is the true, essential God: Now Father, Son, and Spirit have the same; therefore the three are the one Jehovah.

Indeed, one did not know how to say much about it publicly from the Scriptures; nevertheless, it was a known thing among the Jews that God had a Son. We wish to remain with the Scriptures of the Old Testament for now and take from them that single passage, Proverbs 30:4, where Solomon asks in great wonder: **"What is his son’s name?"**

He found himself in a very deep contemplation of nature and its Creator: he considered the space between heaven and earth, how immeasurable and inaccessible it was; yet he saw their connection and union. He saw the power of the wind, that it could not be held by hands and could not be restricted by any power; yet he noticed that, at its time, it suddenly had to be checked and lay down its proud wings, no differently than if it were being grasped by hands. He saw the waters, both above and below, that they had to be held in their power, no differently than if they were wrapped in a cloth or garment. He considered the ends of the earth, but could not comprehend how they were so wonderfully fixed and ordered. Even though he already knew that someone had done this and it had not happened by chance, he had to experience that he knew even less of the Creator than of the creation, which he at least saw before his eyes. Above all this, his soul was struck with holy awe; he humbled himself, recognized his misery and ignorance, and said: "I am the most foolish of all, and human understanding is not in me." <note>Solomon is quoting Proverbs 30:2-3 here, expressing his humility before the vastness of divine wisdom.</note> 

So this wisest king saw in his humiliation—when he experienced that even in his great wisdom he was still very far from perfection—he saw, I say, that there was a path between heaven and earth, that the wind was held in the hands of God, that the waters were bound together as if in a garment, and that the ends of the world were established by God. He knew that God did all this, who must take His name from His essence. Finally, he also knew that this Creator or God had a Son; only he could not comprehend how God’s works were so wonderful, and what kind of being God must be to do such great things, and likewise, in what circumstances the Son must be, through whom the Father accomplished all this.
