# General Sketch of God, etc.

...of the holy Word: There is one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is also God, and yet they are not three Gods, but there is one God. One should judge this analogy <note>Referring to the analogy of light, the sun, and heat from the previous page.</note> with humility, and consider that Holy Scripture itself makes use of it in 1 John 1:5 and Malachi 4:2; thus one will recognize that it is better suited for this purpose than all others.

§. 20. We wish to take another analogy from man himself, and specifically from the human soul. Here we must necessarily place our thoughts on its nature first—so far as we must make a comparison with it here—because it is being debated today. We hold, therefore, that the soul has no more than two powers, which we will name with the usual terms, **Understanding** and **Will**. 

However, we do not do this with the intention of mixing the "rest of the soul" <note>original: *acquiescentiam*, referring to a state of quiet satisfaction or peace.</note> with the will in the common way; for these are, according to all sensory feeling, entirely distinct. Rather, we recognize that this rest <note>original: *acquiescentia*</note> or peace of the soul is a state in which the soul finds itself when it recognizes that which it willed, and consequently possesses that which it recognized. (For the human soul plays with no mere images; but since it is truthful and eternal, it finds rest in no thing unless it is likewise truthful and eternal. From this it also comes that those who do not have His Spirit dwelling within them cannot satisfy their soul with the memory of God.) 

This very fact—that this rest is not an essential power of the soul, but only a certain state of it—we see from its opposite, **unrest**, <note>original: *turbatione*, meaning disturbance or agitation.</note> which is that state where the soul does not recognize what it desires, and therefore does not have what could still its longing. Properly, however, the soul must be in constant rest, as that is what it was created for. Thus we now find in the soul: the **soul itself**, its **understanding**, and the **will**, which evermore seeks the participation in the light and the joy, peace, and righteousness (or right order) flowing from it. And just as the will seeks them, so also (insofar as it finds itself in its right state) it wants to communicate these same things to others in turn. Just as the understanding evermore contemplates all things, directs its plans toward them, and disposes the whole soul between that which is outside the soul, which [may] bring the soul rest or unrest...

...can [perceive] <note>The text continues from the previous page, describing the function of the faculty of understanding.</note> and stands in the middle within the soul itself, compares things with one another or separates them from one another, and is thus the soul’s Word, Wisdom, Counselor, and Mouth; whereas the Will is the soul’s Spirit, which flows forth in the faculty of the soul and gathers everything that creates the soul’s rest and pleasure for union with the same. Both of these, however, the **Understanding** and the **Will**, originate **from the soul; the soul is their root,** and allots to each its power; therefore they are of one essence with the soul, yet are nevertheless not the soul itself. The **glory** of the soul, however, shines forth particularly **in the understanding**, which for that reason may fittingly be called the radiance of glory in the soul. For, as we experience daily, all the excellence of the soul depends <note>original: *dependiret*</note> upon the understanding. Not indeed that the understanding is more than the soul, since the understanding arises from the soul; but rather that the glory of the soul reveals itself in the understanding; for which reason all the radiance of the understanding does not remain in itself, but illuminates the whole soul and bestows its renown upon it. We could now apply <note>original: *appliciren*</note> all of this at great length; but we hope that he who has the understanding to judge the entire analogy will be able to piece together the particular circumstances without effort: since, regardless, we cannot seek out everything, but have been content with what occurred to us while writing. Overall we conclude that this is once again a testimony that a Trinity <note>original: *Dreyheit*, literally "threefoldness."</note> in unity is found even in nature. Therefore, just as there is only one soul—the soul itself, the understanding, and the will—so that the soul itself is soul, the understanding is soul, and the will is soul, although they are not three but only one soul: so also there is only one GOD, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the Father is GOD, the Son is GOD, etc. This analogy must have been very well known to the ancients, from which we find that the Son is called the **Understanding** <note>This refers to the concept of the *Logos* (Word/Reason) or *Nous* (Mind) in Greek philosophy and Jewish Hellenistic thought, which early Christians identified with the Son.</note> by both Jews and heathens. Let us, however, proceed again to the matter itself.

# General Outline of GOD, etc.

[The] Word or the Son in the fullness of time **became man;** of which Chapter IV will treat more extensively. Here we wish to prove with only a single verse from the Old Testament that the Messiah must have been the true GOD, and consequently the one of whom we have heard in the preceding section—that GOD does and speaks everything through him as his eternal Word. Since then—because the Messiah is the Son of Man—it follows irrefutably that the **Word** of the Father, or his only-begotten Son, has become man. Our proof-text <note>original Latin: *dictum*</note> shall be Isaiah 40:3: **The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way for the Lord, make a straight path in the desert <note>original: *Gefilde*, literally "fields" or "open country," here used in the context of the biblical wilderness</note> for our GOD.** With these words the prophet says that at the time of the redemption of faithful Israel, a preacher would be found in the wilderness who should announce to men that they should prepare the way for the Lord who wishes to help them, and make a straight path for their God in the desert. 

No one will doubt that this preacher is John the Baptist, who preached in the wilderness that the Jewish people should make themselves ready to receive their Lord and Redeemer. Now, sound reason dictates that he must be understood as the **Lord** and the **God of Israel** before whom John went and whose name he proclaimed. Since he went before no one else and proclaimed no one other than the Messiah, then necessarily the Messiah, **Jesus Christ, must be the Lord and the true GOD of Israel.** 

That this is so is confirmed by the Holy Scripture of the New Testament in Mark 1:3, where Mark expressly says that this is the beginning of the Gospel. Now, were these words to be understood as referring to someone other than the Messiah, they would not be the beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of GOD. If one wishes to say it could nonetheless still be the beginning because both Jesus and John led to GOD, one thereby separates the service of John from the Gospel of Jesus Christ and gives him a separate office—as if he had not prepared the way for Christ; whereas the Evangelist expressly presupposes that John was sent before the face of Jesus. From this we conclude once more that John prepared the way for the one before whose face he was sent; since this was the face of Jesus, the Son of GOD, then absolutely that same Jesus is the Lord and GOD of Israel of whom John was to preach.

Was it **Christ Jesus**? Or did **John** proclaim another? Truly, it was neither this one nor that one <note>The author uses a rhetorical flourish here to suggest that if it wasn't Jesus, the prophecy would be empty; it must be Him.</note>. Here, surely, no one will deny that the glory of that **Lord** is understood as the one for whom the way was to be prepared; likewise, that the glory cannot be separated from the **Lord** himself, because the way was to be prepared for the very **Lord** who wished to reveal his glory. Furthermore, what other glory of the **Lord** can one understand in the **Old Testament** than that which rests inseparably upon the essence of **God**? Now, however, let one say what kind of glory of the **Lord** became revealed in the times of **John**? Has anyone seen any other glory than that of which **John** says: **We saw his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.** Further: who has been revealed? Is it the Father? We know of no other than **the Life that has appeared or been revealed,** which the apostles have seen (1 **John** 1:2). Who is the **Lord’s Mouth** whom all **flesh** has seen speaking? Truly no one other than our **Lord** and **Savior Christ Jesus**. For never has all flesh seen the mouth of the **Lord** speak, except when the **Word became flesh** and thus could be seen by the flesh. Therefore it remains: **GOD is revealed in the flesh; the Son of God is born a man.**

...so that they all might believe through him. He was not the Light, but [was sent] that he might bear witness to the Light. That was the true Light, which enlightens all people who come into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, but the world knew him not. He came unto his own, but his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them gave he the power to become the children of God, namely to those who believed in his name: Who were born not of bloods <note>original German: "aus den Geblüten"—a plural form suggesting biological lineage or ancestry</note>, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God. And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten Son of the Father, (for he was) full of grace and truth.

Let us now see how gloriously these words hang together in their clarity, and then, how irrefutably they prove that Jesus Christ is the true God, who became man as the Word and the only-begotten Son of the Father. First, we clearly find that of which John speaks, namely **of the Word.** <term>The "Word" refers to the "Logos," a term the author uses to describe the pre-existent Christ.</term> He describes this Word according to its circumstances: (1) that it was before all time, and therefore necessarily from eternity, in that he says of the same, **that it was in the beginning.** For the beginning is the *point of time* <term>original Latin: "Punctum der Zeit"—the infinitesimal instant at which time began</term>, before which no time has a place: He who already exists in the beginning does not belong to time, but to eternity. This is further confirmed when it is said (2): **And the Word was with God.** With which, on one hand, its eternity is firmly established, and on the other, its communion with God is demonstrated. The nature of such communion, however, is excellently depicted when he says (3): **And God was the Word.** For whether one lets the words stand as we have given them, or one reverses them and places them thus: **The Word was God;** it is thereby clearly stated that the Word itself has partaken in the Divine Essence and is itself the true God. Not indeed the same in Person as He of whom it is said that it [the Word] was with Him; yet nevertheless the same according to essence and unity.

...that they are made, indeed, so much so that not a single thing may be named of which one could say that it was made without the same? Must not Scripture be explained by Scripture <note>A fundamental principle of the Reformation was *Scriptura sacra sui ipsius interpres* (Sacred Scripture is its own interpreter).</note>, which says that the heavens were made through **the Word of the Lord**? <note>original: "das Wort des HErrn" — referencing Psalm 33:6.</note> Does this statement of the Apostle not contain exactly what we have hitherto powerfully proven: that God did and spoke everything through His eternal Word, that is, His only-begotten Son? I know, in the presence of eternal Truth, that everyone will feel the emphasis of these words in their soul; therefore, I will not dwell on it any longer. Our Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel, traditionally identified as John.</note> continues and describes the divine majesty of the Word by showing in what manner the world and all things were made through Him; that they were not made through Him as if through a dead and foreign tool, but rather as through the origin of the life imparted to the creatures, when He says: **In Him was life.** By which life itself is understood as the source of all perceptible life, which was in the Word in such a way that it was life itself, as stated in the following: **And the life was the light of men;** for no one is the light of men except Jesus, who is the light of the world (John 8:12). By this he means to say that this Word, as the Life which gave life or essence to all things, was not only the life that brought them forth but also preserved the life within them through His life-giving light, with which He wished to increasingly enlighten men toward life. Therefore, he says further: **And the light shines in the darkness;** thereby indicating that the light unceasingly shines upon men to enlighten them toward life: but at the same time, he laments that they were buried in such thick darkness that they could not grasp the light, when he says: **But the darkness did not comprehend it.**

§. 25. Let us now further note: John had just said that the darkness did not comprehend the light; now he continues and shows how the light nevertheless did not cease to break through the darkness with its rays in order to enlighten men. But he points out the manner in which the light broke through, saying: **There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.** For this John was the morning star that went before the Sun of Righteousness <note>original: "Sonnen der Gerechtigkeit" — a messianic title from Malachi 4:2, frequently used by Pietists to refer to Christ.</note>; he was the voice that cried out that one should prepare the way for the Lord.

§. 27. Here I will now let everyone judge for themselves: are these words written in a confused, dark, and incomprehensible manner? If there is someone who thinks that not everything is connected with more intelligible particles <note>In grammar, particles are small words like "and," "but," or "if" that connect ideas.</note>, let him consider not only that the Hebrew idiom—which at that time was often used by the Jews in Syriac and Greek—carries with it the habit of using the particle *and* in almost all connections; but also consider that all such clarity exists more for the sake of the unlearned than the learned, so that he might finally stop mocking divine wisdom. > "Certainly, this is the same <term>Word</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (Logos)</note> which is from eternity, according to which everything that exists was made, as Heraclitus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who first used the term "Logos" to describe the rational principle governing the universe.</note> held. §. 28. Now that these glorious words have been analyzed and their firm connections discovered within the whole context, we must specifically show how it follows irrefutably that **Jesus** is the true **God**, and that He, as **God**, became man. Although this is already as good as proven, we nevertheless wish to briefly present the main points <note>original: "Haupt-Momenta" — the central arguments or essential factors.</note> and thereby conclude this first chapter. Thus, it is first (1) said of this **Word** **that it was in the beginning.** Since a "beginning" is named here simply, without specifying this or that, it must necessarily be an absolute beginning, before anything existed which itself has a beginning. Therefore, since the Word already existed when any beginning emerged, or when anything started to be, it is thereby excluded from having any beginning itself and belongs to eternity, where no beginning has a place. Therefore, He must be **God**, as one who has neither beginning nor end, as will shortly follow. For it was said (2), **the Word was with God.** The circumstances must show us in what manner He was with **God**. He was with **God** in the beginning, and thus in eternity, for which reason He must be co-eternal with **God**. He was with **God** in such a concept that He shared His essence and His incomprehensible, eternal origin with Him. Finally, He was with **God** in such a way that He was personally distinct from Him, even though, as **God’s Word**, He otherwise could not be separated from Him. Therefore it is further called (3) **and God was the Word**, or the **Word** was **God**, to indicate that **God** Himself was the Word, since **God** and His **Word** cannot be separated from one another; yet this is to be understood in such a way that they are not blended together <note>The author is clarifying the distinction between the Father and the Son while maintaining they are of one substance.</note>, as we find (4) added once more: **The same was in the beginning with God.**

<meta>This page continues the author’s theological defense of the Trinity and the divinity of the Word (Jesus Christ) as presented in the Gospel of John. Thus, while the Word was indeed one with God—even God Himself—it was nonetheless not personally the same God with whom it was in the beginning. This is what we teach: that God is one in essence <term>Wesen: the fundamental nature or "being" of God</term> but more, or three, in persons. However absurd this may seem to some, the explicit letter of Scripture confirms it, and to contradict it is folly—especially since it can be demonstrated through analogies <note>original: "Gleichnissen" — parables or comparisons used to explain spiritual mysteries</note> how such a thing is possible. We do, however, readily admit that one cannot fully represent the incomprehensible nature of God through mere images. 

That these explicit words are not to be twisted is further shown by (5) the divine works. For it could never occur to anyone—even one who speaks against this mystery—that there is no distinction between God and the Word. Furthermore, we see that the work of Creation is attributed to the Word; from this, He must necessarily be recognized as the true God, because in Holy Scripture, God claims the work of Creation for Himself alone. If the Word performed the Creation, and God (with whom the Word resided) also performed it, then God and the Word must necessarily be one, even though they are distinguished within themselves in an incomprehensible way, such that the Word is *with* God. 

We could also (6) demonstrate the divine majesty of the Word from the phrase: **In him was life, etc.** But because we will deal with that specifically below, we will not dwell on it here. We also wish (7) to merely mention the glorious words: **He was in the world, and the world was made through the same,** because the power of these words has already been shown.

Against this, someone might perhaps object that God is sufficient in Himself, and thus there is nothing imperfect in Him, whether He be a Unity or a Trinity. For—arguing here purely from reason—if a human being, even though he consists of three parts and is endowed with three powers of the soul, is nonetheless not satisfied in this "threeness" but, as a lonely individual, seeks a real threeness <note>The author implies that a person seeks companionship outside themselves, such as in marriage, to find completion.</note>; then it seems likely to follow that in God, too, there is a more real and manifest Threeness than is currently found in either the soul or the whole human being. (Whereby it should be briefly noted: if someone should think that a person does not always find satisfaction in marriage, I say that the orderly state of things must not be confused with disorder, nor the spiritual with the physical.)

In the meantime, there is reason to believe that those who compare the divine Trinity with the three powers of the soul are modest enough to remember that the Godhead cannot be placed in full comparison with humanity. How much greater, then, is the distinction between God and the human soul...

# The Doctrine, etc., is Proven Through a Rational Conclusion
->I 2<-
<meta>catchword: a</meta>

We further see that she <note>Wisdom (Sophia), often personified as feminine in the biblical tradition.</note> is a divine Person, as it is emphatically stated:
> I alone encompass the circuit of heaven, and walk in the depths of the abyss, etc.

We see further that this divine Person, while distinct from the Most High, is nevertheless so united with Him that she cannot be separated from Him, in that she **comes forth from the mouth of the Most High**, and therefore belongs to the divine essence and is Himself **God**. We also see how we are to imagine her in relation to the Most High, namely as **God's** only child, and the image of His glory, in that it says she was **created by God**, although it previously said that she **went forth from the mouth of the Most High**; from which we can judge that the <term>Author</term> <note>original: *Auctor*; here referring to the writer of the text or the divine source.</note> uses the word **create** in a figurative sense and understands it as birth; as we can also infer from the divine attributes attributed to her, which no one can have but the true **God**. We finally see that this Wisdom is the true **God of Israel**, who has revealed Himself to the hearts of all men, especially to the Jewish people; who is **God’s** mouth, Word, and power; who carries all things with His powerful word; who rules the heavens and makes Himself known to **Israel** in the pillar of cloud; who alone is **God**, and in whom everything lives and moves; who chose for Himself a dwelling and inheritance, and found it in **Jacob**; who dwelt in the Tabernacle <note>original: *Stiffts-Hütten*; the portable sanctuary used by the Israelites.</note> and in the Temple at Jerusalem, and there proved His power; who held the people of **Israel** as His own property, and through whose glorification has become ever more glorious among all nations. All of this shines forth from the entire description. However, for the sake of completeness, we wish to make a small additional remark regarding the "dwelling." the Targum <note>An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible. Early Christian scholars used Targums to argue that ancient Jews recognized the "Word of God" as a distinct divine entity.</note> uses this expression: **"I am with you," says the Lord of Hosts, "with the Word which made a covenant with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit, which dwells in your midst."** In this, we must observe that among the Christians there are excellent interpreters who seek the same meaning in the Hebrew text itself which the Jewish Targum so clearly expresses. For, firstly, the Lord Sabaoth speaks, saying that He is with them: yet not He alone, but **"with the Word, through which He made a covenant with them,"** who can be no one other than the God who led the children of Israel out of Egypt, as He is the only one with whom the covenant was made, so that nothing else was presented as the covenant. If one wanted to understand "the word" merely as the spoken word through which the covenant was declared and made intelligible, not only would violence be done to the particle *et* <note>original: את (the Hebrew particle 'et'). §. 13. First of all, we note that he speaks of the **Sephiroth** as Persons, as is customary for them; and indeed in such a way that he explicitly proposes that the second **Sephirah**, **Wisdom**, shall be united with the **Messiah**. This is nothing other than what we teach regarding the personal union of the divine and human natures, and what **Christ** taught of himself: that the body or human nature is the temple in which the glory of the Father—that is, his firstborn Son—dwells, **John 2:19.** How he dwelt in him, however—namely, not as in a mere hut or a dwelling separated and distinct from himself, but in personal union—is known elsewhere, and is likewise presented by this Kabbalist when he says the **Messiah** will be united with the second **Sephirah**. This is also confirmed by **Rabbi Solomon Jarchi** <note>Also known as Rashi (1040–1105), the most famous medieval commentator on the Tanakh and Talmud.</note> regarding **Isaiah 11**, when he says: **"That the Wisdom, which is the second Sephirah, will be in the midst of the Messiah."**

As for the **Sephiroth**, <note>In Kabbalah, the ten emanations or attributes through which the Infinite (Ein Sof) reveals Himself.</note> which have been mentioned previously as the occasion arose, the ancient Hebrews actually intended to represent the Divine Essence through them. The word actually means "Numbers," and there are ten of them. Of these, they say that the last seven are attributes <note>or "properties"</note>, but the first three are not attributes, but rather *Sichlioth* <note>original: Sichlioth, intellectuales; from the Hebrew *Sekhliyot*, meaning intellectual or intelligible entities</note>, which Mr. Zierold <note>Johann Wilhelm Zierold (1669–1731), a German theologian and church historian</note> in his *Introduction to Thorough Church History*, Chapter 3, §. 39, renders thus: **that which one must only understand; which is much to say: those things which one could represent to oneself in the understanding as essential and personal, even if one were not allowed to depict them in any physical form.** It is best understood as **intelligible and self-subsisting persons;** therefore the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy, who influenced early Christian thought on the "Logos."</note> speak much of the "Intellect" when they call the first and second persons of the Godhead the **first and second intellect.** 

Furthermore, Mr. Zierold has noted from the Rabbis that they assign a single throne <note>original: כסא אחד; *Kisse echad*</note> to the first three, and say that these same ones had revealed themselves in the last seven, in that **the Trinity is, as it were, the soul of these.** Likewise, they provide information that man, in the state of innocence, was able to reach the last seven through his prophetic spirit, but not the first three. They say, **these three have only one head.** <note>original: שלשתם ראש אחד; *Sheloshtam rosh echad*</note> They report that the ancients, in order to indicate the perfect **unity**, had **made one head out of the Trinity.** <note>original: שלשתן ראש אחד; *Sheloshtan rosh echad*</note>

They sometimes call this Wisdom **Sekhel** <note>original: שכל</note> or the "Divine Intellect" which enlightens, the "Crown of Creation," and the "Radiance of Unity" that is elevated above all dominion. To them, Wisdom is the great sea of the supreme Wisdom, so that Israel may be washed in that same water as if in a spring that flows from the Highest Wisdom, and thus He has mercy on Israel. Indeed, the head of the hellish Serpent is broken or crushed by the water of the great sea. For when we are washed in such water through faith, the power of the Devil ceases.

It certainly happened in later times within the monasteries—where, due to universal ignorance, they wrote and scribbled whatever they pleased—but such things could not be practiced in **Justin's** time, when one had to contend daily with learned Jews and Pagans. Likewise, even if in subsequent times no one felt a pang of conscience about adorning religion with lies, one cannot judge from this that the first Christians, who were still quite pure from such superstition, would have done the same. 

When, however, it appears that some things are clearer than one might expect to find among the Pagans, this is—to put it briefly—the result of an unbelief that is grounded in nothing. The reader may consider for themselves whether this brief paraphrase expresses the meaning of the philosopher, or whether another explanation is necessary. We have sought to clarify it as much as possible, as it seems somewhat difficult to grasp. However one may interpret it, this remains the ultimate opinion: **that all things consist of three, and that therein time and eternity, or God and the creature, agree with one another.**

Whatever further testimonies may be lacking regarding Pythagoras, he has silently and fully confirmed them; for he not only loved the writings of Orpheus so much, but also lived among those people and later benefited from the wisdom of those whom we have just heard taught on this point. ...reveals a human being and lets what is in his essence be seen; (3) the *Name* <note>original Greek: ὄνομα (onoma)</note>, which flows from the essence and its character, making the power of his essence comprehensible to the intellect. *Alcinous* <note>Alcinous was a Middle Platonist philosopher of the 2nd century AD; his "Handbook of Platonism" was a primary source for early modern scholars understanding Plato.</note> reports simultaneously of *Socrates* and *Plato* that they taught that **GOD** is an Intellect, and in this same Intellect is a single *Idea*, which, when it is applied to **GOD**, is the *knowledge* of Himself. But when this Idea is held up against the world, it is the world’s *Archetype* <term>Archetype: an original pattern or model; in Platonic thought, the eternal blue-print in the mind of God</term>, the essential prototype according to which the world was formed as a shadow (for this is how they usually explained themselves), and in regard to itself, this *Idea* is a Being.

*Mornay* <note>Philippe de Mornay (1549–1623) was a prominent French Protestant theologian who sought to prove Christian truths through ancient philosophy.</note> summarizes it briefly thus: This *Idea* in the intellect or in **GOD** is a Being which **GOD** begets through the *knowledge* of Himself, and through which **GOD** made the world (*Chapter VI, page 113*). But *Plato* himself explains it more clearly when he says: **Every star completes its course according to the order which the most divine** *logos* <note>original Greek: λόγος; usually translated as "Word" or "Reason," here referring to the divine organizing principle.</note> **has prescribed.** Indeed, he compares the Good—that is, **GOD**—with the sun; but the Son of the Good with the power through whose communication we see (*ibid.*).

What need is there for many testimonies? He presents this doctrine so clearly that his opponents even want to name him as its author. However, *Plato* either received this doctrine from the Oriental peoples, *specifically* <note>original Latin: *in specie*</note> from the Jews—which then proves that they taught such things and that it did not seem as absurd to him, who was after all a highly intelligent man, as others wish to claim—or he arrived at it by himself, which would then prove that this doctrine is either a universal *tradition* or is recognizable through sound reason. The opponents will be unwilling to admit either of these points, and yet they will find it difficult to find an excuse.

But he himself confirms that he received it from the Jews and other Oriental peoples, or generally through the *tradition* they inherited from their ancestors, in that he always appeals to the *ancient and most ancient word* <note>original Greek: λόγον παλαιὸν und παλαιότατον (logon palaion kai palaiotaton)</note> or to the *ancients and elders* <note>original Greek: ἀρχαίους und πρεσβυτέρους (archaious kai presbyterous)</note>; that is, in a word, to Antiquity; therefore, he cannot be the author. This doctrine must have been very well known, because even *Aristotle* not only accepts it but also presents it as such a simple and obvious matter—though only in passing—when he speaks somewhere [of] how even...

## ...but the Law is *Fate* itself.

When we first recall from these words that he mentions three gods, it is not so much as if he posits <note>original Latin: *statuire*</note> three distinct gods according to the impression of the common and unlearned crowd, but rather to express their actual distinction which they possess within their unity; just as he gives them names that necessarily indicate unity, because providence and understanding are normally found within one rational being. If, I say, we recall this beforehand, then we can well say that there are as many important things as there are words in this man’s expression, which reveal his intellect. He calls the Father the origin of all things, as the Scripture does—see <note>original Latin: *vid.*</note> 1 Corinthians 8:6. He also calls Him an ineffable God, as one of whose essence we could say nothing, just as the Scripture also calls Him a hidden God, and one who dwells in a light which no man can approach. He very beautifully calls the Son *Providence* or the foresight of God, since He is the Son of the house, through whose hand everything passes, who—as we have heard before in Chapter 1—does and speaks everything in which God reveals Himself, and exists as the sole Ruler, whom heaven and earth, as the work of His hands, must serve and honor as their God. Therefore, he beautifully adds that this other God, as he calls Him, is **the giver of the Law, and of both temporal and eternal life.** For what does he say by this other than that God has given His Law (whether he understands the Law of nature, or has received news of the Law given on Mount Sinai, or perhaps had other thoughts) through His Son, as the one who is the Prince of Life, or the life and light of the world, as Holy Scripture says. Finally, along with others, he calls the third person *Secundam Mentem Intellectumque* <note>original Latin: "the second Mind and Understanding"</note>, **the other Understanding**, which is also not a bad expression, but rather borrowed from Scripture, as we see that the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:16 and the Septuagint <note>The "LXX" refers to the Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in Isaiah 40:13 likewise call the Spirit of God. But the naming is not so much to be wondered at as the effect or the office ascribed to this *Mind and Understanding*, namely, that it is a **guardian of the eternal law.** Truly, this one must preserve the law if it is to be kept. What help was the Law of Moses, which was composed in letters? Could it even keep men in obedience? Not at all; the Spirit of...

To this then comes the Holy Spirit and carries it out according to the Father's will and the Son's decree. Yet in this, He conducted Himself as an emissary, angel, or messenger of God as His Heavenly Father. Whenever something was to happen—for example, when Samson was commanded to carry out this or that—the Holy Spirit had to express it through him; He *intimated* <note>In this context, *intimate* (from the Latin *intimare*) means to press into the soul or to make known internally</note> the power of God to him, so that he was capable of carrying it out, as it is written: **The Spirit of the Lord came upon him.** That was the *Intimation*. In the New Testament, it is clearer; for the Father's will is our sanctification, the Son orders it and makes ways so that we can attain it, and the Holy Spirit is poured out upon us, so that we may walk in holiness and bring forth the fruits of the Spirit. 

Finally, the last-quoted words of the author are also remarkable: **The souls perform the Law, but the Law itself is Fate.** <note>original Latin: *Fatum*</note> Wherein he shows that he has a different concept of *Fate* than the other ignorant philosophers, who lived without the Law and therefore had to devise a foolish *Fate* in their folly. To be sure, I cannot express the wise man's opinion with certainty, because I do not have his writings at hand, and I cannot devote any time to reading them for now. However, we may take the words as we will, yet this understanding will flow from them: that the Law (perhaps he understands God Himself by this) is *Fate*, upon which everything necessarily and irrefutably depends <note>original: *dependire*</note>; so that if one wishes to be happy, one must necessarily perform the Law, but if one does not wish to act according to it, then nothing other than misfortune could follow upon it. And therefore the souls acted according to that same *Fate* or Law, in that they mirrored themselves in its image and made themselves conformable to it. §. 23. After all these presented testimonies, I might finally ask the reader whether they could be considered universal or not? We have observed regarding Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism</note> that his teaching was accepted throughout the entire Orient—at least the most prominent part of it—and was maintained until the birth of Christ. In the case of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure representing the fusion of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient sacred writings</note>, we have noted his antiquity and immemorial age; but his fame, as well as the fame of the Egyptians, is greater than we can imagine. Likewise, what is generally called "Barbarian Philosophy" <note>A term used by ancient scholars to describe the wisdom of non-Greek cultures like the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians</note> has always won the prize among the wise. The Greeks have indeed always boasted of their imagined wisdom; but when it comes to true merit, it is well known how the "Barbarians" have, with greater right, boasted against the Greeks. Holy Scripture, whose verdict must have priority for us, praises the wisdom of the Egyptians and mentions other places famous for their wisdom: it gives account of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous for astronomy and astrology</note> that they even took their learning to the point of idle curiosity, wanting to attribute all of God’s judgments to a self-invented natural constellation. Indeed, it shows us in the time of Solomon a Queen from Arabia <note>The Queen of Sheba</note> who was found capable of putting the wisest king to the test. Let these be testimonies enough that among these people there was not only the greatest love for wisdom but that real wisdom was actually found among them. But what do the Greeks say to this? Their great Oracle, I mean that of Apollo, says that **only the Chaldeans and Hebrews have partaken of wisdom.** <note>original: "allein die Chaldäer und Hebräer der Weisheit theilhafftig geworden"</note> see Mornæus <note>Philippe de Mornay, a French Protestant writer</note>, chapter VI, page 108. Plato himself admits that the sciences came from the Barbarians to the Greeks. And who does not know that the most famous philosophers among the Greeks fetched their learning from Egypt, Chaldea, Judea, and Arabia? Therefore, in our thesis, we have called upon all of Greece as witnesses, since not only all the Pythagoreans and Platonists have agreed with us, but Aristotle himself takes it as a known matter. Regarding the Romans, it is known that they parroted the Greeks; for which reason one can be certain that their opinions coincide with those of the Greeks. One should consult the profoundly learned Mr. Abraham Hinckelmann <note>A German theologian and orientalist (1652–1695)</note> in the cited—

### The doctrine &c. is proven through a rational conclusion ###

...conducted in the *Detection of the Boehmenist Foundation* <note>original: "detect. fund. Böhm." Referring to a critique of the mystic philosopher Jacob Boehme</note> in the refutation number IV, § 1 and following; so one will not only find this confirmed, but also hear that the Druids, Bards, Eubages <note>term: An ancient order of Celtic priests and natural philosophers often associated with the Druids</note>, and Eumolpids <note>term: A priestly family in ancient Eleusis, Greece, who oversaw the Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, from whom the European Heathens in Spain, France, Britain, Germany, and the Northern lands mostly derived their wisdom, are all of Oriental origin and name. From this, it follows that even to these, such a doctrine <note>The doctrine of the Trinity</note> must not have been so entirely unknown. I therefore ask everyone for their opinion: whether that which—alongside the Jews—the Chaldeans and other famous peoples of the Orient, as well as the Egyptians so highly renowned for their wisdom, and finally the Greeks and Romans, have confirmed, should not be regarded as a universal consensus of the Heathens? I do not see that anyone can raise any other objection than this: that the Heathens nevertheless unanimously established such a great number of gods, which cannot coexist with the divine Trinity. I confess that if nothing else can be objected, this alone can pass for a significant objection; although the testimonies brought forward previously lose nothing by it. However, to answer this properly, let us take the entire Heathen system of gods before us and see whether we cannot encounter the traces of this truth therein? This undertaking might seem futile and absurd to many; but we will nonetheless attempt to see how far it can be done, in the hope that if we demonstrate it and show it clearly, people will more freely grant us that the doctrine of the Holy Trinity is also confirmed, among other things, by a universal testimony of the Heathens.

§. 23. We assume, therefore, that all rational Heathens at all times recognized one supreme Being, and recognized the same as the only true GOD. > *Jupiter omnipotens, Regum Rex ipse Deusque,*
> *Progenitor, Genitrixque Deûm , Deus unus & omnes,*
> <note>Translation: Almighty Jupiter, King of Kings and God himself, the Father and Mother of the gods, the one God who is all gods.</note>

<meta>This page continues the argument that while the common people of ancient "heathen" cultures practiced polytheism, their underlying philosophical systems often acknowledged a single supreme deity. The author draws a parallel between the religious indifference and traditionalism of the ancients and the nominal Christians of his own 18th-century context.</meta>

### The doctrine, etc., is proven by a conclusion of reason

It cannot be denied that the common masses among the heathens were very much given to polytheism <term>Vielgötterey: the worship of many gods</term> in their lack of understanding; but it happened among them just as it does among Christians and others even today. These people do not concern themselves with **GOD**, nor with His essence, His name, attributes, or works; they care neither for the correct doctrine nor for its pure presentation, so long as they can live according to the lusts of their flesh and create for themselves a sweet imagination of a future glory. Nevertheless, they profess **GOD**, whom they do not know; they defend what they do not respect; they want that to be honored which they flee from as their enemy; they allow a *system of doctrines* <note>original Latin: *Systema doctrinarum*</note> to be written for them in the catechism and larger books, which they neither understand nor believe; they swear upon that which they curse in their hearts through disobedience; and finally, they threaten with death all those who do not wish to do as they do. 

Behold, this is how it went among the heathens. They knew neither whether there was one **GOD** nor none at all; they cared as little for their many gods as for a single **GOD**. But because they had been given news of many gods by their ancestors, they were happy to let that report stand, and they defended the web of their fathers with all zeal, according to the usual pride and stubbornness of men. However, even though they established so many gods and even sentenced others to death who confessed that there was only one **GOD**, it does not follow that they held all gods to be equal, or that they did not believe these depended upon the One. Rather, it is well known that Jupiter was unanimously held to be the **GOD** of all gods. 

When they persecuted someone who believed in only one true **GOD**, they believed that he despised the lesser gods (who were called such, just as happens in the Scripture itself), much as the Catholics think of their saints when one says that they should not be worshipped. And such a conceit had to serve as a pretext so that they could more easily ruin honest people who wished to honor the one **GOD** whom they confessed, and who reproached the others for their hypocrisy and malice. Moreover, they were often concerned with honor and profit, because they wanted the gods they had devised for themselves to be honored, and did not want the shame of being instructed in divine service by other nations; or because, like that certain goldsmith <note>A reference to Acts 19:24-27, where Demetrius the silversmith incited a riot in Ephesus because the preaching of the Apostle Paul threatened his business of making shrines for the goddess Diana/Artemis.</note>, they feared that their livelihood would suffer a great loss. These are the kinds of tragedies <note>original: *Tragœdien*</note> that are still played out daily by all nations under different masks in this vanity. However, to say nothing of other circumstances, it is an established fact that the doctrine of the heathen gods must not be judged according to the practice <note>original Latin: *Praxi*</note> of the common people.

Righteousness grows forth as pleasant flowers in the garden of God. Furthermore, she is called **the goddess of joy;** now it is well known that the Holy Spirit is a truly joyful spirit, in whom alone true joy is found. Certainly the myth-makers <note>original: "Fabel-Schmiede," literally "fable-smiths"</note> would have used their five senses poorly if they had not looked upon true things with their inner light; for joy and jealousy, along with strife and hatred, go poorly together. When it is claimed of her **that she was wounded by Hercules**, we find the secret interpretation therein: that the Spirit of God is hindered in His works by militant, worldly men; which is why we are emphatically accustomed to sing:

> **There is great misery and danger where pestilence reigns, but it is truly much greater where war is waged; there, what is right and laudable is despised and ignored. There, no one asks for decency, for discipline, or for judgment; your Word also lies neglected at such a time and does not prevail.**

The many nymphs who are assigned to her service are the many gifts through which the Holy Spirit reveals His power and glory. This same thing is partially indicated by the **peacock attributed to her, which has feathers of many colors, but is yet ugly at its feet;** the latter of which is meant to signify that the gifts of the Holy Spirit on earth are unregarded and "ugly" in the eyes of men. The pride which is noted in the attribution of this bird may not inappropriately be interpreted as the elevation of the spirit toward God and heavenly things. It is especially to be noted **that it was the custom to build Juno's temples without a door or roof**, to indicate that the Holy Spirit does not have His temple in temples made with hands, but has His dwelling everywhere He wills, and works without hindrance wherever it pleases Him.

§. 32. The reader may now judge for themselves whether our explanation holds together or not. It is certain that scholars have noticed for a long time that the Pagans did not believe as absurdly as they wrote; for which reason they sought the secret meaning in nature. Now, some might say that in such a way, one could make anything out of it, in that what we apply to God, others have **applied** to the **creature** <note>original: "Creatur," meaning the created world or natural things as opposed to the Creator</note>. However, without mentioning how one often cannot find a way out when explaining nature, I only remind you of this: that the objection does not affect us, but rather confirms our opinion. For we have often appealed to the harmony between nature and God; if we now find that many things in these fables which refer to God can also be **applied** to natural things, it certainly serves as a testimony for us. It may meanwhile certainly be true that many among the Pagans of later times hit upon the thought that all such fables were intended to be riddles of nature, because they found that some things could be interpreted quite well in that way; for indeed, even today, the **naturalists** and **atheists** do the same, who for all their imagined cleverness are not so clever as to consider: even if animals have all the **structure** and limbs that one finds in humans, it remains true that an animal is not a human. If the immoral world applies the pronouncements of Scripture regarding the love of God to unchaste love, this cannot result in a disadvantage for the Scripture or the love of God among the sensible. Added to this is the fact that in their fleshly minds they have created many **scruples** <note>original: "Scrupel," meaning doubts or philosophical difficulties</note> and then undertook to resolve them according to such a mindset, from which finally nothing other than such **confusion** could arise. Meanwhile, one will surely see that the first inventors had their intention directed toward the Divine Being; but they had to speak more absurdly of Him the less true knowledge they had of Him, and they had to borrow everything from others who had already smeared it with their filth. Therefore, there is no lack among scholars of those who have sought God and spiritual things therein; even if they perhaps did not do it in the same way as we have endeavored to do in this piece. We also know that such testimony is not needed where one is illuminated by the bright light of divine revelation. The sole cause of this investigation is the sophistry <term>Spitzfündigkeit: overly subtle or deceptive reasoning</term> of the adversaries, who constantly boast that the doctrine of the Holy Trinity is so entirely against all reason—which, however, given these circumstances, does not seem to be true. May God strengthen our faith; that is the foremost thing, indeed, everything in everything.

## CHAPTER III.

### The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity is proven from Holy Scripture and from the Testimony of Christians.

### §. 1.

When Reason <term>Vernunfft; here referring to human logic unaided by divine grace</term>, as it stands in its corruption, has sufficiently exercised itself and has, as much as in it lies, twisted and perverted the clear letter of Holy Scripture, it then wishes to appear perfectly wise and not give the impression that it contradicts Scripture. Not only that, but it even demands scriptural passages for itself, insisting that one must prove with clear and exactly as many measured words that there is a Trinity, that the Son is of the same essence as the Father, and whatever else there may be. Certainly, the Socinians <note>A non-trinitarian movement following the teachings of Fausto Sozzini, which emphasized the use of reason in biblical interpretation.</note>, with whom we are dealing here, are true masters of this, as was proven not long ago by the anonymous author who attacked the sermons of the late Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), a leading figure in German Pietism.</note>, which can be read in his book *On the Divinity of Christ* <note>original: *von der Gottheit Christi*</note>, page 9. Whoever reads the writings of these people cannot notice without annoyance how cruelly they torture and pull at those passages which ascribe to Christ the Creation, the leading of the children of Israel out of Egypt, and the fact that He existed before He was born as a man, and more of the like; how cruelly, I say, they torment and pull at such passages. If one asks them: who gives you the power to make such forced and incomprehensible interpretations? they know no other cause than this: that otherwise it would be against Reason, and therefore it must necessarily be interpreted in such a way. This is now not only supposed to be a sufficient answer; but as if everything were well settled and they were abundantly in the right, they say: "Prove with clear words of Scripture that God is one in essence and three in persons." If one then ignores their mockery (which some among them use instead of proof) and shows them such places in Holy Scripture from which that which they want proven with explicit words *necessarily follows*, they are quickly ready with an answer, saying it is "rationalizing" <note>original: *Vernünffteley*; a derogatory term for human logic used to dismiss theological deductions.</note> and that one must stay with God’s Word—just as if they alone (not to mention other things) were the innocent people who did not cloud God’s Word with any human inventions.

[is] distinct from that of which she speaks. But if she is to be regarded as a **self-subsistent person** <term>selbstständige Person</term> <note>A "self-subsistent person" refers to a distinct individual existence or "hypostasis" within the Trinity, possessing its own will and action, rather than being a mere quality like "kindness" or "intelligence."</note>, then she is in no way a mere attribute. This, however, is clear as day from the following verse 23:

Here I now ask the sincere reader whether an attribute can be presented in such a way that it says of itself:
> **I have been established:**

Can human understanding say of itself: "I have been established by my human"? Or can Wisdom, as an attribute of God, say of God that she was established by Him? Would that not be just as much as saying: "God is established by God"? Therefore, it remains certain that it cannot possibly be understood as a divine attribute. But if this is not the case, then the Wisdom speaking here must be a **self-subsistent person**, who is as certainly distinguished from God in a divine manner as one who is established is distinguished from the one who establishes him. 

If we pay close attention, Wisdom names herself in the very word she speaks of herself as the Son of God, the Messiah, and the Savior of the world. For just as the heavenly Father says of His Son in Psalm 2:6:
> **I have established my King,**

and thereby makes a personal distinction between Himself and His Son; so also here does heavenly Wisdom, as the Son of God, make a real and personal distinction between himself, who is established, and the one who has established him. 

Indeed, it is to be noted that this same word in Hebrew signifies an **anointing** <note>The author is discussing the Hebrew word *nassak* (נסך) in Proverbs 8:23, which can be translated as "set up" or "poured out/anointed." This links Wisdom directly to the title "Messiah," which literally means "The Anointed One."</note>; and that just as it is rendered in the other Psalm:
> **I have anointed my King,**

it must also be rendered here:
> **I have been anointed;**

with which the office of the Messiah is explicitly presented. However, it was not poorly rendered by Luther <note>Martin Luther, whose German translation of the Bible was the standard for the author’s audience.</note>:
> **I have been established;**

for through anointing, people were established as kings, priests, and prophets. This is also why the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament often used by early Christians.</note> rendered it:
> **He has founded me.**

Should one ask how the Son of God, according to His divine nature, could be anointed or established? The answer is that such occurred through His **eternal birth**; as this eternity is recalled here with three emphatic words. In which birth He comes forth from His heavenly Father so that He may order, appoint, and accomplish everything, as He says of Himself here. Thus it is certain from this that here the Son of God, the Messiah and Savior of the world, is to be understood; who, therefore, is also necessarily a self-subsistent person—as no one denies regarding the Messiah—and not a mere divine attribute.

# Holy Scripture and from the Testimony of Christians.

It is very easy to see what motivates the modern Jews and the Socinians <note>A non-Trinitarian movement that emerged during the Reformation, which denied the pre-existence and essential divinity of Christ.</note> to insist that this Psalm refers simply to *David* and should only be *applied* <note>original: "appliciren" (Latin)</note> to *Christ*. They did this so that, if such a point were granted, they could conclude that the title of a "Son of God" makes the *Messiah* a true, essential God no more than it made *David* one. However, even if one were willing to grant them this, their conclusion would not even be correct, as we will perhaps take the opportunity to prove below; furthermore, what they *claim* <note>original: "prætendiren" (Latin)</note> is contrary to all evidence. Regarding this, we must first—along with others who have dealt with this matter—insist that we must take the word "Son" in its proper, literal sense, as it signifies one who is begotten from the essence of his father. The adversaries do indeed bring forward reasons, but we shall see in the proper place that these are not reasons at all, but empty pretexts. Added to this is the fact that the Holy Spirit explains Himself and indicates that He means a real and essential Son when He speaks: **I have begotten thee.** One easily sees that the added words: **Today I have begotten thee,** are not included without reason, and are intended to be an explanation of the Son—namely, what kind of Son he is; so that one is to understand the *pronoun* <note>original: "Pronomen" (Latin)</note> <term>ani (Hebrew: אני), meaning "I"</term> within it: **Thou art my Son, whom I have begotten today.** These explanatory words immediately give the impression to the mind that the discussion is not about a merely adopted son. But if he is not a merely adopted son, then he is necessarily a properly begotten Son, as it says: **I have begotten thee.** Here, everyone immediately hears that God expressly says He has begotten him; and begetting is in itself nothing other than the communication of essence. To accomplish this more appropriately, we will first demonstrate that the promise refers primarily and perfectly to Jesus Christ; then it shall be shown how it is to be understood that the promise is also applied to Solomon.

The first point is to be proven with various reasons. First, the preceding context shows us expressly that the promise should not be understood as referring to a physical temple. For when David intended to honor God especially by building Him a house of cedar, God was indeed pleased with his good intention; but He simultaneously pointed out to him through the prophet Nathan that David was not the one suited to build Him such a house in which He would actually take delight. The reason was that God was not concerned with a house of cedar; as He had demonstrated since the time of the Judges, when He had never desired such a thing from them, but had been content with the Tabernacle <note>The "Hütte" or Tabernacle was the portable tent-shrine used by the Israelites before the construction of the Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, which was established not so much for His sake as for the sake of the undiscerning people. Therefore, it says in verses 5 and following:

that is: Do you think that you, as a miserable human being—though you are indeed a king—could build a house for me to dwell in? The Lord has torn ten tribes from you and left you only two; and this was likewise prophesied under the image of a torn cloak. <note>A reference to 1 Kings 11:30–31, where the prophet Ahijah tears his new cloak into twelve pieces to symbolize the division of Solomon's kingdom.</note> Even if *Solomon* <note>original: "Salomo"</note> was not completely rejected, this happened only as a prefigurement <term>Fürbilde</term> <note>A "prefigurement" or "type" is a historical person or event in the Bible seen as a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ.</note> of the *Messiah* <note>original: "Messia"</note>, so that He would not be rejected; but insofar as Solomon fell from the mercy of God, he had to serve as a sign that the "Son of David" <note>A messianic title.</note> was not yet present. §. 13. Therefore, nothing remains but for us to examine why these words are still interpreted as referring to Solomon? To be sure, Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a prominent Lutheran theologian known for defending orthodox doctrine.</note> said, not without cause, that the passages where it seemed this promise was assigned to *Solomon* were not identical to this passage, but rather indicated a special promise made specifically to *Solomon*. For many circumstances are recounted there which are omitted here; likewise, much is said here that is omitted there. One finds in both nothing more than a similarity, which must necessarily exist because *Solomon* is a prefigurement of the *Messiah*. For where do we find the words that David cites on both occasions when he speaks of it in 1 Chronicles 22:8 and 28:3: **You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed much blood**? Rather, in this promise <note>Referring to the primary messianic prophecy in 2 Samuel 7.</note> a completely different reason is given, as we heard above. Where in our promise do we find the name *Solomon* or his description as in 1 Chronicles 22:9? Where does the condition stand: **If he will be steadfast in doing...**? Where is it written what *Solomon* himself says at the dedication of the Temple in 1 Kings 8:18: **That you had it in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart**? Indeed, something like this is hidden within it, but if we look at it only superficially, we also notice the opposite in express words, namely: you have acted foolishly in thinking that I would be served by a house of cedar. Thus we see a great disparity; but the similarity must necessarily be there, as in a prefigurement. Indeed, the Holy Spirit is natural to God, for he is one God; but it is foolishness to draw one's own conclusions about God when one does not know what is in God. Is it not a presumption to make a comparison between God and man, especially regarding the spirit, when one knows neither the Spirit of God nor the spirit of man? Is it not a miserable conclusion to assert—simply because Scripture makes a comparison between the Spirit of God and that of man—that the Spirit of God is in God in the same way the spirit of man is in man? Does any comparison imply a total equality? Or is God a man? Yet the adversaries admit with such testimony that the Holy Spirit is the true God, because he must be (according to the comparison they have set up, with which we do not agree) a part of Him, as it were. For just as the spirit of man is the true man, so also the Spirit of God is the true God. For just as it was stated before: The Spirit of God is compared with the spirit of man, therefore he must naturally be in God, just as the spirit of man is naturally in man; so it must now also be said: To the Spirit of God are attributed such personal qualities that cannot be attributed to the spirit of man; therefore, this distinction must be found in the Spirit of God as compared to the spirit of man: that the former is to be seen as a divine person, while the latter is seen as a part of man. Thus have our opponents given us the opportunity to present the truth using their own logic; for this is what we desire and what Holy Scripture teaches us.

Nothing can be rightfully objected against this based on the truth, even though the adversaries would very much like to. As for the general objections, a separate chapter will follow below; but as for the specific objections they make from certain verses to prove that the Holy Spirit is not a person, the mere recounting of them can serve instead of a refutation. Does it not follow rather that he is a person? Since it is said of him that he bears witness, which properly belongs to no one else but a person. Does not this conclusion follow: because the Holy Spirit is compared with persons, he is likewise a person in a divine manner? Our opponents cannot reject such a conclusion, as we have cited similar ones from them in this very paragraph. However, if we take their other cited verses, namely 1 John 4:13 and John 3:34, we find that they seek the strength of their proof in the word *Giving*, from which they conclude that the Holy Spirit cannot be given if he is a person.

# Holy Scripture and from the Testimony of Christians.

...might fall. We have proven that the Father is <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The sacred Hebrew name for God, often translated as "the LORD."</note>, the Son is Jehovah, and that the Holy Spirit is Jehovah; here one might think: Are there then three Jehovahs? Scripture indeed speaks only of one Jehovah, and in the cited passage, mention is likewise only made of the Lord along with his Word and Spirit? To which it serves as an answer: that there is only one Jehovah—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But just as the three are one essence, so they also have one name: and just as they are not separated in their essence by their personal distinction, so they are also not divided from one another by sharing in one name. We can take an analogy for this from man, who can be considered as a man either according to the soul or according to the body, yet there are not two men, but one man. For example, when one speaks of the diseases of the body, one says of the whole man that a man is subject to many weaknesses; likewise, in view of the passions of the soul, one can say that a man is surrounded by much misery. Thus the name of "man" belongs to the soul as well as to the body, and yet they are not two, but one man. If we take this analogy as far as it can apply here, we find that it fits the present matter very well.

Consequently, must it not follow that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit stand in an undivided Trinity, or are the one true GOD? Truly, if one wishes to engage in speech and opinion with opponents, one must say that Christ and his Apostles have placed many stumbling blocks before us by using words that—in their own natural sense, obvious to everyone—necessarily create a different concept than the one they <note>The opponents/Socinians</note> wish to have understood. But the best part is that other people also have their own Reason, according to which they know how to judge the meaning of words. Indeed, it is even better that **God** himself strengthens his own people in this mystery, and allows the contradiction of the opponents to serve them toward a wholesome purification and strengthening in the truth. 

Just as they, through this very saying of the Apostle Paul and through insight into divine love, clearly perceive that this Son must be the same <note>of the same essence as the Father</note>, even if he were not already called "his own." For what kind of prize of divine love would it be if He had taken one out from the midst of men and let him suffer for his brothers? One might certainly say that **God's** mercy is to be praised for wanting to forgive men their sins; but in doing so, one would have to consider the entire work of <term>Redemption<note>The theological concept of humanity being "bought back" from sin through Christ's sacrifice.</note></term> a mere child’s play, or else leave the honor to the human race that they became blessed through merit and not through grace. 

For in one man <note>Adam</note> they all died through transgression, even if they did not sin with the same sin; what wonder would it be then that they all lived through one man in righteousness, even if they had not fulfilled that very same righteousness? Or should **God** be unjust, that He would indeed impose sin upon them generally as their own property, but want to seize their righteousness for Himself? Far be it! 

But when **God** let his own Son come into our poor flesh and blood and suffer therein, then one can comprehend what Paul means when he says: **He who also did not spare his own Son.** In the <term>Socinian understanding<note>Followers of Socinianism, a rationalist movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing Him as a human prophet who was granted divinity after his resurrection.</note></term>, he would have had to say: "He who also did not spare humanity itself, but took one from their midst and let him be so terribly martyred, so that He might gradually draw the others after him and deliver them to death." Regarding the Holy Spirit, we have already heard previously that he is presented as distinct from the Father, insofar as it is clear that the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove as a self-subsisting, perfect Being <term>Being: "Wesen," referring to a complete, autonomous existence or substance</term>, while the Father's voice was distinct in itself from the dove. From this, however, it follows that the Holy Spirit is true God, namely because he is God's Spirit, as we have already concluded before. Indeed, because we have irrefutably proven that the Son of God is the true and essential God, we recognize from the descent of the Spirit upon the Son of God that the Spirit is true God; for in God there is nothing but himself. Just as we also see, conversely, from that same descent of the Spirit upon Jesus, that he did not receive the Spirit by measure <note>A reference to John 3:34: "For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure."</note>, but that he came upon him fully and personally; from which it follows that Jesus Christ is the true God, because no creature is capable of [containing] the infinite Spirit of God. Thus the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is also God, and yet they are not three separate gods, but one God. If the Holy Spirit is then a person, then he is a divine person and God himself, because he is God's Spirit, and as the **Socinians** <term>Socinians: A non-trinitarian movement that denied the full divinity of Christ and the personality of the Holy Spirit, viewing the Spirit instead as an impersonal power of God.</term> say, is intrinsic to God (1 Corinthians 2:11). Furthermore, we rightly conclude that the proof of the divinity of these persons flows from the work assigned to them, and this is because baptism or **rebirth** <term>rebirth: Known in theology as regeneration, the spiritual act of being "born again" into a new life in Christ.</term> is a new creation, which belongs to no one but God. Therefore, it is folly to object that the Israelites were also "baptized into Moses," yet it does not follow that he was God. For they were not baptized for rebirth, but for a physical **polity** <term>polity: The civil, social, and legal administration of the Hebrew nation under the Mosaic Law.</term>; and to that extent, Moses was indeed their God <note>original: "Moſes allerdings ihr GOtt." A reference to Exodus 7:1, where God tells Moses he has made him as a "god" to Pharaoh, signifying his role as a divine representative with ultimate authority.</note>. However high and noble Moses was, his law could not bring life, because he was only a human being. And this very thing serves as an irrefutable testimony that no man, however great and noble he may be, can carry out the work of rebirth and redemption.

Therefore, we conclude with certainty: In whose name one is to be baptized for rebirth, that same one must be God. One is to be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; therefore, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be God. This conclusion can be called into doubt all the less, the more one believes of the Father that he is the true God. For one rightly concludes in this place that the Son and Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, because they are placed at his side as his equals in one and the same matter. Indeed, Moses is certainly also placed at God's side; but the difference is obvious. Where has one read that Moses was placed between the Father and the Holy Spirit?

It is certain, however, that the Spirit himself is God, because he is God's Spirit. Indeed, if we are to speak of it in a human way, the Spirit is, as it were, the noblest part of God, just as the spirit of man is likewise his noblest part. To be sure, one might ask: if he were the noblest part, why would he be placed last? However, because we believe in one God, one can easily reason that we recognize no other precedence in God than the precedence of order; and since the Spirit is the innermost, he is therefore placed last in the order, just as one also [arranges] <note>The catchword "nen" at the bottom of the page completes the word "ord-nen" (to arrange/to order) on the following page.</note> the parts of man...

### Holy Scripture and the Testimony of Christians

...but rather that of others who are completely beyond suspicion. Although we must certainly remind ourselves beforehand / that the constant propagation of this doctrine / not only under the Papacy / but also at the time of the Reformation, is the most glorious testimony / which can be given to it according to the Scriptures. For / if one were to object / that the propagation of this doctrine over such long periods could give it no special advantage / because in those previous dark times many other untruths had likewise been propagated; then that is and remains a mere pretext. 

This doctrine has an entirely different status / than other doctrines / which may indeed be stained with impurity / but have been preserved in great purity by the children of God; whereas this doctrine has at all times been acknowledged by the most holy and pious / as well as by the wicked. Indeed, many among the pious have written about this mystery from experience / or rather from the most certain conviction, and have presented it powerfully. 

Furthermore, it is well to note / that / since there has always been bickering and strife among the manifold parties, this doctrine has nevertheless remained untouched. The Greeks <note>The author refers here to the Eastern Orthodox Church.</note> immersed themselves in the contradiction regarding the proceeding of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son <note>This refers to the "Filioque" controversy, a major cause of the Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity.</note> to such an extent / that it, alongside other things / resulted in an eternal hatred between them and the Latins <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note>: Yet nonetheless, the doctrine of the Holy Trinity remained an eternal truth among them. 

There were otherwise so many sects and heretics / who made no conscience of bringing quite absurd things onto the scene; yet in this point they remained constant. The opponents, on the contrary, had no peace among themselves / and contradict one another to this very day: And even though the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> had such great power / that they even persecuted others / they were nevertheless so scattered with their doctrine through divine providence / that nothing was heard of them until the times of the Reformation.

So it stands now until this very day / that the entire Christian world [holds] the Holy Trinity—

> When I (says Mr. Sanson, p. 239 and following), concerning matters involving our affairs, visited a Persian lord named **Reza Kouli Begue**, a **Dervish** <note>A member of a Muslim religious order, often associated with asceticism and philosophy.</note> was present—a man of good understanding and a skilled **philosopher**, well-versed in the **Holy Scripture**—who led the conversation toward matters of religion. He began with great praise for the Christian religion, saying that he recognized it to be very much in accordance with reason, except for the doctrine of the divinity of Jesus Christ. I said to him: "It is true that we believe in the divinity of Jesus Christ; this point is the foundation of our religion; and (which causes me wonder) you yourselves say as much in your **Quran** <note>original: *Alcoran*.</note>, and yet you do not believe it. For in good faith, what does ***Rohu Allah*** <note>Arabic: *Rūḥ Allāh*, literally "Spirit of God." In Islamic theology, this is a title specifically given to Jesus (Isa).</note> mean, which is the name Muhammad gives to Christ Jesus?" He answered me: "This Arabic word (for I have studied the Arabic language from its foundations) means **the Spirit, or the Soul of God.**" To which I replied: "This Spirit, or this Soul of God—is it distinct from God, or is it one with God?" He answered: "The Soul and the Spirit of God cannot be distinguished from God." "Well then," I added, "thus Jesus Christ is God; for what is one with God, that is God." He seemed moved by the logic of this. I praised his sincerity in being willing to give me the true meaning of the word ***Rohu Allah***, and said to him: "I do not find the same sincerity among other Muhammadans; they give these words an entirely different meaning in order to mock the conclusion I draw from them." **Reza Kouli Begue** continued the discourse and said: "As many as we are, we recognize Jesus Christ as a divine man and have a great esteem for him, whereas you Christians have nothing but contempt for Muhammad." # CHAPTER IV.

## That the Messiah Jesus must be the eternal Son of God is reasonably concluded from the work of Redemption; likewise from the fact that he sent the Holy Spirit as his Spirit and poured it out upon his own.

->§. I.<-

Thus far, we have dealt with the Holy Trinity in general; henceforth, we shall only be concerned with demonstrating the eternal divinity of the Son, Jesus Christ, from which the doctrine of the Holy Trinity follows of its own accord. We wish to begin this proof with the work of Redemption <term>Redemption: The theological concept of humanity being "bought back" or saved from sin by Christ</term>, which properly belongs to him. This work, if we possess understanding and faith, convinces us in and of itself that Jesus Christ must be true God. For since the Holy Scripture tells us everywhere that the work of Creation is God’s own work, in which creatures have no part—and even our adversaries <note>Likely referring to Socinians or other groups who denied the divinity of Christ during the Enlightenment.</note> agree with us on this point—we must conclude most reasonably that the work of Redemption is also God's work, provided we know what Redemption is. I say even more: we must reasonably judge that the very same Creator is also the Redeemer. It is necessary, however, that we clearly show that Redemption is a true and actual new Creation, so that everyone may more easily conclude that the Redeemer is as truly God because of the Redemption as the Creator is because of the Creation; indeed, that the Creator is also the Redeemer, who brings his corrupted creature once again...

Admittedly, our opponents—who always lack *arguments* <note>original: *Argumentis*</note> but never lack for words and contradictions—pretend that it is only called a new creation through some similarity, and that in itself it does not *signify* <note>original: *importire*</note> as much.
