§. 3. Those who understand the **mystery of wickedness** <note>original: *Geheimniß der Boßheit*; likely a reference to the "mystery of iniquity" from 2 Thessalonians 2:7, referring to the spiritual state of fallen humanity</note> will not find it at all necessary for one to set the importance of Redemption before their eyes; for they will understand of their own accord that the awakening from death into life requires just as much a **creative power** <note>original: *Schöpffungs-Krafft*</note> as the simple bringing forth into life. To strengthen this with an example and **analogy** <note>original: *Gleichniß*</note>: it is indeed obvious to all the world that a father can certainly beget a child from his own essence, but he cannot awaken it back to life from death.

All creatures bring forth their own kind daily in indescribable numbers into the light; but if something is to be brought forth again from death, then an extraordinary divine power must be added to it, such as was present in the prophets and apostles through the Spirit of **JESUS**. Even the sun, which brings forth an innumerable multitude of **vermin** <note>original: *Gewürmer*; this refers to the early modern belief in spontaneous generation, where the sun's heat was thought to generate insects or worms from the earth</note> with its rays, can bring none of them back from death. It adorns the **earth** <note>original: *Erdkreiß*; literally "the circle of the earth"</note> with countless beautiful flowers and herbs, but once one is cut down or otherwise died away, the sun cannot plant it back into life. From this it clearly appears that the awakening from death into life not only requires just as much power as the first creation of life, but even a greater one. Now it follows that—since humanity and everything else had perished in total death, and were to be awakened not only to life but *out of* death—the Redemption must be, if not a greater, then certainly just as great a work as the Creation was.

But I must fear that someone who does not yet fully see the power and consequence of this argument will raise the objection that the prophets also raised the dead, and that, just as **GOD** did such through them, He also did it through **JESUS** in a greater measure. However, just as this objection can be made by no one other than he who is blind and inexperienced in the **mystery of restoration** <note>original: *Herwiederbringung*; often used in this period to refer to the "restitution of all things" or *apocatastasis*</note>, so it is also easily answered. The prophets who awakened people from death can well be compared with the fathers who beget children, but not with **Christ** in this regard. I may also conclude thus: fathers awaken children to life from that which is not seen, and yet they are not **GOD** for that reason; therefore, even if the heavenly Father created the world, He is not **GOD** for that reason. The same situation applies to **Christ** and his servants. Now, it is well known that the potter prepares his vessel from the clay with easy effort, turning and shaping it according to his pleasure as long as he still has it in his hands and has not yet brought it to its firm and permanent state through the power of fire. at one point it says in **Psalm 69** <note>Original: *Ps. 69.*</note> expressly: **I must pay what I have not robbed.** <note>Psalm 69:4. In this context, the author uses the verse to explain that Christ paid a debt (the desire for equality with God) that He Himself did not owe, but which Adam incurred.</note> That this Psalm refers to Christ is proven by the New Testament, which cites it more than once as a prophecy of Christ. Because Adam’s robbery actually consisted in this—that he wanted to be equal to God—Christ had to pay for this. Just as Adam wanted to steal what he did not have, so Christ had to give away what He *did* have in order to pay for that robbery. From this it follows that Christ was as truly God as Adam was not; this is so convincing that I do not see what anyone would want to object against it. The Apostle Paul refers evidently to this in the cited passage of **Philippians 2** <note>Original: *Phil. 2.*</note> when he says of Christ: **He did not consider it a robbery to be equal to GOD.** With this he means to say that the second Adam, Christ, did not act like the first—who thought he must obtain it through a robbery if he wanted to be like God—but rather viewed it as a gift and present of God’s love that God received humanity into the Godhead. Whereupon he continues and shows that **he emptied himself** <note>original: *er sich selbst entäufert habe*. This refers to "Kenosis," the theological concept of Christ voluntarily setting aside His divine glory to become human.</note>—namely, of that divine equality; which he had to do if he wished to pay for what was stolen. Thus, Christ emptied himself, not of his humanity, nor of his humanity filled with divine power (which he allowed to shine through in his deeds and words); rather, he emptied himself of his divinity. That is: **he, as true man and God, while he was in human likeness, surrendered his divinity to God as a payment for what Adam had stolen, for the sake of reconciliation;** and from then on, he sought that same divinity as a grace and gift which he otherwise possessed as his own property: for which reason God also gave it all back to him and glorified him through suffering and death. This is to be well noted and considered with all diligence, as it provides not only the key to the whole mystery, but also counters many confusions created by blind reason. For when one reads that God gave glory to the Lord Christ for all his suffering, as in **Isaiah 53** <note>Original: *Esai LIII.*</note> and other places, one might conclude that since God only gave it to the Lord Christ after his suffering, he must not have possessed it before; however, this objection disappears once this mystery is explained.

### That the Messiah Jesus must be the eternal Son of God

§. 9. To better understand the matter, we will strive to explain it through a **parable** <term>Gleichniß: an illustrative story used to teach a spiritual or moral lesson</term>. I will therefore propose a case: imagine a distinguished **minister** at a Royal court who had so wronged the King by seeking after his realm and crown that the King became enraged. He condemned him to eternal imprisonment and promised no redemption for him or his descendants, unless he could give a whole kingdom as a **ransom** <note>original: "Ranzion"</note>. 

But it further happened that the **Royal Hereditary Prince**, who was to receive the kingdom after his father, had such mercy on this imprisoned minister that he took his place in the prison and took it upon himself to pay what the other had committed. See, then this Prince who placed himself in prison would be in the place of the wrongdoer who wanted to rob the King of the crown—even though the Prince himself had not robbed it—and yet he would also be the actual Royal Heir. He therefore said to his father, as the King: 

> "Here I sit in the place of your prisoner, and I will pay you for what I have not robbed. You desire a kingdom? Very well! Your own realm, which I should have by right of my **first-birth**, and which I have not lost through any fault, I give over to your will; so that I, as heir, will have no further claim to it, but you yourself shall give it to whomever you please. If you desire anything more from your prisoner, then take me, and do with me as you please."

The Father then gave way to his righteous anger, actually took the kingdom from his son, and tormented him to the extreme danger of death; but finally, he reflected and was moved by the example of his son's mercy, so that he not only granted him his life but also returned to him the hereditary right of the kingdom, and loved him now more than ever before. 

This **parable** is such that it can perfectly explain the nature of the mystery of **Jesus Christ** as the **Redeemer** of the human race. For **Adam** was that same Royal Minister who had so wronged the King of Heaven that he, with all he possessed, could not be redeemed from prison unless he paid back what he had robbed. But that cost too much; therefore, it had to remain unpaid eternally. But then the **Son of the Father** had mercy and placed himself in Adam's stead. Not indeed against the Father's will, but rather with His will; for such was the **good pleasure of God** <note>original: "Wohlgefallen GOttes," referring to the divine will or satisfaction</note>, which we can understand well through God's enlightenment, but not so briefly

# That the Messiah Jesus Must Be the Eternal Son of God

certainly, redemption is God’s work, and He Himself performed it through the man Jesus; thus, we can accept these words in a healthy sense and allow them to stand. But if it is intended to mean that Christ was a mere instrument, like Moses and other men of God—even if to a higher degree and in some closer union—then it is false, and is clearly refuted by what has been cited. For the one God, who has rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of His dear Son, is Himself the **Redeemer of Israel** <note>original Latin: "Goël Israelis"</note>, Isaiah 49:7. Now, if He Himself is the **Avenger of Blood** <note>original German: "Blut-Rächer," referring to the legal right of a relative to claim justice</note>, then He is also Himself the **Kinsman** <note>original German: "Blut-Freund," literally "Blood-Friend"; the relative obligated by law to rescue a family member</note>, and has revealed Himself in the flesh. To be sure, one will ask: Did the Father then become man? I answer, no; but, in that the Word became flesh, He is not excluded from it in such a way that He should be separated from the Word; for the Persons [of the Trinity] are inseparable. Therefore, it is said of Christ Jesus in Colossians 2:9: **that in Him dwells the whole fullness of the Godhead bodily;** which fullness we understand as the Father, Word, and Spirit. For just as in Ephesians 1:23 the word **fullness** <note>original Greek: "πλήρωμα" (pleroma)</note> is taken in such a way that it indicates a multiplicity gathered into one—in that the congregation of Christ is called His body, His fullness—so also here the word "fullness" must be understood as a multiplicity found within the one Godhead. And this is all the more so because it says **all** <note>original Greek: "πᾶν" (pan)</note> fullness. For otherwise, each Person has His own fullness; for example, the Holy Spirit has His fullness as if for Himself, in that He can distribute Himself here and there in various divided gifts, while retaining His fullness for Himself. Likewise, in the Father are various powers which show themselves in His different servants according to His own pleasing distinction; but the fullness of His powers remains in Himself and cannot dwell in any human. But now, in Christ, the fullness dwells; from which it follows, first of all, that He must be God, because otherwise He would not be capable of containing any Divine fullness. There also dwells in Him the whole fullness of the Godhead—namely, of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit—and this by virtue of the inseparable unity which these Persons have in their essence, from which His eternal divinity is fully seen. Therefore, although strictly speaking the Word became flesh and thereby gave Himself as our **Kinsman-Redeemer** <note>original: "Goël"</note>, the Father and Spirit are not separated. Therefore, it is also spoken of as being from the whole...

# That the Messiah Jesus must be the eternal Son of God

...fact, that the Holy Spirit remains all the more unknown to people the less they are willing to allow Him to dwell within their souls. Therefore, mindful of our own weakness, we cannot expect anything other than that we will not be able to carry out this subject with the dignity it deserves. However, we wish to turn to it in humility and attempt what may be useful in a human way to prove the doctrine we intend to present. 

First, we must necessarily point out what no one will deny: that the Holy Spirit is God's Spirit. If anyone, being convinced by what has come before, wishes to accept as truth that the Spirit of God is true God and a distinct Person, so much the better. Yet we do not need to rely on that point here; instead, we shall assume it now along with our adversaries as a known fact: that the Holy Spirit is natural to God and therefore not a created being. <note>The author is arguing that if the Holy Spirit is "natural" to God (part of God's own essence), then only God can "send" Him.</note>

Based on this, we conclude as follows: **Whoever sends the Holy Spirit is God; Jesus Christ sends Him; therefore He is God.** 

That Christ sends the Holy Spirit, no one denies; therefore, we only need to prove that it follows from this that He is true God. Now, I would think that everyone could grasp and feel within themselves that no one can send the spirit that is natural to them except themselves. (For the sake of clarity, I must take the word "send" in a figurative sense here.) Just as no one can send the spirit of a man except the man himself in whom the spirit resides, so even less can anyone send the Spirit of God except God Himself, in whom He resides. This is so clear that I do not know if anyone would have an objection to it. 

But if this cannot be denied, I conclude further: **No one sends the Holy Spirit except God; therefore, he who sends the Holy Spirit must be God.** 

Since this also cannot be denied by virtue of the first point, it must indeed be the truth that **Christ, because He sends the Holy Spirit, is true God.** 

What will one say to this? Perhaps that God alone, and no one else, can send the Holy Spirit, but that God sends His Spirit upon Christ, and through Christ upon His members. <note>The "members" refers to the "Members of the Body of Christ," a common Christian metaphor for the believers or the Church.</note> I answer: yes, that is true; but Christ sends the Holy Spirit as *His* Spirit, and the Spirit of the Father is also the Spirit of the Son. Thus we find that the Spirit of the Father, whom Christ promises to His own in John 15:26, is called the Spirit of the Son,

The former belongs to God and Christ, but the latter belongs to the believers and the children of God.

# 214 That the Messiah Jesus must be the eternal Son of God

It is a fact that the Holy Spirit remains so much the more unknown to people as they are less willing to allow Him to dwell within their souls. Therefore, we ourselves, in remembrance of our own weakness, can expect nothing else than that we will not be able to carry out this matter with the dignity it deserves. However, we wish to turn to it in humility and attempt what may be useful in a human way to prove the doctrine we have set before us. First, we must necessarily remind everyone of this—which no one will deny—that the Holy Spirit is **God’s** Spirit; if anyone, having been convinced by what preceded, wishes to accept as a truth that the Spirit of **God** is the true **God** and a self-subsisting person <note>original: "selbständige Person" — an early theological term for "hypostasis" or a distinct "person" within the Trinity</note>, then so much the better. However, we do not need that at this point; rather, we accept it now with our adversaries as a known matter that the Holy Spirit is natural to **God** <note>original: "in GOtt natürlich" — meaning the Spirit is inherent to God's essential nature and not a created being outside of Him</note> and is thus no creature. Upon this, we conclude as follows:

->**Whoever sends the Holy Spirit is God;**<-
->**Jesus sends Him; therefore He is God.**<-

That **Christ** sends the Holy Spirit is denied by no one; therefore, we must only prove that it follows from this that He is the true **God**. Now, I should think that everyone could grasp and feel within themselves that no one can send the spirit that is natural to them except themselves; (I must here, for the sake of clarity, take the word "send" in a figurative sense). Just as no one can send the spirit of a man except the man himself in whom that spirit resides, so even less can anyone send the Spirit of **God** except **God** Himself, in whom He is. This is so clear that I do not know if anyone would have anything to object against it. But if one cannot deny this, then I conclude further: **No one sends the Holy Spirit but God; therefore, he must be God who sends the Holy Spirit.** Since one cannot deny this either, by virtue of the former premise, it must indeed be the truth that **Christ, because He sends the Holy Spirit, is true God.** What will one say to this? Perhaps this: that **God** indeed sends the Holy Spirit Himself, and no one else can; but **God** sends His Spirit over **Christ**, and through **Christ** over His members. I answer: yes, that is true; but **Christ** sends the Holy Spirit as His own Spirit, and the Father’s Spirit is also the Son’s Spirit, just as we find that the Spirit of the Father—whom **Christ** promises to His own in John 15:26—is called the Spirit of the Son.

The <term>LXX</term> <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> saw clearly that God spoke of himself—that he should be pierced; but because they considered that it would create a strange impression of God in the hearts of the nations if they should read that God would be pierced, they preferred to do violence to the word and give it a metaphorical sense, as if it meant **to revile**, **to insult**, or **to mock and annoy someone to their face.** However, just as one cannot simply say they had no other concept of the word even if they translated it thus, the word cannot lose its true meaning just because they twisted it.

# That Jesus Christ is true God is rationally [demonstrated]

[it must] remain [established] / that if **GOD’s** Son is truly **GOD’s** Son / he must as Son be equal to his Father in essence.

When we consider further in this matter / that the Arians <note>Arians were followers of Arius (c. 250–336 AD), who taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than eternally divine.</note> not only admit / that the Son of **GOD** existed before his human birth / but also confess / that he created the world / as the **Word of the Lord**; then we must wonder even more / how it was possible / for them to judge him as anything other / than that he is eternal with his Father. How can the Word of **GOD** now be viewed as outside of **GOD**? Or how can one say / that the Word should be after **GOD** and not simultaneously with **GOD**? Certainly the Arian system looks so strange / that one / if human ignorance were not so well known / and so many testimonies were not clear as day / should almost doubt / whether they ever taught such absurdities. It might be / that they shared this <term>presupposition</term> <note>original: "Præsuppositum"; an underlying assumption or prior condition in an argument.</note> with the *Socinians* <note>Socinians were a non-trinitarian group who believed Jesus was a human who was granted divinity after his resurrection, placing great emphasis on human reason.</note> / that they necessarily had to believe differently / than they otherwise should according to the letter of the Scripture / because they could not grasp / how one could be in three / and three could be in one. But these, along with the others, should have considered / that we hardly grasp what is on Earth and close at hand / much less what is in heaven / and least of all what is in **GOD**. Just consider / whether one can even grasp / how it happens / that from one man’s blood so many countless people come? Yes, one says / how should we not grasp that? However / if one does not otherwise give it much reflection / let one imagine / as if one had been the first human / or had seen the first human / as he stood there for himself / and then investigate / whether one / since the nature of reproduction was then unknown / could have believed / that from one person so many countless others should come forth? It is certain / that everyone / who wishes to reflect on the matter with seriousness / will find / that as well-known as the manner of multiplication is now / it must have remained unknown in itself / if it had not been unlocked by **GOD** in human nature. There are very many such things / which / although they are now regarded as easy / were nevertheless incomprehensible before their discovery. Walking on a sphere / and turning one's feet upward <note>This is a common historical illustration used to show that physical realities (like the spherical earth and gravity) can seem impossible or "against reason" to someone who does not understand the underlying laws, just as divine mysteries might seem impossible to limited human intellect.</note> is not possible for a human; meanwhile, he does walk upon the ball of the earth / and likewise turns his feet upward / even if he does not think about it / and according to his nature certainly keeps his feet below and on the ground. So it is in natural things / what then should one say of divine things? If one wants to say / that it is of a different nature with **GOD** than with man; then that is true / but nothing else follows from it but this / that **GOD** does not beget in a human way / which is an eternal truth even for us. Nevertheless, the Son of **GOD** / if he is indeed **GOD’s** Son / must be equal in essence to the Father: unless / **GOD** purposefully intended to deceive us <note>original: "mit Fleiß habe wollen hinters Licht führen"; literally "to lead behind the light," an idiom for deception.</note>; which is far from the case. We stick to the words / and must stick to them; but whoever says / that **GOD’s** Son is not the actual and essential Son of **GOD** / departs from the pattern of sound doctrine <note>original: "Fürbilde der heylsamen Lehre"; a reference to 2 Timothy 1:13.</note>. Therefore, the accusation / as if one had invented foreign words / falls away of its own accord: And if others form such ideas of the Son of **GOD** / which are not fitting / one certainly has reason to seek out such words / with which one may correctly represent the matter; for which no one is to blame / but the error of the adversary.

### That Jesus Christ is true **God** / is rationally [demonstrated]

§. 6. What we have now said of the essence <note>original: *Wesen*; the fundamental nature or substance of a being.</note> / must also be true of eternity. For if **God** has begotten a Son of his essence / then that Son must also be equal to him in eternity. This usually appears quite incomprehensible to those / who cannot yet judge further than what they see with their eyes / because they conclude according to human ways / that the son must come after the father. However / just as we see in all of nature / that not all begetting requires the same amount of time / but one begets earlier / the other later; so it is to be observed from this / that each brings forth its own kind in the time appointed for it by nature. Just as each thing begets its own kind according to its own time; so must **God** also beget his Son according to his likeness in eternity. The beginning of creatures is with time; but **God’s** beginning is in himself as in unfathomable eternity. If **God** is now to beget his equal / he must exist with him in an unconditional and unlimited eternity. Indeed, this begetting must be eternal in the eternal [being] / and never age through time / just as the eternal **God** remains without time / cessation / or obsolescence / as he is. If one wishes to say / that he had his beginning in eternity / that is quite improperly spoken; for every beginning gives birth to its own time / and thereby ceases to be pure eternity. Therefore, as Christ is without time as **God’s** Son / he exists in absolute eternity / and has no beginning. Should he have a beginning in time / he would also have to be subject to the end of time / like all other things / which arise with time; but let this be far from the Creator of all things. From this we see / that the birth of the Son of **God** does not make him lesser than the Father / but rather makes him equal to the Father in himself. The same condition applies to dignity; since the Son / who is of the same essence and equal eternity with the Father / must also necessarily be of the very same dignity. If there is a difference therein / that the Father is not the Son / and the Son is not the Father; then that difference is within the Godhead <term>Godhead: The divine nature or essence of God; here referring to the internal relationships of the Trinity.</term> itself / and does not concern us. It is also not fitting for us to judge it / so that we do not err. Meanwhile / because the Son is presented to us as the Father’s Word / we can easily form a rational judgment in this matter as well, following such guidance. A man’s word is not the man himself / yet it is in and with the man / and belongs to the man; therefore one must give the word the same honor / that one gives to the man / and the word also has in

### That JESUS Christ is true GOD is rationally [demonstrated]

...[from the] old Jewish Church, adding from Mr. Allix’s <note>Pierre Allix (1641–1717) was a prominent theologian who argued in his 1699 work *The Judgement of the Ancient Jewish Church* that ancient Judaism held views compatible with the Trinity.</note> oft-praised treatise against the Unitarians <note>Unitarians: a group that believes God is a single person and rejects the Trinity.</note>, namely regarding this: that **GOD** truly begat a Son. Thus, he shows from Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> that he considers the Son of **GOD**—whose name **Solomon** asks after in Proverbs 30:4—to be the *Logos* <note>original: *λόγος*; the Word</note>, and that he says the **Word** by which they swear was begotten. Likewise: that **GOD** begat His **Wisdom** in Proverbs 8, which is nothing other than the **Word**; furthermore, that the *Logos* (**Word**) is the most ancient **Son**, the eternal **Son of GOD**, whereas the world is the **Son of GOD** within time. Also: that His **Word** is His image and His firstborn. To this one can also add: that the **Word** is the **Son of GOD** even before the **angels**; while no one of an Arian <note>Arians: followers of a 4th-century belief that Jesus was a created being, not equal to God the Father.</note> mindset would deny this, they must nonetheless admit that the Jew Philo spoke of it in a completely different sense than an Arian usually confesses.

Excellent and as an undeniable testimony is the passage in the Jerusalem **Targum** <note>Targums: ancient Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible that often interpret the text through the lens of Jewish tradition.</note> on Genesis 3:22: "And **GOD** the **LORD** spoke, behold, **Adam** has become like one of us." For this is paraphrased as follows: "**The Word of Jehovah** says: here is **Adam**, whom I have created; he is the **only-begotten son** in the world, just as I am the only-begotten son <note>original Hebrew: *יחיד* (Yachid); unique or only-begotten</note> in the high heavens." Here we find that the **LORD** who created the world is regarded not so much as the Father, but rather as the Son, which agrees with the testimonies of the New Testament. We find that **GOD** must have truly begotten a Son of His own essence, who must be as truly the eternal **GOD** as one truly confesses that the **Lord Jehovah**, who spoke so that heaven and earth should come to be, is the true and only **GOD**.

We find finally confirmed once more what we have said and proven above: that every revelation of **GOD** in works and words found in the Old Testament occurred through the **Son** as the **Word**. **Philo** also calls the **Word** the eternal **Word** of the eternal **GOD**, born of the Father; and to the question: **Why is Wisdom spoken of in the feminine gender—** <note>original: *in Fœminino*; the author is likely about to address why "Wisdom" (Sophia/Chokmah) is a feminine noun in Greek and Hebrew while referring to the Son.</note>

## That Jesus Christ is Truly God is Proved in a Rational

Way. But where then would the clear decree of **GOD** remain, that He will not give His glory to another? <note>A reference to Isaiah 42:8: "I am the Lord: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another."</note> Or can we say with any right to the truth that **God** gives His glory to no other if He shares it with a human—which is what they claim Jesus Christ was? Even our adversaries must confess—by virtue of the very principles they have established to twist the Scripture—that all divine honor is simply attributed to the Son. This is because everything that, at first glance, cannot possibly be understood as anything other than **God** is attributed to the Lord Christ in the New Testament. How then can the Scripture say that **God** will not give His glory to another? Therefore, it must remain absolutely true that, if **God** is one **God**, the Son must be of one essence with the Father. 

For, just as our opponents conclude that it is inconceivable for three persons to be in one essence, we likewise conclude: it is inconceivable that **God** should have a Son who is not one with Him, and yet that there is still only one **God**. According to human understanding, a father may indeed hold an office of honor which the son does not simultaneously hold; however, a son cannot be of a different essence <term>essence; original: *Wesen*—referring to the fundamental nature or substance of a being</term> than the father. But because in **God** there is no external dignity that does not arise from the essence itself, it is impossible for there to be anything in the Father that the Son would not also possess. Therefore, as long as it remains true that **God** is one **God** and yet has a Son, it must also remain true that Father and Son are of one essence and one dignity, and consequently of one eternity. 

Should the Son not be equal to the Father in eternity, even though they are necessarily equal in essence, it would have to follow that there was some growth in **God**. It would be as if that which was first in **God** was called the Father, and that which was added later was called the Son. To imagine such a thing, however, would be monstrous, absurd, and even blasphemous. This observation applies to both the **Socinians** <note>A non-trinitarian movement following the teachings of Fausto Sozzini which denied the pre-existence and divinity of Christ.</note> and the **Arians** <note>Followers of the 4th-century priest Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father and not co-eternal.</note>. For no matter how one tries to conceive of it, this must remain: if Christ is not one in essence with the Father, there are simply two gods, and **God** has given His glory to another. They must see for themselves then how they—while pretending to be worshipers of the one **God** above all others—can remain free from idolatry. This is especially true since they feel how difficult it is for them to avoid establishing two gods; hence there is such a quarrel among the **Socinians** regarding the worship of **Jesus Christ**.

Likewise, we also find that even when only one divine person is spoken of, the plural *Elohim* is nonetheless used; this serves as a reminder to us that although the persons have their specific works and distinct differences, they still always remain in one undivided essence. For example, in the 45th Psalm, we find that both the Father and the Son (as the Messiah) are named with the name *Elohim*, each individually, for no other reason than that in their true distinction they are nevertheless not separated but one. # The Eternal Divinity of Christ Proven from His Titles

Among these, the first shall be that we find written of Him that He is the Life, John 1:4 and 14:6. From this we conclude that, if Christ is truly the Life, He must thereby truly be **GOD**; for **GOD** is the Life, and the Life is **GOD**. No one will deny this except for someone who does not know that all things have life from **GOD**, or that **GOD** is the fountainhead of life; therefore even our adversaries will not want to deny that Life, in and of itself, is none other than **GOD**. 

See now, they must admit that no one other than **GOD** is the Life; they must admit that Christ is the Life without condition, because He calls Himself so without condition; unless they want to say that Christ did not speak correctly: yet they still do not want to admit that Christ is true **GOD** and eternal life. What is this other than flatly contradicting the Holy Scripture? 

We conclude thus: Whoever is the Life is **GOD**; the reason: because no one other than **GOD** is the Life. But now Christ is the Life, which they cannot deny because the Scripture says it; therefore Christ is **GOD**. They must confess everything here; however, to escape the conclusion drawn from it, they cannot help themselves except by <term>limiting: a logical tactic (Latin: limitare) used to restrict the meaning of a word to avoid a specific conclusion</term> and using flowery explanations. From this one sees that it is the truth when we previously said that it is difficult for them because they must always twist the Scripture with cleverness. 

But let us hear how they set about it here. They can say nothing else than that He has the fact that He is the Life from **GOD**, and not from Himself. But we ask: Did **GOD** then strip Himself and give Himself to Christ? For if **GOD** gave Christ "to be the Life," then He gave Him "to be **GOD**." Thus **GOD** would have ceased to be what He was before, and been swallowed up by Christ: or else there are now two, and no longer one **GOD**. The first is absurd in itself, and the second is against Scripture. 

But if one wishes to say that **GOD** communicated to Him a particular power of life out of Himself, but not the entire divine fountainhead of life, then one acts again against the Scripture, which not only says of Him without condition that He is the Life, but also that the entire fullness of the Godhead dwells in Him, and indeed bodily <note>original: "leibhafftig"; a reference to Colossians 2:9, emphasizing that Christ's divinity is not just a spirit or power, but a physical reality</note>. 

In short: according to the power of the letter <note>This refers to the "literal" or "plain" sense of the biblical text</note>, it follows that Christ is the true **GOD** and the eternal life: and if the opponents do not want to admit that, then they must twist it, restrict it, invent foreign explanations for it, and do the best they can; if they achieve nothing more, they have at least contradicted and caused confusion. # The eternal divinity of Christ proven from His names.

GOD has never been seen by anyone except by the Son; much less could an angel, as a creature, ever have contained GOD within himself. To be sure, one might again object to this and say: is the Son not GOD just as much as the Father? I answer: He is certainly GOD, and of one essence with the Father; yet He is the one through whom GOD reveals Himself, and in His incarnation He has shown that He can clothe Himself in our flesh and blood; how much more, then, could He use the service of angels for His revelation in the Old Testament, even without assuming their essence <note>The author is distinguishing between Christ taking on human nature (incarnation) and simply using an angelic form or messenger as a temporary vehicle for communication.</note>. Moreover, we must not go further in investigating the nature of this mystery than our eyes reach, and we must let it be enough for us that the Scripture says no one has ever seen GOD; from which it follows that it was not the Father, but the Son, as the radiance of glory <note>A reference to Hebrews 1:3, describing the Son as the "radiance of God's glory."</note>, who must have revealed Himself in the Old Testament. 

Before we leave this subject, let us briefly recall that according to the explanation we have given regarding the angel, great clarity can be found in several matters. For one thing, the word "Angel" retains its ordinary meaning, so that one does not need to investigate in what way the Son of God was called an angel or was one. Secondly, one does not always have to argue whether a created or uncreated angel is meant, as usually happens. Finally, the passage in Exodus 33:2-3 <note>original: *2. B. Mos. XXXIII. 2. 3.* refers to the Second Book of Moses.</note> will present no difficulty, from which opponents usually conclude that because GOD distinguishes Himself from the angel in such a way, it shows the angel cannot be God's Son. Although I must confess that even if the other explanation is used <note>The "other explanation" refers to the view that Christ is the Angel of the Lord Himself, rather than just appearing through one.</note>, nevertheless no advantage arises for them from this passage. I further confess that in the other opinion—according to which one recognizes the angel so-named as the Son of GOD Himself—there is no small amount of evidence, especially considering Genesis 48:15-16 <note>original: *1. B. Mos. XLVIII. 15. 16.* refers to the First Book of Moses.</note>. So, whichever view one takes, the *Socinians* <note>Socinians: A 16th- and 17th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, viewing Him as a man endowed with divine power rather than being God Himself.</note> cannot save themselves. —

...the Father's bosom, has declared it, or has led the Word <note>The author is analyzing John 1:18, specifically the phrase "He has declared Him."</note>. For the Greek word *exēgēsato* <note>original: *εξήγησατ.*</note> means as much as: to preside, to be a leader, to govern, to administer, or also to interpret, explain, recite, and relate. And—which is particularly well-worth noting—this very word is used in reference to the Law, and means to recite the words of the Law so that another may correctly grasp and repeat them. *See Johannes Scapula's Greek-Latin Lexicon <note>A standard 17th-century scholarly reference for Greek.</note> under the entry exēgēsai (where he cites from Demosthenes that "to declare the law" signifies: I proclaim the law, i.e., the herald of the law's words).* 

From this, anyone may see for themselves whether this meaning is not contained therein: that although Moses gave the Law, the Truth was brought through Christ, as He is the only one who knows God because He lies in the bosom of the Father. Therefore, even Moses had not seen God, but rather the Law which he gave was recited to him by Christ, so that he had to repeat it to the Jewish people. Now, I do not wish to say simply that the word *exēgēsato* refers to nothing more than the Law of Moses; rather, it encompasses everything that Christ has proclaimed to us from His Heavenly Father. But because He is the one who alone is in the <term>bosom of God</term> <note>A biblical metaphor for the most intimate possible relationship and shared essence.</note>, sees God, and relates and recites to us what He hears and sees from His Father, then Moses must also have received it from Him, if this statement of John, His <term>forerunner</term> <note>Referring to John the Baptist.</note>, is to remain true. I will say no more; but let one take the entire discourse and weigh it according to the light of sound reason, and then see for oneself what is contained within it concerning this truth. **John bears witness of Him and cried out, saying: "This was He of whom I said: He who comes after me was before me, for He was earlier than I. And of His fullness have we all received, and indeed grace for grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ."**

§. 12. Finally, we wish to make one more quite general conclusion, which, because of its importance and clarity, well deserves to be appended. The priests served Him; He allowed Himself to be attended with all glory, splendor, and music. Now let us note that God did all this Himself, and not through Moses or those who otherwise belonged to the Levitical service <term>Levitischen Gottesdienst: The religious duties and ceremonies performed by the tribe of Levi as prescribed in the Old Testament law.</term> and Jewish government. From this I then conclude: what happened then happened only figuratively <note>original: "bildlich." In this context, it refers to "typology," a method of interpretation where Old Testament events are seen as "types" or symbolic precursors to the "reality" of the New Testament.</note>, and as a sign that in the time of the New Testament it should be thus truly and essentially fulfilled. It must therefore follow that because the revelation of God at that time was true and yet only figurative among the children of men, the revelation of the New Testament must have occurred through an actual "becoming-equal"—that is, that God actually came from heaven and became human. 

For God reveals Himself in the Old Testament, and did it, as said, not through others. Had He now not become human Himself, and had He only revealed Himself through a glorified human being <note>The author is likely arguing against Socinian or Arian views, which suggested Jesus was a highly exalted human rather than God Himself.</note>, then not only would the prefiguration of that time not be fulfilled, but one would also have to confess that the Old Testament revelation of that time was far more glorious than that which now occurs in the New Testament. 

Let us speak of this a bit more clearly, and to that end compare the indwelling of God in the Temple and in the man Jesus with one another. See, God truly dwelt in the Temple and deemed the children of Israel worthy of His essential presence; He spoke with them and let Himself be found among them at all times. Now, if God were to dwell in Christ Jesus no differently than He dwelt in the Temple at that time, what then would be the difference? But now, by virtue of the Scripture—which teaches us that then was the shadow, but now is the body <note>A reference to Colossians 2:17, "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ." 1. That it was the Shekhinah who redeemed Israel from Egypt.
2. That the Shekhinah was prefigured by the Passover Lamb. Rabbi Menahem, folio 5, column 1.

Rabbi Menahem, folio 2, columns 1 and 2.

"He speaks of himself **as the Manna,** and likewise **that he has come from heaven,** and thereby indicates that he is the Shekhinah. # The Eternal Divinity of Christ Proven from His Titles

...[who] say that at the time of the Messiah, **God** shall be one and His name shall be only one. Zechariah 14. Rabbi Menahem, folio 135, column 4.

We see in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7:52, how St. Stephen rebukes the Jews for having sold the **Righteous One** for money. What is the basis upon which St. Stephen builds his argument? According to the notions of the Jews, it is clear: they give the name of "the Righteous One" to the <term>Shekhinah: the Divine Presence of God dwelling among His people</term>, and they interpret the words of Amos 2:6 as referring to Him, where it is said that the Righteous One is sold for money. Rabbi Menahem, folio 17, column 3, and folio 19, column 1.

St. Paul in Acts 20:28 says that **God** redeemed the church through His own blood; and this is according to Jewish notions, whose constant teaching is that the salvation of **Israel** shall be accomplished by **God** Himself. To this end, they cite Psalm 22 and Zechariah 9:9, and maintain that the Shekhinah shall be their Redeemer. Rabbi Menahem, folio 19, column 4; folio 58, column 4; and folio 59, column 1.

Likewise, St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 calls **Jesus** Christ the "Adam from above." By this, he indicates that he is here retaining the Jewish notion which calls the Shekhinah the **Adam from above, the heavenly Adam, and the highly-praised Adam**; <note>The author is likely referring to the mystical concept of *Adam Kadmon*, the "Primordial Man," used in Kabbalah to describe a divine level of reality.</note> these are titles which they attribute to **God** alone. Rabbi Menahem, folio 14, column 3.

In Ephesians 5, he offers a great and high contemplation on the love of **Jesus Christ** for His Church, for which He gave Himself up as its Redeemer. He views the Church as His wife and seeks in the first marriage between Adam and Eve a great and high mystery, and a prefiguration of the union that is found between Christ **Jesus** and His Church. In all of this, he follows the Jewish notions which view the Shekhinah **as the bridegroom of the Church.** Rabbi Menahem, folio 15, column 3.

St. Paul, in Hebrews 6 and 7, regards Melchizedek as a prefiguration <note>original: "Fürbild"</note> of Christ **Jesus**; and this is according to the notion of the Jews, who agree that Melchizedek was a prefiguration of the Shekhinah, whom they **call a King of Peace and the Righteous One.** Rabbi Menahem, folio 18, column 1; folio 31, column 1.

# Chapter VII.
## Certain pitfalls, in which dull and unteachable reason becomes entangled, are cleared out of the way.

->§ I.<-

We have, therefore, in the preceding chapters, proven the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the eternal divinity of Jesus Christ, our highly praised Savior, with firm and immovable grounds. We could now leave it at that; in the bright light of this truth, we would have no need to trouble ourselves with the dark clouds stirred up by the blindness of unenlightened reason. However, so that nothing is lacking, we shall briefly seek to clear the most prominent stumbling blocks out of the way. Regarding the counterarguments which adversaries typically bring against the reasons already cited, they are of such a nature that they were only devised and forced with great effort for their own protection. Consequently, when one asks why they so twist the clear letter of the text, they know nothing else to say except that they must necessarily do so for the sake of other passages that seem contrary to these. For this reason, it is unnecessary to answer them once those passages—the ones for which they twist the others—have been clearly answered and explained. Nevertheless, here and there, as can be seen from this treatise itself, answers have been provided even for those things which seem to have an ambiguity due to the controversy raised against them. 

The assault on this mystery becomes almost dreadfully difficult for its authors. Even after more than a thousand years of working at it, they must still employ great art and labor just to present the "correct" sense or the meaning of their objections in a way that is even comprehensible. They even admit themselves that it is difficult for them; yet, they remain stuck in their delusion. Mr. Dr. Spener <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), a prominent German theologian and the "Father of Pietism."</note> cites Lælius Socinus <note>Lælius Socinus (1525–1562) was an Italian theologian whose skeptical inquiries into the Trinity influenced the later Socinian movement, which denied Christ's full divinity.</note> in Section I, Chapter IV, regarding the passage in John 8:58: **"Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."** Socinus confesses that the explanation he brought forth cost him much effort, many days of reflection, and prayer. To this, the blessed man [Spener] adds that such a perversion of the text should not be considered a divine answer to prayer—

### Some Pitfalls in which Feeble Reason Becomes Entangled

[Reason believes it] has all the more right, the more it imagines that others—especially those who engage much with the **Scripture** and yet do not act according to it—make far too much of the **Scripture**. Truly, this is an extremely dangerous <term>error</term><note>original: "Irrthum"</note>, which will bring unspeakable damage to the **Church**, and in part has already brought it. Such a proceeding seems to me just as if someone in the night wanted to cast the light aside and say: "Why do I need the light? Do I not have my eyes, which **GOD** placed the sun in the heavens to enlighten?" **Peter** said not to the unbelievers, but to the believers, that they should take heed of the sure **prophetic word** (2 Peter 1:19). If anyone now wishes to say that the **morning star** <note>A reference to Christ or spiritual enlightenment as mentioned in 2 Peter 1:19: "...until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts."</note> has already risen in him and the day has already broken, he must truly know no more of any darkness or any doubt, and according to such knowledge, he must also walk in the light. 

As long as someone still feels darkness both in his will and understanding, and yet does not want to diligently heed the light of the **Holy Scripture**, he remains free to the **Devil** and his own <term>imaginations</term><note>original: "Einbildungen"; in this context, it refers to deceptive mental constructs or delusions.</note>, and consequently gives out his own **fantasy** <note>original: "Phantasie"</note> as **Divine inspirations**. Here, no one will easily allow himself to be blamed; but it depends upon each person’s examination of himself. I say it with all boldness, that the **Holy Scripture** is not held highly enough even by many well-intentioned souls. 

Furthermore, one falls next not only generally upon other human books, but when one has hardly begun to recognize that one should **fear GOD**, one immediately takes all kinds of **dispute-books** <note>original: "Streit-Bücher"; refers to polemical writings or theological treatises focused on debating doctrine.</note> in hand, and wishes already to pass judgment on **doctrines of faith**. It then happens that children who do not want to hold onto chairs and benches fall from a height, and many times even break their necks. Oh, how many a man has afterward lamented his **curiosity** <note>original: "Fürwitz"; implies an impertinent or reckless desire to know things beyond one's station or maturity.</note>, when he finally noticed with how much unnecessary unrest he had to pay for it. 

But as long as one does not want to heed this, the cry is: "Should I not test what is right? Should I bind myself to other people's statutes?" But my dear man! By what do you wish to conduct the test? If you do it according to your own heart, you must necessarily err; if you wish to do it according to the **Scripture**, you must first know the **Scripture** before you can judge other books by it. Therefore, read the **Holy Scripture** until you are a master of it, and leave other dispute-books unread for that long. 

Next, you must guard yourself so that when you fall into **temptation**, you do not immediately let your hands sink, become terrified, fearful, and faint-hearted; but rather approach the struggle with earnestness, examine everything diligently, ask **GOD** for assistance, and persevere with supplication and sighing.

### ...are cleared out of the way.

[...be] convinced that your understanding can grasp no other concept from the **Scripture** than that **Jesus** is the true **Son of God**, then let rising contrary thoughts frighten you no further, but rather thrust them out of your mind. Do not concern yourself if they return often, for the **Devil** and your own unbelief are impudent guests. Guard yourself also against impatience. For it is custom<unclear>ar</unclear>y that one pours out the unrest of his heart in restless words, thereby causing all kinds of misfortune for oneself and others. We possess a stubborn and proud nature that does not like to recant what it has once spoken. Therefore, if a new idea occurs to you, take care that you do not make it known immediately, unless you wish to seek the counsel of wise men in the matter. Do not think that by accepting and spreading such a jarring idea you will escape the unrest of your heart; for you will realize that you still cannot get free of it. Many a soul returns after having searched through every corner, solitude, foreign company, and wilderness in its impatience, and says: "I sought him in the chamber and found him not; I sought him in the desert and he was not there." Rest, therefore, with patience until he reveals himself; but seek him in the **Scripture**, which bears witness of him. 

Finally, in these days, one must guard oneself very carefully against the wretched ***Indifferentism*** <note>original: "Indifferentismo"; the 18th-century theological term for the belief that it does not matter what religion or denomination one belongs to, as long as one is "good."</note>, where people think it is all the same what one believes, as long as one fears **God**. Yet all **fear of God** must be grounded in **Truth**, and there is only one Truth. **Satan** has brought things so far that, whereas people were previously far too **superstitious**, they now begin to throw everything away, and thus push away the **fear of God** along with the **Truth**. Certainly, those people who are devoted to ***Indifferentism*** profess tolerance and the fear of God with their mouths, but in truth, they do not care enough about it to be properly concerned. Thus it happens, regarding the mystery we have presented, that many of them, when they hear of the **Socinian doctrine** <note>original: "Socinianiſche Lehre"; a rationalist movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, which the author views as a dangerous heresy.</note>, first think it signifies nothing—that it is enough to believe in a **God** and fear him. Thereupon they are easily persuaded to let someone talk them into it, or even to read about it when the fancy takes them. Because both their **reason** and their literal knowledge do not go far, yet they imagine themselves to know something, they easily fall into agreement and secretly confess what they dare not acknowledge publicly. ### Some pitfalls in which weak reason becomes entangled

§. 7. It is now time that we clear out of the way the stumbling blocks over which our opponents and others trip. We must regard this as the most significant obstacle hindering them: they cannot grasp how One should be in Three and yet not be three Gods. Furthermore, they do not wish to take their reason captive under the obedience of faith, nor believe what the **Scripture** says beyond their own comprehension. *Valentinus Smalcius* <note>A prominent Socinian theologian (1572–1622) known for his rationalist approach to scripture.</note> therefore says in the preface against *Franz*, as *Spenerus* <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the "Father of Pietism."</note> cites in §. 4. Cap. I: *Religion and Holy Scripture have many things above reason, and by this very fact it commends itself most highly; but against reason, nothing. Indeed, if religion were contrary to reason, it would by that very fact betray its own falsehood and would not be religion.* <note>original Latin: "Supra rationem multa habet religio, & S. scriptura, & hoc ipso se ipsam maxime commendat, at contra rationem nihil, imo si religio rationi adversaretur, hoc ipso falsitatem suam proderet & religio non esset"</note> That is: **The Christian religion has much that goes above reason, and makes itself particularly distinguished and beloved by that very fact; but it has nothing that is against reason: indeed, if it were against reason, it would thereby betray its own falsehood and would be no religion at all.** Well stated, but poorly applied. Anyone who wishes to conclude from such a sentence that the mystery of the **Holy Trinity** is not **Scriptural** must first prove that it is *against* reason; however, we have shown this to be quite different. Even if we were entirely unable to grasp with our reason that it were possible in any way to find One in Three and Three in One, should we then think that it is *against* reason? Or should we not rather conclude that it is merely *above* reason? *Smalcius* admits that the **Scripture** has much that is *above* reason; why then does he not wish to categorize the mystery of the **Holy Trinity** there as well? Or can he say that he is so completely the master of reason that he knows everything that agrees with it or not? **Holy Scripture** otherwise shows itself to be reasonable in all things and bears the testimony that it is **God's Word**; if something stands within it that our reason does not comprehend, we must believe it until we do comprehend it, and not rebel against the clear letter <note>The "clear letter" refers to the literal text of the Bible.</note> under the pretense that it is against reason. The worldly man <term>worldly man (German: *Welt-Mensch*); a person governed by secular desires rather than spiritual insight</term> hears that one should not resist evil, but rather, if one receives a blow to the right cheek, one should offer the other as well. To him, this is not only beyond reason, but even so much against reason that it seems a folly and *absurd* <note>original: *absurd*</note> to him. Now, such a person would have much more right to misuse the *axiom* <note>original: *axioma*; a self-evident truth or established principle</note> provided by *Smalcius*, because he knows how to bring forth so many reasons apparent to human wit, with which he can fully persuade not only others but also himself that this rule of **Christ** is against reason and therefore not to be accepted. 

But against whose reason is this rule? Against all reason? Not at all; it only transcends the reason of a person who knows nothing more than the world. On the other hand, there are so many others who well understand that it is highly rational. Here, the **Socinians** <note>A non-Trinitarian sect that emphasized rationalism in interpreting the Bible</note> are much worse than the former; for those at least confess that even if it were against reason, it must still remain as it is because it stands in God’s Word. But the **Socinians** say: "This is against my reason, therefore it is against all reason, and must for that reason be cast out of the Scripture," whether it happens directly or through crooked detours and distortions. 

But let someone say for once: is it against reason that God exists with His Word and Spirit? Should God then be without Word and Spirit? Or does one wish to quarrel with God because the Word became flesh? Or accuse the Scripture of a lie because it testifies to such things? Or finally, should the Creator direct Himself according to His creature more than pleases Him—that He should sit in a body like a man, forming and speaking a word through the air and the tools of the mouth, and carrying the Spirit around as if bound in his vessel? 

If, however, one admits that God has a different nature than man, why would one want to create self-devised *concepts* <note>original: *concepte*</note> of God, when one does not even know oneself? Will God let it go unpunished that the Holy Revelation of His Word has been so dragged and twisted according to one's own will? In this, one acts according to all the whims of corrupted reason, and even dares to freely set down special *maxims* <note>original: *Maximen*; fundamental rules of conduct or belief</note> accordingly, in order to *legitimize* <note>original: *legitimiren*</note> such an undertaking; yet this is often done so that one does not appear to be basing oneself only on reason. However, one may easily judge the vanity of the building itself from this sandy foundation.

For firstly, it is evident that the entire **Holy Scripture** of the Old Testament is not so much concerned with describing **God's** essence and nature as it is with testifying that no one is **God** among all those falsely worshiped gods of the **nations** except alone the true **God** of Israel, whose name is **Jehovah**. Such was also recognized by the Jewish Church, as we have seen in the preceding § 8 from the cited testimony of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture</note>. If we pay attention to the consequences drawn from this sentence—that **Jehovah** alone is **Jehovah**—we find it thoroughly confirmed. For it is immediately said in verse 5, **"You shall love God with all your heart, with all your soul,"** etc., and in verse 12, there is a serious reminder not to forget the **Lord**; which follows very beautifully from the fact that **Jehovah** is uniquely and solely **God**, and none else besides. On the other hand, if the words of the 4th verse are viewed only as a point of doctrine—that **God** is one in essence—there is no connection between them and the following exhortations. For it does not immediately follow from the unity of essence that one must love Him and not forget Him.

Furthermore, the false gods are also placed in opposition to this **God** of Israel in the very same passage in verse 14: **"And you shall not follow after other gods;"** which gives an indication that **Moses**, with the words "**Jehovah** our **God** is **one God**," intended to show that He alone and no other is **God**, and therefore they had no others to worship. Psalm 83, verse 19, seems to give the same explanation of this saying when it says: **"So they shall know that You, who alone are named the Lord, or, that Your name alone (and no other's) is Jehovah."** Indeed, the New Testament gives us almost the most certain information regarding this. What they object, however—that "one" cannot be more than one—they may settle that with the text of **Moses**, where **Jehovah** is named **in the plural** <note>original: "in plurali"</note>, "our Gods" <note>The author refers to the plural Hebrew name *Elohenu* used alongside the singular *Jehovah*.</note>. For even if they wish to speak against it, it has partly been answered for them in the first chapter, and partly it does not apply here, because where they lack declarations of Scripture, their **inability to grasp** or **claims of reason** are only to be lamented, but not used for the refutation of a mystery revealed through the Spirit of God. However, according to such an explanation, the first **Jehovah** is to be regarded as a **proper name** <note>original: "Nomen proprium"</note>, or God's actual and special name, which the God (of the gods) of **Israel** bears; and indeed in such a way that, even though several are thought of who bear the name **Jehovah** as the true God, there is nevertheless only one **Jehovah**, because those who are so named are One. In such thoughts, we might perhaps paraphrase the saying thus:

->**The Essence of all essences, which alone exists for itself, which is, and which was, and which is to come, and yet according to time neither is, nor was, nor will be, but always is what it is—the Essence, I say, Note: which is your Gods, is One Essence, which is not divided, but remains in its unified Essence as it is.**<-

Therefore you, O **Israel**, should not imagine gods for yourself after the manner of the heathens, which are divided in a human way like Father, Son, and Mother, or fight with one another, or are subject to one another. We, however, consider the first explanation to be the most correct.

From the first and second verses <note>original: "Versiculs"</note> of the first chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, they form in their minds an immovable conclusion against the divinity of Jesus Christ. The words read as follows: **"After God at various times and in various ways spoke in times past to the fathers through the prophets, he has in these last days spoken to us through the Son, whom he has appointed heir over all things, through whom he also made the world."** From this, they conclude: If God spoke through his Son at the last, then he did not speak through him in the Old Testament. They wish, therefore, to render powerless the strength we draw from the revelations of the Son of God in the Old Testament, and I know not by what kind of further logical deduction they conclude that the Son of God is not true God.

However, firstly, even if this were granted according to their understanding, it still could not be forced from it that Christ was not true God. Furthermore, the proposition that the Son of God was present in the Old Testament, and as the Word of the Lord directed all things, is so powerfully proven that it would have to be overturned by much more significant arguments <note>original: "Argumenta"</note>. What else would they conclude from this, other than that God's Son finally spoke through himself, and no longer solely through the prophets? The Son stands here in contrast to the prophets, and must therefore be explained according to the comparison with them. Now, however, the prophets were men, and God spoke through them; thus, God has finally done through his Son that which he formerly did through the prophets as if through others <note>The author distinguishes between God using external agents (prophets) and God acting through His own Son, who shares His essence.</note>. The Son had not yet taken on flesh and blood in the Old Testament and in the times of the prophets, so he could not speak to men, who understand no language other than that of a human being. But when he became man in these last days, he was then able to proclaim the will of God to mankind.

Does it then follow: "The Son spoke last after the prophets, therefore he did not exist before the prophets"? Or does even this follow: "The Son spoke for the first time in the last days, therefore he did not reveal himself beforehand; therefore he did not, as the true God of Israel, direct their affairs"? Certainly just as little as this: "God spoke through the prophets, therefore he did not speak himself." Finally, it is a shame that one would seek an opportunity to assault the divinity of Christ from such a text, in which it is so emphatically confirmed. <note>The author points out the irony that his opponents use a verse to deny Christ's divinity even though that same verse credits Christ with the creation of the world.</note>

was, he did not consider it a robbery to be equal with God. <note>This is a reference to Philippians 2:6, a key verse in debates over whether Jesus was equal to God the Father.</note> What wonder was it then that Christ said the Father was greater than he? Certainly, the distinction between the natures <note>The "Two Natures" doctrine: the belief that Jesus is simultaneously fully God and fully human.</note> is well-observed, even though they stand with one another in the most precise and personal union. This is done so that one may always consider what undeserved grace has happened to the human race, and not consider it a robbery. Because our opponents <note>Referring to the Socinians, a 16th- and 17th-century group that rejected the Trinity and Christ's divinity.</note> refuse to understand this, they say that what is written of the mere humanity is to be understood literally, but what is written of the pure divinity is to be understood figuratively <note>original: "uneigentlich"</note> and must only be **accommodated** <note>original: "accomodiret"; in theology, "accommodation" suggests that divine language is adjusted or simplified for human understanding rather than being strictly literal.</note> to Christ: the reader may judge this **axiom** <note>original: "Axiomate"; a fundamental principle or starting assumption.</note> for himself.

Christ himself took this into account exactly, and therefore sometimes spoke very humbly and lowly of himself, but at other times made such pronouncements that show his entirely divine nature and glory; these can in no way be understood without the knowledge of his twofold nature and the distinction between them. In this, his apostles followed him in every way, as their writings testify. Therefore, the Christian Church has always applied diligence so that, on the one hand, one should not separate the natures, but on the other hand, one should not confuse or mix them. <note>This reflects the "Definition of Chalcedon" from 451 AD, which sought to balance the two natures of Christ without blending them together into a third thing.</note> 

It is, however, to be regretted that those passages which are recorded for our assurance—that Jesus Christ is truly a man and our brother, so that we should be all the more assured of God's grace and all divine promises—are so shamefully twisted that we use them on the other hand to dispute his divine nature. That he is true God is our strength and power, since without divinity he could accomplish nothing and would always leave us with some doubt of his inability; but that he is true man is our confidence and firm anchor of hope, by which all doubt of his reluctance is taken from us. Therefore, it is necessary that we be assured of both his divinity and humanity, and allow ourselves neither to be led into denying the divinity through the powerful representation of his humanity, nor to be led into despising the humanity through the irreproachable testimonies of his divinity.

However, the **Socinians** are accustomed to gathering even more from the Scripture beyond the objections just cited and dismissed, especially from the Epistle to the Hebrews, because that very book gives them much trouble. ...the first and second verses of the first chapter to the **Hebrews**, they form in their thoughts an immovable conclusion against the divinity of **Jesus Christ**. The words read as follows: **"After God at various times and in various ways spoke in times past to the fathers through the prophets, he has in these last days spoken to us through his Son, whom he has appointed heir over all things, through whom he also made the world."** From this, they conclude: if **God** spoke through his **Son** last, then he did not speak through him in the Old Testament. With this, they intend to nullify the evidence we take from the revelations of the **Son of God** in the Old Testament, and I know not by what kind of further inference they conclude that the **Son of God** is not true **God**. 

But first, even if one were to grant their understanding of this passage, it still could not be forced to mean that **Christ** was not true **God**. Furthermore, the principle that the **Son of God** was present in the Old Testament—and, as the **Word of the Lord**, directed all things—is so powerfully proven that it would require far weightier arguments to be overturned. What else do they wish to conclude from this, other than that the **Son of God** finally spoke through himself, and no longer solely through the prophets? 

The Son is placed here in contrast to the prophets, and must therefore be explained according to his equality with them. <note>The author argues that if the prophets were the medium of God's voice, the Son is now the medium, but a superior one.</note> Now, the prophets were men, and **God** spoke through them; thus, **God** has finally done through his Son what he previously did through the prophets as intermediaries. In the Old Testament and in the time of the prophets, the Son had not yet taken on flesh and blood; therefore, he could not speak to men who understand no language other than that of a human being. But when he became man in these last days, he was then able to proclaim the will of **God** to mankind. 

Does it then follow that because the Son spoke last after the prophets, he did not exist before the prophets? Or does even this follow: that because the Son first spoke [directly] in the last days, he did not reveal himself before then? Or that he did not, as the true **God of Israel**, direct those very affairs? Certainly no more than this: **God** spoke through the prophets, therefore he did not speak himself. Finally, it is a shame that one seeks an opportunity to assault the divinity of **Christ** from such a text, in which that divinity is so emphatically confirmed.

[He re]minded them of such things, that they should not deviate from this faith and think that everything had already occurred; rather, they should apply all the more diligence so that they might enter into this rest and not despise the sharp discipline of the living Word of God through unbelief. In the same way, the Apostle intends, through this foundation of the majesty of the Son of God, to encourage his **Hebrews** that they should take all the more heed of the word they hear, so that they do not drift away (Chapter II, verse 1). To that end, he compares the **Old Covenant** with the **New** and concludes thus: If the **Old Covenant**, which was spoken through the **angels**, possessed such great holiness, then the **New Covenant**, which was established by the **Son of God** himself, must have a so much greater holiness. One can easily imagine that he had to present such things to them that were familiar to them and believed by the Jewish Church; otherwise, they would have rejected his entire discourse as being built on a false foundation. 

According to this observation, it is now an infallible truth that the Jewish Church at that time believed that the second, the forty-fifth, the hundred-and-second, and the hundred-and-tenth **Psalm** dealt absolutely with the **Messiah**; whereby the whole of <term>Socinianism</term> <note>Socinianism was a rationalist Christian movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, arguing that Jesus was a mere human who was granted divinity after his resurrection.</note> is overturned at once. But the fact that the **Messiah** is compared with the **angels** is necessary to make the comparison of the **Old** and **New Testaments** all the more evident. For example: making a comparison between an earthly king and God is unnecessary in itself, for everyone believes that God is greater than a king. However, if I hold the favor of God and a king side by side—perhaps advising someone that they should rather lose the king’s favor than God’s—I must certainly make a comparison between God and the king and say: "for God is more than the king." 

So it is also with this comparison of the **Son of God** and the **angels**. The Apostle says: Apply diligence so that you take heed of the word even more than in the **Old Covenant**. Why? For the word of the **Old Covenant** was only spoken through the **angels**, and yet every transgression and disobedience received its just reward; but now the **New Covenant** has been established by the **Son of God** himself. How then shall we escape if we neglect such a salvation? Therefore, we can also say that the comparison of the **Son of God** with the **angels** does not happen so much to make the Son great, but rather to [make] the angels [small] against him—

A son is the father's image, therefore he is not the father himself; nevertheless, he is a man, just like the father. According to such an observation, it would follow more than all too certainly from this naming of the Son of **God** that he is the essential **God**; but if this does not please our **criticizing** adversaries, they may judge from it what a miserable **argument** they bring to the floor in such an important matter. They **argue** no better when they say: **"Christ is a visible image of the invisible God, therefore he can neither be the highest God, nor be of the same essence with Him."** For it is true by all confession that **Christ** became a visible image; however, the opponents must leave it quite unproven that he was not also previously an invisible image. The Scripture says: **God was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16)**; thus, the one who became manifest in the flesh is the invisible **God**; this, however, is not the Father, but the Son, who was justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the **Gentiles** <note>original: "Heyden" (Heathens/pagans)</note>, believed on in the world, and taken up into glory. According to this and the preceding observation, the conclusion they made—**that he can neither be the highest God nor of the same essence with Him—falls away entirely.**

§. 17. Other objections that are still made are quite foolish and not worthy of being answered. Of such a kind is when they say: **"The Word would have had to stop being the Word if it had become flesh."** My goodness! How does that follow? Must one who becomes something which he was not before therefore stop being what he already is? Does the human spirit not nevertheless remain a spiritual and incorporeal being, even though it dwells in the body and, together with the body, constitutes the person of a human being? Why put such cobwebs <note>A metaphor for flimsy, weak arguments</note> in the way, to strike against such a fundamental and "super-fundamental" **article of faith**?
