->### Some Pitfalls in which dull Reason entangles itself /<-

...be **God**, and have existed before his birth. My dear! What is the point of this sophistry? Isn't that the very matter under dispute? Should one and the same statement be both the premise and its own proof? It is no better concluded when one says: **There is only one God, therefore there is only one person in the Godhead**; for that is exactly the question at issue and must therefore not be cited as a proof. But if that logic were to hold, then we could also conclude thus: The <term>Socinians</term> <note>Followers of Socinianism, a 17th-century theological movement that denied the Trinity and the pre-existence of Christ, favoring a rationalist interpretation of Scripture.</note> are heretics; why? Because they are erroneous teachers. But they would soon answer and say: Prove that first, and only then say that we are heretics; for a heretic and an erroneous teacher are one and the same thing. Or: The <term>Socinians</term> are heretics, why? Because they say **Christ** is not true **God**. Would they allow such a thing to stand, and not first demand that one should show that such teaching of theirs is indeed erroneous?

Another strange objection is the following: **If Christ were God, he could not have been born, crucified, and died;** just as if one does not experience every day that a human being—though his spirit can suffer no physical injury—nevertheless feels the pains of his body at the same time in his spirit, because of the personal union <note>The "personal union" (unio personalis) refers to the Christian doctrine that Christ is one person with two natures, divine and human.</note>. Thus also the human being dies, though he cannot die according to the spirit; nevertheless, the spirit must walk the path of death because it is separated from the body through death. 

See! That is how poorly these people succeed with their logical conclusions; nonetheless, it seems that they (especially <term>Felbinger</term> <note>Jeremias Felbinger (1616–1690), a prominent Socinian writer known for his German translation of the New Testament.</note>) take great pleasure in this, because they not only repeat it often but also accuse us of many absurdities in the process. Finally, in order to better understand these people's desperate fighting, we must cite one more thing; which is that, when they wish to weaken the verse, **that in Christ all the fullness of the Godhead dwells** <note>A reference to Colossians 2:9.</note>, they object that it does not say it dwells in the **man**, but in **Christ**. Instead of an answer, however, we will leave it to the reader to consider, so that he may better weigh what one ought to judge of their arguments. We turn now to something better.

# Chapter VIII.

## On some use of this doctrine for faith / and for godliness.

### § 1.

So, my reader, you have now received the mystery of the **Trinity**, having seen it not only proven but also defended against objections: but know that you have received nothing more than a pedagogy <note>A method of instruction or a basic introductory guide.</note> and a helping hand herewith; for this matter is not accomplished through external disputing and instruction alone. To be sure, we do not mean to say that the **Divine Word**, from which we have drawn our proof, does not carry its own living and Divine power to convince our souls; but it remains true that we can weaken its power within ourselves and hinder the work of the **Holy Spirit**, which is linked to that Word, through our own wickedness.

There are indeed many who not only confess the triune **God**, but are also skilled at explaining the mystery with the words of **Scripture** and defending it against the counter-arguments of adversaries; nevertheless, they cannot convince their own hearts. When they try to persuade themselves of it, it is a purely forced matter which keeps a constant doubt and unbelief hidden within. Against such doubt and unbelief, one must certainly fight with **God’s** Word as with the "sword of the Spirit" <note>A reference to Ephesians 6:17, describing the Word of God as a spiritual weapon.</note>; but because neither faith nor the right knowledge of the Word of **God** lies within our own power, we must give room to the **Holy Spirit** to dwell in our souls and perform His work through heartfelt prayer and true repentance.

**Scripture** testifies indeed that no one knows what is in **God** except the **Spirit of God**, 1 Cor. 2:10, 11. And the Christian Church has always believed that the **Spirit of God** flees the idolatrous and departs from the wicked <note>original: "B. der Weißh. I. 5." refers to the Book of Wisdom 1:5, a book of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon often used in the 17th century to illustrate moral wisdom.</note>. Thus, one recognizes indeed how one must prepare oneself with a holy life in the fear of the **Lord**, so that the **Holy Spirit**—by reminding and presenting us with that which stands in **Scripture**—may divinely establish us in the salutary doctrine of the **Holy Trinity** and strengthen us in faith against the "gates of hell." I have experienced this many times in my own...

...and other examples, it is noticed that God often permits all kinds of confusion to arise for the sake of sin, perhaps so that one might turn all the more earnestly to God in such distress and withdraw oneself from the distractions of the fleeting heart; as the Scripture also warns in 2 Thessalonians 2:11 <note>The passage refers to God sending a "strong delusion" to those who did not love the truth.</note>. One must not think that God Himself stirs up this confusion and error within us, or places something in us from the outside that was not already there; no! Everything called doubt and unbelief lies within us, and if it is not always noticed, this is only because of the light shining upon us through God’s grace, which holds back the power of darkness so that we do not entirely perish—or it arises from our own inattentiveness, by which we gaze at external things and forget what is inside us, which God allows to happen with patience until the time of His wrath breaks forth.

Therefore, we see that when a person begins to pay attention to their heart and wishes to turn toward God, unimaginable filth foams forth from the heart at that very moment. Then, evil thoughts of denying God and His Word, and doubts regarding all Divine mysteries, come forth with great power. Often, a truly hellish unbelief is found even in matters of which one was previously so certain that they wondered how any person could possibly harbor a single doubt about such truths. One often doubts without knowing why, so that if one were to take counsel with oneself at such a time and ask, "Why do you doubt?" one would know no other reason than this: "I doubt." 

In this, one must experience that faith is a <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>original: "Hypostasis"; a Greek term used in Hebrews 11:1, often translated as "substance," "assurance," or "reality." Peter had surely learned that the Messiah was to be the Son of God; others in the Jewish Church had learned the same alongside him. The teachers and scribes had the Scriptures before their eyes daily and knew every report concerning the Messiah. Nevertheless, most did not find the Lord Christ, and when Peter found Him, it was said: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven" <note>A reference to Matthew 16:17, where Jesus explains that Peter's recognition of Him as the Messiah was a divine revelation.</note>. § 2. One should consider what a weighty matter it must be to truly and rightly recognize **J**esus **C**hrist, since 1 John 2:14 ascribes the knowledge of Him who is from the beginning to the "fathers," while saying of the "children" that they know the Father. One should reflect on how much must depend on Him of whom the Father, Word, and Spirit testify, and toward whom the three witnesses on earth are likewise directed (1 John 5:7–8). One should weigh what depths of the unfathomable Godhead must be in Him, whom no one knows except the Father (Matthew 11:27). From this, one can further judge that the investigation of the truth concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity is highly necessary and useful, and that one must take care not to regard the study of this doctrine as a useless dispute, lest one insult the Father in the Son; for whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father either. On this matter, Mr. Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a famous radical Pietist theologian known for his "Impartial History of the Church and Heresy."</note> provided an excellent confession in his preface to Mr. Allix’s book against the <term>Unitarians</term> <note>original: "Unitarios"; those who believe God is one person and deny the Trinity.</note>, especially in the first and second sections.

> „The most high mystery,“ he says, „of the

> all reason be put to shame, and all unbelief come to nothing, so
> that no one among angels or men may boast that they have known it
> without the Divine Spirit Himself. Indeed, for this very reason, it is the supreme <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "Mysterium"</note> among

If we, without looking toward this Trinity, consider the depths of the Godhead—such as its eternity, its revelation, its invisible essence, infinity, immeasurability, unspeakable glory, absolute omnipotence, omnipresence, omniscience, most reverent holiness, unfathomability, and finally, that He is a Spirit who is incomprehensible to all spirits and is no further recognizable than He wishes to reveal Himself—if we, I say, consider these and similar things in themselves, then our heart is set in a deeply wondering awe; but when the contemplation of this deepest mystery is added to it, then the most humble concealment and covering of all understanding, all knowledge, and all reason must fully follow. ### Of Some Use of This Teaching for Faith ###

...ther yet be so equal, because no one knows You but Your Father. And who can doubt, O **Holy Spirit**, that You are equally glorious and incomprehensible? For it is You who searches the depths of the Godhead, and thus are as incomprehensible as those whom You search through. O **Most Holy Trinity**, who shall not revere Your hiddenness with deepest humility! Who shall not testify to the unsearchability of Your being with astonishing wonder? See, in this and similar ways, the wonder of our heart and thoughts breaks out; but as this **Most Holy Being** opens anyone's eyes more and more to His certain knowledge, so the wonder and praise of **God** is increased more and more. It does not stop at such *meditation* <note>original: "meditation"; the author uses the Latin term to describe a structured, prayerful reflection on divine mysteries.</note> alone, but the soul longs to know such a mystery, and it sighs within itself: Oh, when will I reach the point where I behold **God's** face. If it now sees in the face of **Jesus Christ**, and from the clear Word of **God**, that we shall know **God** as He is, then it purifies itself in such hope, so that it may be pure as He is pure, 1 John 3:2-3. Oh Father, grant us to know You with Your Son and Spirit, then we shall follow You and be truly blessed. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see **God**.

§. 4. When we thus approach the contemplation of this mystery with a stir of our spirit, we then find the **Holy Trinity** in all the works of **God**; and the works, conversely, only become truly known to us through the knowledge of the **Triune God**. In Creation, we see how everything came from the Father, went forth through the Son, and was brought to light by the **Holy Spirit**. There are **Three**, each of whom has His own office <note>The word "Geschäffte" here refers to the specific roles or operations attributed to each person of the Trinity in the act of creation.</note>, and yet they have only one work; no office could exist without the other, and the offices of all three were as the office of a single one; from which it becomes clear how there are three Persons and yet not three Gods. But because everything is made by this **Triune God**, the power of the Father, Son, and Spirit lies in all things, so that they have their origin from the Father, are made through the Son, and have their life and breath <note>original: "Othem"; an archaic word for breath, signifying the divine spark of life sustained by the Spirit.</note> in the eternal Spirit of **God**. It is the same in daily preservation, where everything is preserved by the Father, carried by the Son, and warmed and strengthened to life by the Spirit. In government <note>original: "Regierung"; refers to Divine Providence, or God's ongoing guidance and ruling of the created world.</note>, everything is commanded by the Father, done through the Son, and driven in living motion by the **Holy Spirit**. See, through this observation, we now find opportunity in all things to revere the **Triune God**, to [rest] ourselves in him...

to encourage him, to commend oneself to His goodness, and to expect everything from Him. There we recognize how all things are from **God**, and without Him nothing can happen; there we recognize His most precise **providence** <note>original: "Vorsehung"</note> over all things through the **Son**, and the unceasing stirring and moving of His **Spirit**; there we notice the depths of the inaccessible light in the **Father**, and the revelation of the **radiance** <term>radiance (Ausschein): a term reflecting Hebrews 1:3, describing the Son as the out-shining of the Father's glory</term> in the **Son**. Now, when we perceive within ourselves the promptings of the conscience, and at the same time the inability to satisfy it, we see from the contemplation of the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "Heiligen Drey-Einigkeit"</note> that such a state could not have been so in the beginning. For whatever was created by the **Father** through the **Word** is also animated to its life through the **Spirit**. Since a life is now demanded which is not present, it must have been there once, and have been corrupted by a poison and calamity. At this point, the insight into our total corruption and **original sin** <note>original: "Erb-Sünde"</note> opens up to us, and how it has permeated all humanity. 

However, the very demand for a good life that we feel in our conscience shows us the **Father's** will for our **rebirth** <note>original: "Wiedergebuhr"</note> and for the renewal of our corrupted life; it shows us the origin of death and of a necessary judgment over all the perverted life of the flesh and of sin. It shows us the certain execution of this life to be reawakened through the **Word**, which happened through **redemption** <note>original: "Erlößung"</note>; for what the **Father** wills, the **Son** carries out. It shows us the final completion of this making-alive through the **Holy Spirit**, because the **Spirit** likewise animates to actual life what the **Father** speaks through His **Word**. 

This teaches man to cease from his own doing and to surrender himself to his **God** in the humblest **yieldedness** <term>yieldedness (Gelassenheit): a key Pietist concept of letting go of self-will and resting in God's will</term>. This gives man the knowledge of the **judgments of God** and makes him fit to pass a right judgment on the wrath of the **Heavenly Father** and the **mercy** <note>original: "Barmhertzigkeit"</note> that stands alongside it. This teaches man to distinguish the judgment of the **Father** from the judgment of the **Son** and from the judgment of the **Holy Spirit**, and yet to regard them as one judgment and the judgment of the only **God**. 

There, the whole order of salvation opens up; one sees in **God** nothing but holiness, truth, justice, vengeance, and fiery zeal, and yet alongside these nothing but love, compassion, patience, forbearance, and gentleness. One looks upon all of this without taking offense, and no longer says as before, "How does **God's** mercy rhyme with His justice?" but rather one cries out and says: **Holy is God the Lord Sabaoth** <note>original: "Heilig ist GOtt der HERR Zebaoth"; a reference to the angelic song in Isaiah 6:3</note>, all His judgments are righteous, and His mercy has no end. # and to Godliness

This is a completely incomprehensible matter without insight into the Divine Mystery <term>Mystery: refers to the "Göttliches Geheimniß," the hidden truths of God, specifically the Trinity, which cannot be known through reason alone</term>. Without the knowledge of this truth, who can raise their voice with the thousands of angels and say: *The Lamb that was slain is worthy to receive power and riches, and wisdom and strength and honor and praise and glory?* *Revelation V. 11, 12.* Like a blind man, one must grope at the wall when reading that in Christ all things shall be gathered together, both which are in heaven and which are on earth, through Himself *Ephesians I, 10,* if one is inexperienced in this mystery. One is deaf when one is meant to hear every creature in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and all that are in them, saying to Him who sat on the throne and to the Lamb: *Blessing and honor and glory and power from eternity to eternity.* *Revelation V. 13.* All Scripture is locked away and tangled with unsolvable knots; every creature stands before our eyes in sheer confusion, so that we do not know what to think or say of it. Our heart remains in error as before, and everything is offensive and suspicious to it.

§ 7. In this mystery, we first learn to recognize that God is Love. For if God did not spare His only-begotten Son—and thus Himself—in that He gave His Son for us all, then it is indeed manifest that the entire Divine Being is nothing but pure love. Had God only adopted a human as His son, making him His own son through a special birth and placing all His glory, goods, and grace upon him, it would be much; but not so much that we could say in the true sense, "God is Love." But now, since God did not spare His own Son, we see with an unveiled face that He is essentially Love. **In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him.** <note>original citation: 1 John 4:9</note> How I wish I were capable of presenting this love in such words that the reader could recognize it as if with seeing eyes! But it is God’s work that the Father be glorified in the Son. Meanwhile, behold the love of God in Jesus Christ as much as you can. God your Creator, whom you have grossly offended even unto hell and eternal damnation, follows after you of His own accord, calls you with longing desire out of your ruin; He wants nothing from you, no payment or satisfaction <term>satisfaction: in a legal or theological sense, "Genugthuung" refers to the debt or punishment required to balance a transgression</term>, only this one thing: that you would turn back and turn toward Him again, so that He, your Creator, must not see you, His creature, lying forever in misery with such heartache...

# On some uses of this teaching for faith

§. 8. If we pay even closer attention to this mystery, we find a remarkable clarity <note>The German *Klarheit* here carries the sense of "divine brightness" or "glory," referencing 2 Corinthians 4:6.</note> of God in the face of Jesus Christ, through the rays of divine humility and meekness, which are otherwise not easily seen. I do not mean now only that the Son, as for Himself and in His own person, humbled Himself and took the form of a servant—which is indeed much, and is the effect of divine humility. Some might even doubt whether it is fitting to attribute humility to God, since He surely has no one before whom He must humble Himself. But just as such a person has far too poor a notion of noble humility—since it is more a generous condescension and lowliness of oneself than a *slavish submission* <note>original: "sclavische submission"</note>—so he also does not consider that Christ, as the image of the Father, says of Himself: **I am meek and lowly of heart.** (Matthew 9 <note>The author cites Matthew 9, though this specific phrase is found in Matthew 11:29.</note>). In what then does the **meekness and humility of Jesus Christ** consist? In this: that He endured our sins with great patience, did not avenge the insults done to Him, and moreover, in order to redeem us, lowered Himself so deeply and appeared among us in the form of a servant. But let us now climb a little higher through Christ and in Christ into the pure Godhead, and examine the Father’s humility and meekness, which we find mirrored in Christ. For this is His meekness: that He in no way avenged the injustice done to Him, and even more, He Himself excused, reconciled, and mediated the crime. "Ah," you say, "did He not rightfully let His wrath and zeal go out against sin?" I answer: Yes, rightly; He showed His wrath against sin, but not against His creature. Must not a shepherd strike his little sheep hard if he is to tear it from the lion’s maw? But he pities the sheep that he had to strike so hard. Just so must a doctor cause pain to his patient, not because he wants to inflict suffering, but because he wants to take the suffering away from him. But what is this compared to the meek God, who sets aside the injustice done to Him and then, to take away the pains of His sick child, takes those very pains upon Himself. The Father draws us through pain, the Son bears the pain, and the Holy Spirit intercedes with painful sighs for the creature groaning in its blood and death. O you most holy and most sweet Trinity, how great and high will your praise be when we one day see you face to face! Yours is the glory—

Let us take note from this that the knowledge of this mystery unlocks much that moves us to great wonder at divine grace, miracles, and works.

§. 9. Here we recognize, first, that God is in earnest regarding the preaching of the forgiveness of sins. For as long as God sought to be paid, as it were, with "foreign skin"—which the Son’s would have to be if He were not simultaneously true God—or with that which is taken from what is ours, we would have to form very poor thoughts of the highly praised forgiveness of sins. But now, since God Himself has found and made reconciliation through His own blood, and for our sake has, so to speak, torn the heart out of His body, the heart of His love stands open to us; and we step forward with joy and hear the word of the forgiveness of sins. This is what makes us look so confidently toward the exalted Son of God on the Cross, so that by looking upon Him we might be healed of the wounds received from sin. For when we look up to the Son of Man, who came from heaven from His Father’s bosom, we find the opened heart of God and look into all His love without hindrance; therefore we have no doubt at all of gracious forgiveness, just as we are certainly assured that God did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all.

# On some use of this doctrine for faith

§. 8. If we pay further attention to this mystery, we find a remarkable radiance of God in the face of Jesus Christ, through the rays of divine humility and gentleness, which are otherwise not easily perceived. I do not mean now merely that the Son, as for himself and in his own particular person, humbled himself and took on the **form of a servant** <note>This refers to the "Kenosis" or self-emptying of Christ described in Philippians 2:7.</note>, which is indeed a great deal and the effect of divine humility. Some might even doubt whether it is fitting to attribute humility to God, since he has no one before whom he must humble himself. However, just as such a person has far too poor a conception of noble humility—since it is more a **generous condescension** and a lowering of oneself than a slavish submission—so he also does not consider that Christ, as the image of the Father, says of himself: **"I am gentle and humble of heart."** Matthew 11. But in what does the **gentleness and humility of Jesus Christ** consist? In this: that he endures our sin with great patience, does not avenge the insults done to him, and moreover, in order to redeem us, lets himself down so low and appears among us in the form of a servant.

His gentleness, then, is this: that he in no way avenged the injustice done to him, but even further, excused, reconciled, and represented the crime within himself. "Ah," you say, "did he not rightfully let his wrath and zeal go forth against sin?" I answer: yes, rightly so; he let his anger be seen against sin, but not against his creature. Must not a shepherd grip his little sheep hard if he is to tear it out of the lion's jaws? But he grieves that he must grip the sheep so hard. Similarly, a doctor must cause his patient pain—not because he wants to inflict suffering, but because he wants to take the suffering away from him. 

But what is this compared to the gentle God, who sets aside the injustice done to him and then, to take the pain away from his sick child, takes that very pain upon himself? The Father lures with pain, the Son bears the pain, and the Holy Spirit, with painful sighs, represents the creature who is groaning painfully in his blood and death. header: and to godliness.

Glory in eternity / Amen! The **humility of God** has been revealed in this: that he did not consider himself too high to unite himself with human beings, and to set humanity with him upon his throne; which occurred when **the Word became flesh** <note>original: "das Wort ist Fleisch geworden"; a reference to John 1:14</note>, and was united into **one person** with the man Christ Jesus. See, here the Holy God justifies himself, showing that he is not to blame for the fall and ruin of humanity. The **first Adam** sought to become like God in a forbidden way, by wishing to seize by force <note>original: "rauben"; literally to rob or plunder</note> that which was yet too high for him, and which could not be given except by grace; this was his fall and ruin, for which God was not to blame. He afterwards showed in the **second Adam** <note>A theological term referring to Jesus Christ, who undoes the spiritual damage caused by the first man, Adam.</note> that he had not withheld his likeness from man out of pride, in that he freely took up humanity into divine union. Because this one did not consider it a robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, and took on the **form of a servant**, etc., God therefore exalted him, and gave him a **name which is above every name**, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that **Jesus Christ is the Lord** to the glory of God the Father. Philippians 2:6–11. Let us take note from this, that the knowledge of this mystery unlocks much which places us in great wonder at divine grace, miracles, and works.

§. 9. Here we recognize, first of all, that God is in **deadly earnest** with the preaching of the **forgiveness of sins**. For as long as God wanted to settle the debt, as it were, with a "foreign skin" (such as the Son's would have to be if he were not at the same time true God) or with that which is taken from what is ours, we would have very poor thoughts of the so highly praised forgiveness of sins. But now, since God himself has devised and achieved **reconciliation** with his own blood, and for our sake—to speak in such a way—has **torn the heart out of his body**, the heart of his love stands open to us; and we step forward with joy and hear the word of the forgiveness of sins. This is what makes us look so confidently toward the exalted Son of God on the **cross**, so that by looking upon him we may be healed of the received wounds of sin. For when we look up to the **Son of Man**, who has come from heaven from his Father’s bosom, we find the opened heart of God, and look without hindrance into all his love; therefore we have no doubt at all of gracious forgiveness, as we are certainly assured that God did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.

# On some Use of this Doctrine for Faith

...being drawn through the Son / whereby one quiets their heart before the Father in clear knowledge of the Son / and stands in confidence without fear; yet it is another thing / when one is born again of the Spirit / whereby one becomes a partaker of another nature / and puts off the enmity against God's Law <note>The author refers to the spiritual transformation where a person's natural resistance to divine will is removed.</note> / or finds their food and life in the will of God. Although the **Holy Trinity** is undivided and inseparable in its works / nevertheless each person has a distinct time of their particular revelation; (hence one attributes creation to the **Father** / redemption to the **Son** / and sanctification to the **Holy Spirit**:) So the **Holy Trinity** also has its particular time of revelation in every human being. 

The **time of repentance** is of the Father; that is a time / when one is by no means without faith and sanctification / yet nevertheless feels most of all the sharp discipline of the Father with anxiety and distress / while on the other hand, one hardly notices faith and sanctification: The **time of faith** is of the Son; that is a time / when one is by no means without the discipline of the Father and without sanctification / but rather now has more to do with them than before / yet nevertheless feels most of all confidence / comfort and the pacifying of their heart through faith in **Christ Jesus** / but meanwhile accepts the Father's chastening much more peacefully and without such great anxiety / and longingly waits for the promise of the Father / that is / for the **Holy Spirit** / that he should make us completely free from sin / and what is bound up with it: The **time of sanctification** is of the **Holy Spirit**; that is a time / when one is by no means without the Father's discipline / and faith in the Son / but is instead much more eager / that the Father would punish everything unclean and evil / so that one can cleanse themselves from it in the blood of Christ / and stands so firmly grounded in faith / that one is courageous inwardly and outwardly against all the gates of hell / although one thinks little of faith / yet nevertheless perceives most of all in their heart / how it is sanctified by the **Holy Spirit** and led from one glory to another / so that what was previously like death now becomes one's life / or / that one is truly heavenly and divinely minded. <note>original: "conf. 2. Cor. III. 17. 18." — Compare 2 Corinthians 3:17–18, which describes being transformed "from glory to glory" by the Spirit of the Lord.</note> Hence one then longingly waits in the Spirit for the homecoming into the Father’s house / and desires to see the **triune God** / who carries out his work so gloriously / face to face. This is now the reason / why one should take care / that the works of the **Holy Trinity** are not mixed with one another. The longing effort after faith still

<header>and toward Godliness.</header>

...still to the drawing of the Father; the hunger and thirst for sanctification <term>Sanctification: the process of being made holy and purified from sin through the Holy Spirit</term> is an effect of faith in the Son, while actual sanctification is the essential liberation from sin and its wages. This was also recognized by *Luther* <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the central figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> when he said that discipline and punishment are not properly the work of the Holy Spirit; however, the specific place where this is written does not occur to me.

§. 13. This is the small amount which can be accepted as a wholesome use of this most holy doctrine. The more one is deemed worthy to look into this mystery, the more capable he will be to apply everything to his own benefit. St. *Luther* <note>The author uses "S." for "Sanctus" or Saint as a mark of high respect for Luther.</note> said that the holier the godly were, the more they saw the footprints of the Holy Trinity; we may fairly conclude from this that the more one glimpses the footprints and gazes into the mystery itself, the more godly and holy one becomes in spirit and in truth. We know how to be modest, then, in admitting that we have brought forth very little of the glorious benefit of this doctrine out of our great poverty; just as in most things, more of a reminder and instruction than a proper execution has taken place. Now, we would have otherwise been inclined to briefly go through the entire confused *System of Doctrines* <note>original: "Syſtema doctrinarum"</note> of the *Socinians* <term>Socinians: A rationalist Christian sect that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus, viewing him as a man rather than God.</term> and to show how all their false teachings are connected with the denial of the triune God; but let it be enough that we warn them with the prophet *Isaiah*, who had to speak the judgment upon the stubborn Jews from the mouth of the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Zebaoth"</note>, the Son of God, where it says in *Chapter VI. 9. 10.*:

> Go, and tell this people: Hear indeed, but understand not; see indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed.

Let each one now examine themselves as to what is going on in their hearts, whether they have searched God’s Word with earnestness and zeal, and what reflection this has left within them; for according to this, we must all one day allow ourselves to be judged before God’s judgment seat—may God grant it be in pure mercy! Furthermore, our heartfelt request goes to all those who deign to read and look into this humble writing, that they do not [neglect] the investigation of this doctrine...

<header>On some use of these doctrines for faith</header>

...wish to disregard or neglect, as happens with so many—partly through open wantonness, and partly under all sorts of hollow pretexts. For one knows that God is the origin of all things, as well as of all doctrine and godliness <term>Godliness: derived from the German 'Gottseligkeit,' referring to a life of active piety and devotion</term>; this alone should be enough to convince us that we must investigate the mystery of the Godhead with all diligence, as far as the Holy Scripture provides us guidance. Furthermore, we can easily judge that one must well know the nature and character of Him upon whom one is to be grounded for eternal life, who is **JESUS CHRIST, who is GOD over all, blessed in eternity, Amen!**

Romans IX. 5. One should diligently avoid all confusion and mixing in matters of faith, considering that there is no article of faith <term>Article of Faith: a fundamental point of religious doctrine</term> that does not lead to godliness and strengthen the new man <term>New Man: a Pauline concept (Ephesians 4:24) referring to the regenerated spiritual nature of a believer</term>. If one is now confused and muddled in faith and in doctrine, what can one then build upon it? It is indeed no impossibility that the heart becomes firm through grace (Hebrews XIII. 9), if only one begins correctly. But above all things, it is necessary that one becomes truly humble. Oh, how many proud spirits have stumbled, and still stumble, when they wish to judge everything without humility, and consider it a joy when they find something new with which to boast before others and to despise them. 

But if one is humble and employs patience for a while, one can escape many of the snares of Satan and preserve oneself from much unrest. Many a person is tormented by his own impatience, and then certain doctrinal points must serve as a target upon which he wishes to vent everything; when he has then caused himself much vain unrest for a time, he comes to himself and wishes that he might have done it differently, or at the very least, had remained still. Briefly, we can say with Peter in the 2nd letter, Chapter I, verse 5, with some application: Apply all your diligence to this, and supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with temperance, and temperance with patience, and patience with godliness, and godliness with brotherly love, and brotherly love with common love. For where such things are abundant among you, they will not let you be idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, and consequently also in this mystery of the Holy Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

# and toward godliness.

...wish to show regarding this matter. Look in grace upon all my weakness, and help me out of all misery <term>Misery: from the German 'Jammer,' suggesting a state of spiritual wretchedness or lamentation</term> and darkness. Reveal your Holy Name yourself in the hearts of all people, and uncover the depths of the Godhead through your Holy Spirit in faith in the name of the only-begotten Son of GOD. Teach us to grasp with holy hands the contemplation of your most holy essence, so that the fire of your wrath and anger <note>original: 'Grimm- und Zorn-Feuer'</note> does not seize and consume us. Our heart must be a pleasing temple, wherein one hears without ceasing the praise, honor, and glory of the eternal GOD—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to whom belongs the kingdom, the power, and the glory into all eternity, Amen.
